   102→# Shell Usage Standard (Fish)
   103→
   104→This repository uses the Fish shell for interactive commands and automation snippets, aligned with the system configuration. Prefer Fish for new scripts and examples.
   105→
   106→## Policy
   107→- Default shell: Fish (`#!/usr/bin/env fish`).
   108→- Provide Fish snippets for automation examples; keep Bash as optional fallback when helpful.
   109→- Keep one-file, shell-agnostic command sequences unchanged when they work in both shells.
   110→
   111→## Conventions
   112→- Variables: `set NAME value` (no `=`). Export: `set -x NAME value`.
   113→- Arrays/lists: `set items a b c`; append: `set items $items d`.
   114→- Conditionals: `if test -f file; ...; end`; switches: `switch $var; case value; ...; end`.
   115→- Substitution: `set VAR (command ...)`.
   116→- PATH: `set -x PATH /new/bin $PATH`.
   117→
   118→## Shebangs
   119→- Use `#!/usr/bin/env fish` for executable scripts.
   120→
   121→## Compatibility Notes
   122→- Avoid `set -euo pipefail`; Fish handles errors differently. Use explicit checks or `status` as needed.
   123→- When porting Bash snippets, verify quoting and list handling.

   129→# Tool Search Guidelines
   130→
   131→Preferred tools for searching and analyzing code in this repository.
   132→
   133→## Core Tools
   134→
   135→| Tool | Use For | Examples |
   136→|------|---------|----------|
   137→| `fd` | File discovery by name/pattern | `fd config.json`, `fd '*.ts'`, `fd -e md` |
   138→| `rg` | Text search (regex, context) | `rg "function.*export"`, `rg -i "todo" -A 3` |
   139→| `ast-grep` | AST-based code structure search | `ast-grep --lang ts -p 'function $NAME($ARGS) { $$$ }'` |
   140→| `fzf` | Interactive selection/filtering | `fd '*.ts' \| fzf`, `rg -l "export" \| fzf` |
   141→| `jq` / `yq` | JSON / YAML processing | `jq '.dependencies'`, `yq '.database.host'` |
   142→
   143→## ast-grep Language Mapping
   144→
   145→- `.ts` → `--lang ts`, `.tsx` → `--lang tsx`, `.js/.mjs` → `--lang javascript`
   146→- `.rs` → `--lang rust`, `.py` → `--lang python`, `.go` → `--lang go`
   147→
   148→## When to Use Which
   149→
   150→- **ast-grep**: Code patterns, refactoring, type-aware search, avoiding false positives from comments/strings
   151→- **rg**: Plain text, documentation, config files, simple string matching, unsupported languages
   152→- **fd**: Finding files by name, extension, or directory structure
   153→
   154→## Best Practices
   155→
   156→- Default to TypeScript context for ast-grep in this codebase
   157→- Prefer structural (ast-grep) over textual (rg) for code analysis
   158→- Combine tools: `fd '*.ts' | xargs ast-grep --lang ts -p 'pattern'`
   159→- Fallback: if ast-grep fails, use rg

   164→
   165→# Workspace File Reference Rule
   166→
   167→## Overview
   168→
   169→This rule governs how workspace files (such as `.code-workspace` files) should reference directories and paths.
   170→
   171→## Rule
   172→
   173→**DO NOT** refer to the dotagents directory (`../dotagents` or similar) in workspace files. The dotagents directory is for reference only and should not be included as a workspace folder.
   174→
   175→Instead, use the current directory path with "." (e.g., `"."`) or reference the appropriate workspace/directory directly.
   176→
   177→## Examples
   178→
   179→### Incorrect:
   180→```json
   181→{
   182→  "folders": [
   183→    {
   184→      "name": "dotagents",
   185→      "path": "../dotagents"
   186→    }
   187→  ]
   188→}
   189→```
   190→
   191→### Correct:
   192→```json
   193→{
   194→  "folders": [
   195→    {
   196→      "name": "dotfiles",
   197→      "path": "."
   198→    }
   199→  ]
   200→}
   201→```
   202→
   203→## Rationale
   204→
   205→The dotagents directory contains configuration and reference materials that should not be part of the active workspace. Including it can cause confusion and unnecessary clutter in the workspace structure.
   206→

    18→## Core Search Tools
    19→
    20→### File Discovery
    21→- **Primary**: `fd` - Fast and user-friendly alternative to `find`
    22→  - Search for files by name, extension, or pattern
    23→  - Respects `.gitignore` by default
    24→  - Examples: `fd config.json`, `fd '*.ts'`, `fd -e md`
    25→
    26→### Text Search
    27→- **Primary**: `rg` (ripgrep) - High-performance text search
    28→  - Full-text search across files
    29→  - Regular expression support
    30→  - Context options (`-A`, `-B`, `-C` for lines after/before/around matches)
    31→  - Examples: `rg "function.*export"`, `rg -i "todo" -A 3`
    32→
    33→### Code Structure Analysis
    34→- **Primary**: `ast-grep` - AST-based code search and analysis
    35→  - **Default to TypeScript contexts** for this codebase
    36→  - Language-specific parsing for accurate structural matches
    37→  - Pattern-based matching using AST nodes rather than text
    38→
    39→#### Language Mapping for ast-grep:
    40→- **TypeScript files** (`.ts`): `ast-grep --lang ts -p '<pattern>'`
    41→- **React/TSX files** (`.tsx`): `ast-grep --lang tsx -p '<pattern>'`
    42→- **JavaScript files** (`.js`, `.mjs`): `ast-grep --lang javascript -p '<pattern>'`
    43→- **Rust files** (`.rs`): `ast-grep --lang rust -p '<pattern>'`
    44→- **Python files** (`.py`): `ast-grep --lang python -p '<pattern>'`
    45→- **Go files** (`.go`): `ast-grep --lang go -p '<pattern>'`
    46→
    47→#### When to Use ast-grep Over Text Search:
    48→- Finding function definitions, class declarations, or specific code patterns
    49→- Refactoring operations that require understanding code structure
    50→- Type-aware searches (finding usages of specific types, interfaces, etc.)
    51→- Complex code transformations
    52→- Avoiding false positives from comments or strings
    53→
    54→#### ast-grep Pattern Examples:
    55→```bash
    56→# Find all function declarations
    57→ast-grep --lang ts -p 'function $NAME($ARGS) { $$$ }'
    58→
    59→# Find React components with specific props
    60→ast-grep --lang tsx -p '<$COMP $PROPS>$$$</$COMP>'
    61→
    62→# Find class methods
    63→ast-grep --lang ts -p 'class $CLASS { $METHOD($ARGS) { $$$ } }'
    64→```
    65→
    66→### Interactive Selection
    67→- **Primary**: `fzf` - Fuzzy finder for interactive selection
    68→  - Pipe search results through fzf for interactive filtering
    69→  - Examples: `fd '*.ts' | fzf`, `rg -l "export" | fzf`
    70→
    71→### Data Processing
    72→- **JSON**: `jq` - Command-line JSON processor
    73→  - Parse, filter, and transform JSON data
    74→  - Examples: `cat package.json | jq '.dependencies'`
    75→
    76→- **YAML/XML**: `yq` - YAML/XML processor (similar to jq)
    77→  - Handle YAML and XML files with jq-like syntax
    78→  - Examples: `cat config.yaml | yq '.database.host'`
    79→
    80→## Tool Selection Decision Tree
    81→
    82→### 1. Code Structure Search
    83→- **Use ast-grep when:**
    84→  - Searching for specific code patterns (functions, classes, imports)
    85→  - Need to understand code semantics, not just text matches
    86→  - Working with TypeScript/JavaScript code (most common in this repo)
    87→  - Performing refactoring or code transformation tasks
    88→  - Need to avoid false positives from comments or string literals
    89→
    90→### 2. Plain Text Search
    91→- **Use ripgrep (rg) when:**
    92→  - Searching for plain text content (documentation, comments, logs)
    93→  - Simple string matching across multiple files
    94→  - Need contextual lines around matches
    95→  - Working with non-code files (markdown, configuration, etc.)
    96→  - ast-grep doesn't support the target language
    97→
    98→### 3. File Discovery
    99→- **Use fd when:**
   100→  - Finding files by name patterns
   101→  - Listing files by extension
   102→  - Exploring directory structures
   103→  - Building file lists for further processing
   104→
   105→## Best Practices
   106→
   107→### Performance Optimization
   108→- **Combine tools efficiently**: `fd '*.ts' | xargs ast-grep --lang ts -p 'pattern'`
   109→- **Use appropriate scoping**: Limit searches to relevant directories when possible
   110→- **Leverage caching**: Tools like `fd` and `rg` are already optimized for speed
   111→
   112→### Accuracy and Precision
   113→- **Prefer structural over textual**: Use ast-grep for code analysis, rg for content search
   114→- **Validate language detection**: Ensure ast-grep uses the correct `--lang` parameter
   115→- **Test patterns incrementally**: Start with simple patterns and refine as needed
   116→
   117→### Integration Workflows
   118→```bash
   119→# Example: Find all TypeScript files with export statements, then select interactively
   120→fd '*.ts' | xargs ast-grep --lang ts -l -p 'export $$$' | fzf
   121→
   122→# Example: Search for TODO comments and show context
   123→rg -i "todo|fixme" -C 2 --type typescript
   124→
   125→# Example: Find and process configuration files
   126→fd 'config.*\.json' | xargs jq '.version' | sort -u
   127→```
   128→
   129→### Error Handling
   130→- **Fallback strategy**: If ast-grep fails or language is unsupported, fall back to rg
   131→- **Validate tool availability**: Check tool installation before usage
   132→- **Handle edge cases**: Account for mixed-language files and unusual extensions
   133→
   134→## Tool Installation Verification
   135→
   136→Before using these tools in scripts or automation:
   137→
   138→```bash
   139→# Check tool availability
   140→command -v fd >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "fd not installed"; exit 1; }
   141→command -v rg >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "ripgrep not installed"; exit 1; }
   142→command -v ast-grep >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "ast-grep not installed"; exit 1; }
   143→command -v fzf >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "fzf not installed"; exit 1; }
   144→```

   146→## Additional Tools
   147→
   148→While the core tools above cover most use cases, these additional tools may be useful for specialized tasks:
   149→
   150→- **`grep`**: Fallback for basic text search when rg is unavailable
   151→- **`find`**: Fallback for file discovery when fd is unavailable  
   152→- **`sed`/`awk`**: Text processing and transformation
   153→- **`sort`/`uniq`**: Result deduplication and sorting
   154→- **`xargs`**: Efficient command chaining for large result sets

1→# CLAUDE.md - AI Assistant Guide for Gemini Voyager
     2→
     3→> **Last Updated**: 2026-02-09
     4→> **Version**: 1.2.2
     5→> **Purpose**: Comprehensive guide for AI assistants working with the Gemini Voyager codebase
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## 1. Role & Core Mandates
    10→
    11→**Role**: You are an expert Full-Stack Engineer and Chrome Extension Specialist working on Gemini Voyager. Your goal is to deliver high-quality, robust, and idiomatic code that enhances the Google Gemini experience.
    12→
    13→**Core Mandates**:
    14→
    15→1.  **Safety First**: Never commit secrets. Validate all system operations.
    16→2.  **Code Consistency**: Strictly follow the project's architectural patterns (Services, Stores, functional React).
    17→3.  **Type Safety**: No `any`. Use `unknown` with narrowing. Use Branded Types for IDs.
    18→4.  **Testing**: Every feature and fix must include tests.
    19→5.  **Documentation**: Keep documentation and translations in sync with code changes.
    20→
    21→---
    22→
    23→## 2. Operational Methodology
    24→
    25→Before writing code, apply this "Linus-style" problem-solving framework to ensure robust and simple solutions.
    26→
    27→### Phase 1: The Three Questions
    28→
    29→Ask yourself before starting:
    30→
    31→1.  **"Is this a real problem?"** - Reject over-engineering.
    32→2.  **"Is there a simpler way?"** - Always seek the simplest solution (KISS).
    33→3.  **"Will it break anything?"** - Backward compatibility is an iron law.
    34→
    35→### Phase 2: Requirements Analysis
    36→
    37→When analyzing a request:
    38→
    39→1.  **Data Structure First**: "Bad programmers worry about the code. Good programmers worry about data structures."
    40→    - What is the core data? Who owns it?
    41→    - Can we redesign data structures to eliminate branches/complexity?
    42→2.  **Eliminate Special Cases**: "Good code has no special cases."
    43→    - Identify `if/else` branches that patch bad design.
    44→    - Refactor to make the "special case" the normal case.
    45→3.  **Destructive Analysis**:
    46→    - List all existing features that might be affected.
    47→    - Ensure zero destructiveness to user data (especially `localStorage`).
    48→
    49→### Phase 3: Decision Output
    50→
    51→If a task is complex or ambiguous, present your analysis in this format:
    52→
    53→```text
    54→【Core Judgment】
    55→✅ Worth doing: [reason] / ❌ Not worth doing: [reason]
    56→
    57→【Key Insights】
    58→- Data structure: [most critical data relationships]
    59→- Complexity: [complexity that can be eliminated]
    60→- Risks: [potential breaking changes]
    61→
    62→【Plan】
    63→1. Simplify data structures...
    64→2. Eliminate special cases...
    65→3. Implementation steps...
    66→```
    67→
    68→---
    69→
    70→## 3. Tool Usage & Verification Protocols
    71→
    72→Strictly adhere to these protocols to prevent errors and ensure data integrity.
    73→
    74→### 🛡️ The "Read-Write-Verify" Loop
    75→
    76→1.  **READ**: Always read the target file **before** editing. Do not rely on memory or assumptions.
    77→    - _Tool_: `read_file`
    78→2.  **WRITE**: Apply atomic changes. Use sufficient context for `replace`.
    79→    - _Tool_: `write_file` or `replace`
    80→3.  **VERIFY**: Check the file content **after** editing to ensure the change was applied correctly and didn't break syntax.
    81→    - _Tool_: `read_file` or `run_shell_command` (grep/cat)
    82→
    83→### 🚨 Critical Safety Checks
    84→
    85→- **Never** modify `dist_*` folders directly.
    86→- **Never** commit `.env` or secrets.
    87→- **Always** run `bun run typecheck` after modifying TypeScript definitions.
    88→- **Always** run `bun run lint` before finishing.
    89→
    90→---
    91→
    92→## 4. Module Glossary & Complexity Hotspots
    93→
    94→| Module (Path)                          | Responsibility                                    | Complexity | Notes                                                                          |
    95→| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
    96→| `core/services/StorageService`         | **Single Source of Truth** for persistence.       | 🌶️ High    | Handles sync/local/session logic + migration. **Do not modify lightly.**       |
    97→| `core/services/DataBackupService`      | Multi-layer backup protection.                    | 🌶️ High    | Critical for data safety. Race conditions possible during unload.              |
    98→| `core/services/GoogleDriveSyncService` | Google Drive cloud sync (OAuth2).                 | 🌶️ High    | Handles folders, prompts, and starred messages sync. Requires OAuth2 identity. |
    99→| `features/folder`                      | Drag-and-drop folder logic + cloud sync UI.       | 🌶️ High    | DOM manipulation + State sync is tricky. Watch out for infinite loops.         |
   100→| `features/export`                      | Chat export (JSON/MD/PDF/Image) + Deep Research.  | 🌶️ High    | Image export, message selection, multi-browser compat. Fragile to Gemini UI.   |
   101→| `features/backup`                      | File System Access API.                           | 🟡 Medium  | Browser compatibility issues (Safari fallback).                                |
   102→| `pages/content`                        | **DOM Injection** (22 content script modules).    | 🟡 Medium  | Bridge between Gemini UI and Extension. Each sub-module is self-contained.     |
   103→| `pages/content/mermaid`                | Mermaid diagram rendering.                        | 🟡 Medium  | Dynamic library loading with legacy fallback.                                  |
   104→| `pages/content/watermarkRemover`       | NanoBanana watermark removal via fetch intercept. | 🟡 Medium  | Disabled on Safari. Uses `fetchInterceptor.js` injected into page context.     |
   105→
   106→---
   107→
   108→## 5. Development Standards & Anti-Patterns
   109→
   110→### ✅ DOs
   111→
   112→- **Prefer Plain Objects**: Use interfaces/types for data structures.
   113→- **Immutability**: Use `map`, `filter`, `reduce`.
   114→- **Encapsulation**: Use `private`/`protected` in classes.
   115→- **Type Guarding**: Use `unknown` + narrowing (Zod or custom guards).
   116→- **Named Exports**: `export function X` (easier refactoring).
   117→- **Functional React**: Hooks at top level, strictly functional components.
   118→
   119→### ❌ DON'Ts (Anti-Patterns)
   120→
   121→- **Global State Pollution**: Never use global variables outside of defined Services.
   122→- **Direct Storage Access**: Never use `chrome.storage` directly in UI components. Always use `StorageService`.
   123→- **God Components**: Don't put business logic in UI files. Move it to `features/xxx/services` or custom hooks.
   124→- **Any Type**: Explicitly banned. Use `unknown` if you must, then narrow it.
   125→- **Magic Strings**: Use constants or enums, especially for Storage Keys and CSS Classes.
   126→- **Console Logs**: Remove `console.log` in production code (use `LoggerService` for critical info).
   127→
   128→---
   129→
   130→## 6. Testing Strategy
   131→
   132→**Framework**: Vitest 4.0.6 (jsdom environment)
   133→
   134→### TDD Workflow Guidelines
   135→
   136→1.  **Write the Test First**: Define the expected behavior in `*.test.ts`.
   137→2.  **Fail**: Ensure the test fails (validates the test itself).
   138→3.  **Implement**: Write the minimal code to pass the test.
   139→4.  **Refactor**: Clean up the code while keeping tests green.
   140→
   141→### Mocking Patterns
   142→
   143→This project relies heavily on `vi.mock` for Chrome APIs and external services.
   144→
   145→**Mocking Chrome API**:
   146→The global `chrome` object is mocked in `src/tests/setup.ts`. You can inspect or override it in individual tests.
   147→
   148→```typescript
   149→// Example: Mocking specific storage behavior for a test
   150→beforeEach(() => {
   151→  (chrome.storage.sync.get as any).mockResolvedValue({ someKey: 'value' });
   152→});
   153→```
   154→
   155→**Running Tests**:
   156→
   157→```bash
   158→bun run test                # Run all tests
   159→bun run test <filename>     # Run specific test file
   160→bun run test:watch          # Interactive mode
   161→bun run test:coverage       # Check coverage
   162→```
   163→
   164→---
   165→
   166→## 7. Workflows & Definition of Done
   167→
   168→### Setup
   169→
   170→```bash
   171→bun install
   172→```
   173→
   174→### Development
   175→
   176→```bash
   177→# Start Dev Server
   178→bun run dev:chrome
   179→bun run dev:firefox
   180→bun run dev:safari
   181→
   182→# Build for production
   183→bun run build:chrome
   184→bun run build:firefox
   185→bun run build:safari
   186→bun run build:edge        # Repackages Chrome build for Edge
   187→bun run build:all         # Build all platforms
   188→
   189→# Documentation site (VitePress)
   190→bun run docs:dev
   191→bun run docs:build
   192→```
   193→
   194→_Note: Uses Nodemon for hot-reloading content scripts._
   195→
   196→### Commit Messages (commitlint)
   197→
   198→Use Conventional Commits format:
   199→
   200→```
   201→<type>(<scope>): <imperative summary>
   202→```
   203→
   204→- `type`: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `chore`, `docs`, `test`, `build`, `ci`, `perf`, `style`
   205→- `scope`: short, feature-focused (e.g., `copy`, `export`, `popup`)
   206→- summary: lowercase, imperative, no trailing period
   207→
   208→Examples:
   209→
   210→- `fix(copy): handle clipboard fallback`
   211→- `refactor(copy): introduce temml to convert tex2mathml`
   212→- `chore: update sponsors.svg`
   213→
   214→### Definition of Done (DoD)
   215→
   216→Before claiming a task is complete, verify:
   217→
   218→1.  **Functionality**: Does it meet the requirements?
   219→2.  **Tests**: Are there new tests? Do all tests pass (`bun run test`)?
   220→3.  **Types**: No TypeScript errors (`bun run typecheck`)?
   221→4.  **Linting**: Code formatted and linted (`bun run lint`)?
   222→5.  **Build**: Does it build without error (`bun run build`)?
   223→6.  **Safety**: No secrets committed? No destructive `localStorage` operations?

# AGENTS.md - AI Assistant Guide for Gemini Voyager

> **Last Updated**: 2026-02-15
> **Version**: 1.2.3
> **Purpose**: Comprehensive guide for AI assistants working with the Gemini Voyager codebase

---

## 1. Role & Core Mandates

**Role**: You are an expert Full-Stack Engineer and Chrome Extension Specialist working on Gemini Voyager. Your goal is to deliver high-quality, robust, and idiomatic code that enhances the Google Gemini experience.

**Core Mandates**:

1.  **Safety First**: Never commit secrets. Validate all system operations.
2.  **Code Consistency**: Strictly follow the project's architectural patterns (Services, Stores, functional React).
3.  **Type Safety**: No `any`. Use `unknown` with narrowing. Use Branded Types for IDs.
4.  **Testing**: Every feature and fix must include tests.
5.  **Documentation**: Keep documentation and translations in sync with code changes.

---

## 2. Operational Methodology

Before writing code, apply this "Linus-style" problem-solving framework to ensure robust and simple solutions.

### Phase 1: The Three Questions

Ask yourself before starting:

1.  **"Is this a real problem?"** - Reject over-engineering.
2.  **"Is there a simpler way?"** - Always seek the simplest solution (KISS).
3.  **"Will it break anything?"** - Backward compatibility is an iron law.

### Phase 2: Requirements Analysis

When analyzing a request:

1.  **Data Structure First**: "Bad programmers worry about the code. Good programmers worry about data structures."
    - What is the core data? Who owns it?
    - Can we redesign data structures to eliminate branches/complexity?
2.  **Eliminate Special Cases**: "Good code has no special cases."
    - Identify `if/else` branches that patch bad design.
    - Refactor to make the "special case" the normal case.
3.  **Destructive Analysis**:
    - List all existing features that might be affected.
    - Ensure zero destructiveness to user data (especially `localStorage`).

### Phase 3: Decision Output

If a task is complex or ambiguous, present your analysis in this format:

```text
【Core Judgment】
✅ Worth doing: [reason] / ❌ Not worth doing: [reason]

【Key Insights】
- Data structure: [most critical data relationships]
- Complexity: [complexity that can be eliminated]
- Risks: [potential breaking changes]

【Plan】
1. Simplify data structures...
2. Eliminate special cases...
3. Implementation steps...
```

---

## 3. Tool Usage & Verification Protocols

Strictly adhere to these protocols to prevent errors and ensure data integrity.

### 🛡️ The "Read-Write-Verify" Loop

1.  **READ**: Always read the target file **before** editing. Do not rely on memory or assumptions.
    - _Tool_: `read_file`
2.  **WRITE**: Apply atomic changes. Use sufficient context for `replace`.
    - _Tool_: `write_file` or `replace`
3.  **VERIFY**: Check the file content **after** editing to ensure the change was applied correctly and didn't break syntax.
    - _Tool_: `read_file` or `run_shell_command` (grep/cat)

### 🚨 Critical Safety Checks

- **Never** modify `dist_*` folders directly.
- **Never** commit `.env` or secrets.
- **Always** run `bun run typecheck` after modifying TypeScript definitions.
- **Always** run `bun run lint` before finishing.

---

## 4. Module Glossary & Complexity Hotspots

| Module (Path)                          | Responsibility                                    | Complexity | Notes                                                                          |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------- | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `core/services/StorageService`         | **Single Source of Truth** for persistence.       | 🌶️ High    | Handles sync/local/session logic + migration. **Do not modify lightly.**       |
| `core/services/DataBackupService`      | Multi-layer backup protection.                    | 🌶️ High    | Critical for data safety. Race conditions possible during unload.              |
| `core/services/GoogleDriveSyncService` | Google Drive cloud sync (OAuth2).                 | 🌶️ High    | Handles folders, prompts, and starred messages sync. Requires OAuth2 identity. |
| `features/folder`                      | Drag-and-drop folder logic + cloud sync UI.       | 🌶️ High    | DOM manipulation + State sync is tricky. Watch out for infinite loops.         |
| `features/export`                      | Chat export (JSON/MD/PDF/Image) + Deep Research.  | 🌶️ High    | Image export, message selection, multi-browser compat. Fragile to Gemini UI.   |
| `features/backup`                      | File System Access API.                           | 🟡 Medium  | Browser compatibility issues (Safari fallback).                                |
| `pages/content`                        | **DOM Injection** (24 content script modules).    | 🟡 Medium  | Bridge between Gemini UI and Extension. Each sub-module is self-contained.     |
| `pages/content/mermaid`                | Mermaid diagram rendering.                        | 🟡 Medium  | Dynamic library loading with legacy fallback.                                  |
| `pages/content/watermarkRemover`       | NanoBanana watermark removal via fetch intercept. | 🟡 Medium  | Disabled on Safari. Uses `fetchInterceptor.js` injected into page context.     |

---

## 5. Development Standards & Anti-Patterns

### ✅ DOs

- **Prefer Plain Objects**: Use interfaces/types for data structures.
- **Immutability**: Use `map`, `filter`, `reduce`.
- **Encapsulation**: Use `private`/`protected` in classes.
- **Type Guarding**: Use `unknown` + narrowing (Zod or custom guards).
- **Named Exports**: `export function X` (easier refactoring).
- **Functional React**: Hooks at top level, strictly functional components.

### ❌ DON'Ts (Anti-Patterns)

- **Global State Pollution**: Never use global variables outside of defined Services.
- **Direct Storage Access**: Never use `chrome.storage` directly in UI components. Always use `StorageService`.
- **God Components**: Don't put business logic in UI files. Move it to `features/xxx/services` or custom hooks.
- **Any Type**: Explicitly banned. Use `unknown` if you must, then narrow it.
- **Magic Strings**: Use constants or enums, especially for Storage Keys and CSS Classes.
- **Console Logs**: Remove `console.log` in production code (use `LoggerService` for critical info).

---

## 6. Testing Strategy

**Framework**: Vitest 4.0.6 (jsdom environment)

### TDD Workflow Guidelines

1.  **Write the Test First**: Define the expected behavior in `*.test.ts`.
2.  **Fail**: Ensure the test fails (validates the test itself).
3.  **Implement**: Write the minimal code to pass the test.
4.  **Refactor**: Clean up the code while keeping tests green.

### Mocking Patterns

This project relies heavily on `vi.mock` for Chrome APIs and external services.

**Mocking Chrome API**:
The global `chrome` object is mocked in `src/tests/setup.ts`. You can inspect or override it in individual tests.

```typescript
// Example: Mocking specific storage behavior for a test
beforeEach(() => {
  (chrome.storage.sync.get as any).mockResolvedValue({ someKey: 'value' });
});
```

**Running Tests**:

```bash
bun run test                # Run all tests
bun run test <filename>     # Run specific test file
bun run test:watch          # Interactive mode
bun run test:coverage       # Check coverage
```

## Project overview

`react-native-live-text-view` is an Expo native module that provides an iOS Live Text-enabled wrapper view for images.

- JS/TS public API lives in `src/` and exports `LiveTextView`.
- Native implementation is iOS-only in `ios/`, built with Expo Modules API.
- `example/` is an Expo app used to manually validate behavior.

## Common commands

### Install dependencies

- Root package:
  - `npm install`
- Example app:
  - `npm --prefix example install`

### Library development (root)

- Build library: `npm run build`
- Lint: `npm run lint`
- Run tests: `npm run test`
- Run a single test (pass through Jest args): `npm run test -- <path-or-jest-args>`
- Clean generated artifacts: `npm run clean`
- Prepare package (build + prepare steps): `npm run prepare`

### Example app

- Run iOS example app: `npm --prefix example run ios`
- Start Metro for example app: `npm --prefix example run start`

### iOS native iteration helpers

- Open example iOS workspace in Xcode: `npm run open:ios`
- If testing in Expo development build flow, rebuild iOS native project when native changes are made:
  - `npx expo prebuild -p ios --clean`
  - `npx expo run:ios`

## Architecture notes

### JS/TS layer

- `src/index.ts` exports `LiveTextView` and prop types.
- `src/LiveTextView.tsx` bridges to the native view manager using `requireNativeViewManager('ReactNativeLiveTextView')`.
- Event payload types are defined in `src/LiveText.types.ts`.
- `onHighlightChange` is normalized to emit a boolean (`isHighlight`) instead of the full event object.

### Expo module wiring

- `expo-module.config.json` registers only iOS module `ReactNativeLiveTextViewModule`.
- `ios/ReactNativeLiveTextViewModule.swift` defines:
  - View props: `disabled`, `liveActionButtonHidden`
  - View events: `onStart`, `onReady`, `onError`, `onTextSelectionChange`, `onHighlightChange`

### Native iOS behavior

- Core implementation is in `ios/ReactNativeLiveTextView.swift`.
- The native view:
  - Finds the wrapped `UIImageView` from child subviews.
  - Attaches `ImageAnalysisInteraction`.
  - Runs VisionKit `ImageAnalyzer` with `.text` configuration.
  - Emits analysis lifecycle events and selection/highlight updates back to JS.
  - Observes `UIImageView.image` changes and re-analyzes when image content updates.
- Runtime guards:
  - Live Text analysis requires iOS 16+ (`ImageAnalyzer` availability checks).
  - `selectedText` in `onTextSelectionChange` is populated only on iOS 17+.

### Example app usage pattern

- `example/App.tsx` demonstrates the expected integration pattern:
  - Wrap a React Native `Image` in `<LiveTextView>`.
  - Toggle `disabled` and `liveActionButtonHidden` props.
  - Listen to `onStart`, `onReady`, `onError`, `onHighlightChange`, `onTextSelectionChange` for runtime behavior validation.

## Notes from repository config

- No Cursor rules (`.cursorrules` / `.cursor/rules`) or Copilot instruction file (`.github/copilot-instructions.md`) are present.
- Lint config is in `.eslintrc.js` and ignores `build/` and `README.md`.

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

## Project overview

`react-native-live-text-view` is an Expo Modules-based React Native library that enables iOS Live Text interactions on images.

- Library package at repo root (`src/`, `ios/`, `expo-module.config.json`)
- Demo app in `example/` (used to manually verify behavior on iOS)
- iOS-only native implementation (no Android module)

## Common commands

Run commands from repository root unless noted.

### Library development

- Install deps: `npm install`
- Build JS/types: `npm run build`
- Lint: `npm run lint`
- Run tests: `npm test`
- Run a single test file/pattern: `npm test -- <testPathPattern>`
- Clean generated artifacts: `npm run clean`
- Prepare package artifacts: `npm run prepare`
- Run prepublish checks: `npm run prepublishOnly`

### Example app (manual iOS verification)

Run from `example/`:

- Install deps: `npm install`
- Start Expo dev server: `npm run start`
- Build/run iOS app: `npm run ios`

From repo root, open native iOS workspace for example:

- `npm run open:ios`

## Architecture

### JavaScript/TypeScript layer

- `src/index.ts` exports the public API (`LiveTextView`, `LiveTextViewProps`).
- `src/LiveText.types.ts` defines typed event payloads and props passed between JS and native.
- `src/LiveTextView.tsx` is the main JS wrapper around the native view manager (`requireNativeViewManager('ReactNativeLiveTextView')`).
  - It adapts native events and preserves backward compatibility for consumers accessing payloads via `event.nativeEvent`.

### Native iOS layer

- `ios/ReactNativeLiveTextViewModule.swift` registers the Expo module and view:
  - module name: `ReactNativeLiveTextView`
  - props: `disabled`, `liveActionButtonHidden`
  - events: `onStart`, `onReady`, `onError`, `onTextSelectionChange`, `onHighlightChange`
- `ios/ReactNativeLiveTextView.swift` implements the `ExpoView` and `ImageAnalysisInteractionDelegate` behavior:
  - Locates the underlying `UIImageView` from React subviews
  - Attaches `ImageAnalysisInteraction`
  - Runs async `ImageAnalyzer` analysis for text
  - Emits lifecycle/results/errors back to JS
  - Re-runs analysis when image changes via KVO on `imageView.image`

### Module wiring

- `expo-module.config.json` declares iOS module autolinking and points to `ReactNativeLiveTextViewModule`.
- `ios/ReactNativeLiveTextView.podspec` defines CocoaPods packaging for the module and depends on `ExpoModulesCore`.

## Platform and behavior constraints

- The module is iOS-only.
- Live Text analysis is gated in native code with `@available(iOS 16.0, *)` and `ImageAnalyzer.isSupported` checks.
- `onTextSelectionChange.selectedText` depends on iOS 17+ (`selectedText` is empty on earlier iOS versions).

## Validation workflow for changes

For most code changes, validate with:

1. `npm run lint`
2. `npm run build`
3. `npm test`
4. Manual verification in `example/` on iOS (`npm run ios` from `example/`) for native behavior/event changes

     7→
     8→# CLAUDE.md 및 AGENTS.md 생성 스킬
     9→
    10→$ARGUMENTS 가 주어지면 해당 프로젝트 경로를 대상으로 한다. 없으면 현재 작업 디렉토리를 대상으로 한다.
    11→
    12→## 생성 철학
    13→
    14→이 스킬 전체를 관통하는 4가지 원칙이다 (references/karpathy-guidelines.md 참조).
    15→
    16→- **생각 후 행동**: 가정하지 말고 확인한다. 모호함을 감추지 말고 드러낸다.
    17→- **단순함 우선**: 문제를 해결하는 최소한의 내용만 포함한다. 추측을 배제한다.
    18→- **외과적 정밀함**: 프로젝트에서 관찰된 사실만 포함한다. 린터가 할 일은 린터에게 맡긴다.
    19→- **목표 기반 실행**: 모든 지시사항은 검증 가능해야 한다.
    20→
    21→아래 4단계를 순서대로 수행한다.
    22→
    23→---
    24→
    25→## 1단계: 프로젝트 분석 — Think Before Coding
    26→
    27→대상 디렉토리에서 다음을 자동 탐지한다:
    28→
    29→- 패키지/빌드/테스트/린트·포매터 설정 (package.json, Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, go.mod, .eslintrc, .prettierrc, biome.json, ruff.toml 등)
    30→- 저장소 구조 및 독립성 (모노레포: workspaces, packages/, apps/; 서브모듈: .gitmodules 파싱으로 경로/URL/독립 저장소 여부; 하위 디렉토리의 자체 패키지 매니저 존재 여부)
    31→- 문서/CI 구성 (기존 CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md, contributing-docs/, .cursorrules, 하위 CLAUDE.md 위치/내용, CI/CD: .github/workflows, .gitlab-ci.yml)
    32→
    33→탐지 결과를 간략히 정리하여 사용자에게 보여준다. 이때:
    34→
    35→- 탐지 결과에서 **사실**과 **가정**을 구분하여 표시한다.
    36→- 자동 탐지로 알 수 없는 항목을 명시적으로 나열한다.
    37→- 기존 AGENTS.md가 있으면 구조와 내용을 분석하여 3단계 생성 시 참고한다.
    38→- 중첩 CLAUDE.md 후보 목록을 표로 정리한다:
    39→  | 경로 | 유형 (모노레포 패키지/서브모듈) | 기존 CLAUDE.md 유무 | 생성 권장 여부 |
    40→
    41→---
    42→
    43→## 2단계: 인터뷰 — Think Before Coding
    44→
    45→1단계 자동 탐지로 알 수 없는 항목만 질문한다. WHAT/WHY/HOW 프레임워크를 따른다.
    46→
    47→질문은 다음 범위 내에서 필요한 것만 한다:
    48→
    49→**WHY (자동 탐지 불가)**:
    50→- 이 프로젝트의 목적/역할은 무엇인가?
    51→
    52→**WHAT (자동 탐지로 부족한 부분만)**:
    53→- 모노레포인 경우 각 패키지/앱의 역할
    54→- 서브모듈이 있는 경우 부모 저장소와의 관계 및 독립 운영 여부
    55→- 외부 서비스 의존성 (DB, 메시지 큐, 외부 API 등)
    56→
    57→**HOW (자동 탐지로 부족한 부분만)**:
    58→- 특별한 작업 규칙/워크플로우, 브랜치 전략, PR/커밋 규칙, 환경 설정 특이사항이 있는가?
    59→- 중첩 CLAUDE.md 후보 목록을 보여주고, 각 후보에 대해 생성 여부를 확인한다
    60→
    61→추가 원칙:
    62→- 모호한 항목은 **가능한 해석을 제시한 뒤** 사용자에게 선택을 요청한다.
    63→- 1단계에서 가정한 내용을 사용자에게 확인한다.
    64→
    65→---
    66→
    67→## 3단계: 생성 — Simplicity First + Surgical Changes
    68→
    69→네 가지를 생성한다:
    70→
    71→공통 작성 규칙:
    72→- 코드 스니펫은 직접 포함하지 않고 file:line 참조만 사용한다

    74→### A. 루트 CLAUDE.md

   159→- **중복 금지**: 상위 CLAUDE.md에 있는 내용을 반복하지 않는다. 차이점만 기술한다
   160→- **상위 참조**: 공통 규칙은 상위 CLAUDE.md를 구체적 경로로 참조한다
   161→- **목표 줄 수**: 50줄 이하. 절대 100줄을 넘기지 않는다
   162→- **자기 완결적 제목**: `# CLAUDE.md — {패키지/서브모듈 이름}`으로 시작한다
   163→
   164→#### 구조
   165→
   166→```markdown
   167→# CLAUDE.md — {이름}
   168→
   169→(1줄: 이 디렉토리의 목적/역할)
   170→
   171→## 기술 스택
   172→(상위와 다른 부분만. 동일하면 섹션 생략)
   173→
   174→## 개발 명령
   175→(이 디렉토리 고유의 빌드/테스트/린트 명령)
   176→
   177→## 작업 규칙
   178→(상위와 다른 규칙이 있는 경우만. 없으면 생략)
   179→
   180→## 참조 문서
   181→- **[../CLAUDE.md](../CLAUDE.md)** — 프로젝트 공통 규칙
   182→(하위에 AGENTS.md가 있으면 참조, 없으면 생략)
   183→```
   184→
   185→#### 참조 경로 규칙
   186→
   187→- 상위 CLAUDE.md: 항상 상대 경로 (`../CLAUDE.md`)
   188→- 서브모듈: 부모 저장소 CLAUDE.md를 URL 또는 상대 경로로 참조
   189→- 형제 디렉토리: 직접 참조하지 않는다 (상위를 경유)
   190→
   191→---
   192→
   193→## 4단계: 검증 — Goal-Driven Execution
   194→
   195→생성된 CLAUDE.md와 AGENTS.md에 대해 다음 체크리스트를 줄 단위로 적용한다:
   196→
   197→1. **보편성/필수성/중복**: 모든 작업에 적용되는가? 없으면 실수하는가? 코드를 읽으면 자명한가? → 아니면 삭제 또는 AGENTS.md/contributing-docs/로 이동
   198→2. **린터 역할**: 코드 스타일 규칙인가? → 삭제하고 린터/Hook으로 대체 권장
   199→3. **추측 배제**: 1~2단계에서 확인되지 않은 내용이 포함되는가? → 있으면 삭제
   200→4. **검증 가능성**: 각 지시사항을 따랐는지 판별 가능한가? → 아니면 구체화
   201→5. **분량 제약**: 100줄 이하, 개별 지시사항 50개 이하인가? → 초과하면 통합 또는 삭제
   202→6. **계층/범위**: CLAUDE.md가 contributing-docs/를 직접 참조하는가? AGENTS.md가 Claude 전용 내용만 담는가? 중첩 CLAUDE.md가 자기 디렉토리 밖을 포함하거나 상위 내용을 반복하는가? → 있으면 이동/삭제 또는 상위 참조로 대체
   203→7. **참조 정합성**: 중첩 CLAUDE.md의 상위 참조 경로가 올바른가? → 상대 경로 검증
   204→
   205→자기 테스트 질문:
   206→- "시니어 엔지니어가 이 CLAUDE.md를 보고 '과하다'고 할까?"
   207→- "CLAUDE.md → AGENTS.md → contributing-docs/ 계층이 명확하게 분리되어 있는가?"
   208→- "중첩 CLAUDE.md를 제거해도 상위 CLAUDE.md만으로 해당 디렉토리 작업이 충분한가?" → 충분하면 중첩 파일 삭제 권장
   209→- "중첩 CLAUDE.md 간에 내용이 서로 모순되는가?"
   210→
   211→검증 결과를 사용자에게 보고한다. 탈락 항목이 있으면 해당 줄과 사유를 함께 표시하고, 정제된 최종본을 제시한다.
   212→
   213→---
   214→
   215→## LLM 컨텍스트 원칙
   216→
   217→- LLM은 인컨텍스트 학습자다. 기존 코드 패턴을 검색하면 스타일을 자연스럽게 따라가므로, 스타일 규칙을 CLAUDE.md에 포함할 필요가 없다.
   218→- Claude Code 시스템 프롬프트가 이미 ~50개 지시사항을 포함하며, 보편적이지 않은 내용이 많을수록 전체가 무시될 확률이 높아진다.
   219→- 상위 레벨(CLAUDE.md)의 오류는 하위(계획 → 코드)로 기하급수적으로 증폭된다.
   220→- LLM은 명확한 목표가 있을 때 반복 실행에 탁월하다 (references/karpathy-guidelines.md). 지시사항을 **검증 가능한 목표**로 작성해야 Claude가 자율적으로 올바른 결과에 도달한다.
   221→

1→---
     2→name: commit
     3→description: "한국어 Conventional Commits 규칙에 따라 git 커밋을 생성한다. /commit, 커밋해줘, commit, 변경사항 커밋 요청 시 사용한다."
     4→model: sonnet
     5→allowed-tools: Bash(git status:*), Bash(git diff:*), Bash(git log:*), Bash(git add:*), Bash(git commit:*)
     6→---
     7→
     8→# Git Commit
     9→
    10→프로젝트의 한국어 Conventional Commits 규칙에 따라 커밋을 생성한다.
    11→
    12→## 형식
    13→
    14→`<type>(<scope>): <한국어 제목 -하다>`
    15→
    16→- **type** (필수): feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, test, chore
    17→- **scope** (선택): 프로젝트 CLAUDE.md에 정의된 scope를 따른다
    18→- **제목** (필수): 한국어, `-하다` 종결 어미, 50자 이내, 마침표 없음
    19→- **본문** (선택): 변경 의도가 불명확할 때만 포함한다. why > what > how 우선순위, 72자 줄바꿈
    20→
    21→## 절차
    22→
    23→1. 사용자 인자에서 파일 경로나 지시사항을 확인한다
    24→2. `git status`와 `git diff`로 변경사항을 파악한다
    25→3. `git log --oneline -20`으로 최근 커밋 스타일과 scope를 확인한다
    26→4. 스테이징할 파일이 불명확하면 사용자에게 확인한다
    27→5. 해당 파일만 `git add`로 스테이징한다
    28→6. heredoc으로 커밋한다:
    29→
    30→```bash
    31→git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF'
    32→<type>(<scope>): <한국어 제목>
    33→
    34→<본문 — 필요한 경우만>
    35→EOF
    36→)"
    37→```
    38→
    39→## 금지 사항
    40→
    41→- Co-Authored-By를 추가하지 않는다 (시스템이 자동 처리)
    42→- `git push`를 실행하지 않는다
    43→- 사용자 확인 없이 파일을 스테이징하지 않는다
    44→
    45→## 참고
    46→
    47→커밋 메시지 상세 규칙은 references/gitmessage.md를 따른다.
    48→

1→# claude-flow-guidance-implementation
     2→
     3→Implementation kit for wiring `@claude-flow/guidance` into real repos with repeatable automation for Claude Code hooks, Codex lifecycle events, and guidance optimization workflows.
     4→
     5→## What This Package Is
     6→
     7→This package is an installer and scaffold, not just an API example.  
     8→It creates a working guidance control plane in a target repo, including:
     9→
    10→- hook event wiring (`pre-*` and `post-*`)
    11→- guidance runtime scripts (`analyze`, `optimize`, `ab-benchmark`, modules)
    12→- Codex bridge commands (optional)
    13→- `CLAUDE.local.md` bootstrap for local-only experiments
    14→- verification checks so setup can be validated immediately
    15→
    16→## What `quickstart` is doing
    17→
    18→The quickstart commands do two things:
    19→
    20→- run `init` to install and wire scripts/config into your target repo
    21→- run `verify` to confirm that required files, hooks, and syntax checks pass
    22→
    23→It is meant to produce a runnable integration, not just generate documentation.
    24→
    25→## Quickstart
    26→
    27→Use directly from npm:
    28→
    29→```bash
    30→npx --yes -p claude-flow-guidance-implementation cf-guidance-impl init --target ~/source/my-project --install-deps
    31→npx --yes -p claude-flow-guidance-implementation cf-guidance-impl verify --target ~/source/my-project
    32→```
    33→
    34→Or install as a dev dependency:
    35→
    36→```bash
    37→npm i -D claude-flow-guidance-implementation
    38→npx cf-guidance-impl init --target ~/source/my-project --install-deps
    39→npx cf-guidance-impl verify --target ~/source/my-project
    40→```
    41→
    42→## Integration Modes
    43→
    44→| Mode | What gets wired |
    45→|---|---|
    46→| `both` (default) | Claude hooks + Codex bridge + guidance scripts |
    47→| `claude` | Claude hooks + guidance scripts |
    48→| `codex` | Codex bridge + guidance scripts |
    49→
    50→Examples:
    51→
    52→```bash
    53→npx cf-guidance-impl init --target ~/source/my-project --target-mode both
    54→npx cf-guidance-impl init --target ~/source/my-project --target-mode claude
    55→npx cf-guidance-impl init --target ~/source/my-project --target-mode codex
    56→```
    57→
    58→## CLI Reference
    59→
    60→```bash
    61→cf-guidance-impl init --target <repoPath> [--target-mode both|claude|codex] [--force] [--install-deps] [--no-dual] [--skip-cf-init] [--no-verify]
    62→cf-guidance-impl install --target <repoPath> [--target-mode both|claude|codex] [--force] [--install-deps]
    63→cf-guidance-impl verify --target <repoPath> [--target-mode both|claude|codex]
    64→```
    65→
    66→## What `init` Changes In Your Target Repo
    67→
    68→`cf-guidance-impl init` performs:
    69→
    70→1. Runs `npx @claude-flow/cli@latest init` unless `--skip-cf-init`.
    71→2. Adds CLI mode flags automatically:
    72→   - `both` uses `--dual` unless `--no-dual`
    73→   - `codex` uses `--codex`
    74→   - `claude` uses standard init
    75→3. Copies scaffold runtime files (`scripts/`, `src/guidance/`, docs, hook handler).
    76→4. Merges guidance scripts and dependencies into `package.json`.
    77→5. Merges `.claude/settings.json` env and hooks in Claude-enabled modes.
    78→6. Appends Codex bridge sections to `.agents/config.toml` and `AGENTS.md` in Codex-enabled modes.
    79→7. Creates `CLAUDE.local.md` (if missing) and appends `CLAUDE.local.md` to `.gitignore`.
    80→8. Runs verification unless `--no-verify`.
    81→
    82→## Installed Scripts (Target Repo)
    83→
    84→Core:
    85→
    86→- `guidance:analyze`
    87→- `guidance:optimize`
    88→- `guidance:autopilot:once`
    89→- `guidance:autopilot:daemon`
    90→- `guidance:ab-benchmark`
    91→- `guidance:status`
    92→- `guidance:all`
    93→- `guidance:trust`
    94→- `guidance:adversarial`
    95→- `guidance:proof`
    96→- `guidance:conformance`
    97→- `guidance:evolution`
    98→
    99→Codex lifecycle bridge:
   100→
   101→- `guidance:codex:status`
   102→- `guidance:codex:session-start`
   103→- `guidance:codex:pre-command`
   104→- `guidance:codex:pre-edit`
   105→- `guidance:codex:pre-task`
   106→- `guidance:codex:post-edit`
   107→- `guidance:codex:post-task`
   108→- `guidance:codex:session-end`
   109→
   110→## Manual Runtime Mode (No Copied Runtime Files)
   111→
   112→You can also execute scripts directly from `node_modules`:
   113→
   114→```json
   115→{
   116→  "scripts": {
   117→    "guidance:analyze": "node ./node_modules/claude-flow-guidance-implementation/scaffold/scripts/analyze-guidance.js",
   118→    "guidance:optimize": "node ./node_modules/claude-flow-guidance-implementation/scaffold/scripts/guidance-autopilot.js --once --apply --source manual",
   119→    "guidance:ab-benchmark": "node ./node_modules/claude-flow-guidance-implementation/scaffold/scripts/guidance-ab-benchmark.js",
   120→    "guidance:codex:status": "node ./node_modules/claude-flow-guidance-implementation/scaffold/scripts/guidance-codex-bridge.js status"
   121→  }
   122→}
   123→```
   124→
   125→Project root resolution for scaffold scripts:
   126→
   127→- `GUIDANCE_PROJECT_DIR` if set
   128→- else `CLAUDE_PROJECT_DIR` if set
   129→- else `process.cwd()`
   130→
   131→## Verify + Smoke Test
   132→
   133→```bash
   134→npx cf-guidance-impl verify --target ~/source/my-project
   135→cd ~/source/my-project
   136→npm run guidance:status
   137→npm run guidance:analyze
   138→npm run guidance:codex:status
   139→```
   140→
   141→For Codex bridge smoke checks:
   142→
   143→```bash
   144→npm run guidance:codex:pre-task -- --task-id smoke-1 --description "smoke"
   145→```
   146→
   147→Expected success signals:
   148→
   149→- `handler.ok: true` means local bridge path succeeded
   150→- `claudeFlowHook.ok: true` means optional `@claude-flow/cli` hook call succeeded
   151→
   152→## Installed Files (High-Level)
   153→
   154→| Path | Purpose |
   155→|---|---|
   156→| `.claude/helpers/hook-handler.cjs` | Event entrypoint for hook dispatch |
   157→| `scripts/guidance-integrations.js` | Unified guidance module runner |
   158→| `scripts/guidance-codex-bridge.js` | Codex lifecycle adapter |
   159→| `scripts/guidance-autopilot.js` | Local-rule optimization/promotion loop |
   160→| `src/guidance/phase1-runtime.js` | Compile/retrieve/gates/ledger integration |
   161→| `src/guidance/advanced-runtime.js` | Trust/adversarial/proof/conformance/evolution modules |
   162→| `docs/guidance-control-plane.md` | Operational overview |
   163→| `docs/guidance-implementation-guide.md` | Authoritative implementation guide |

1→# CLAUDE.md — site/
     2→
     3→Marketing website for partio, an open-source CLI that captures AI agent sessions alongside Git commits.
     4→
     5→## Tech stack
     6→
     7→- Next.js 16 (App Router)
     8→- React 19
     9→- TypeScript
    10→- Tailwind CSS v4
    11→- Framer Motion 12
    12→
    13→## Commands
    14→
    15→```bash
    16→npm run dev    # Start dev server on localhost:3000
    17→npm run build  # Production build
    18→npm run lint   # Run ESLint
    19→```
    20→
    21→## Architecture
    22→
    23→- **App Router** — single-page app with `src/app/layout.tsx` (root layout) and `src/app/page.tsx` (home)
    24→- **Components** are organized into three directories:
    25→  - `src/components/layout/` — Navbar, Footer
    26→  - `src/components/sections/` — Hero, Features, HowItWorks, CliDemo, OpenSource
    27→  - `src/components/ui/` — reusable primitives (Button, Badge, Terminal, FeatureCard)
    28→- **Lib** — `src/lib/utils.ts` contains the `cn()` class-merge helper (clsx)
    29→- **Path alias** — `@/*` maps to `./src/*`
    30→
    31→## Conventions
    32→
    33→- **Client components** — most components use `"use client"` because they depend on Framer Motion. The root layout is a server component.
    34→- **Styling** — Tailwind CSS v4 utility classes only. Theme colors are defined as CSS custom properties in `src/app/globals.css` and registered via `@theme inline`. Use the semantic tokens (e.g. `bg-background`, `text-accent`, `border-border`) rather than raw hex values.
    35→- **Animations** — Framer Motion with `motion.div`, `useInView`, and staggered variants. Follow the existing animation patterns when adding new sections.
    36→- **Class merging** — use `cn()` from `@/lib/utils` to merge Tailwind classes.
    37→- **TypeScript** — interfaces are defined inline in component files, not in separate type files.
    38→- **State** — no state management library. Use local `useState` where needed.
    39→- **Static content** — all copy is hardcoded in component files. There is no CMS or content layer.
    40→- **No API routes or server actions** — this is a purely static marketing site.
    41→- **No environment variables** — none are currently used.
    42→

    44→
    45→- Docs: https://docs.partio.io
    46→- CLI repo: https://github.com/ArvosAI/partio

1→# Fix Output Type Bias in Remediation Prompt Generator
     2→
     3→## Context
     4→
     5→The remediation prompt generator has two compounding problems that both bias the AI executor toward "generic update" (inline edits) over creating skills or standards:
     6→
     7→**Problem 1 — `errorDefaultGuidance` bias:** The guidance text added for errors explicitly says "default to generic update," overriding the three-question decision criteria that would correctly classify `git-workflow` issues as skills.
     8→
     9→**Problem 2 — Evaluator Fix suggestions are unaware of skills/standards:** The 19 evaluators that produce issues have no knowledge of the standard/skill/generic classification. Their **Fix** field describes inline edits (e.g., "Add this section to AGENTS.md: ..."), nudging the AI executor to treat everything as a generic update even when a skill would be more appropriate. The prompt never warns the executor about this.
    10→
    11→**Concrete example:** Issue #15 (`git-workflow` — commit message format) has a Fix that says "Specify a commit message format explicitly, e.g.: `### Commit Message Format`..." — this reads as "add a section to AGENTS.md," so the executor does just that, ignoring that a git-workflow skill would be better.
    12→
    13→## Problem Location
    14→
    15→`src/shared/remediation/prompt-generator.ts`
    16→
    17→- **Lines 236–239** — `errorDefaultGuidance` variable (bias toward generic)
    18→- **Lines 478–496** — `## Instructions` section in `buildErrorFixPrompt()` (no warning about evaluator Fix suggestions)
    19→
    20→The issue block header already shows `evaluatorName: category` (e.g., `git-workflow: Workflow Integration`) at line 151, so the evaluator-type signal is already visible.
    21→
    22→## Proposed Changes
    23→
    24→### Change 1: Replace `errorDefaultGuidance` with fix-nature-based guidance
    25→
    26→```typescript
    27→const errorDefaultGuidance =
    28→    context === "error"
    29→        ? `\n\n**Choosing the right type for error fixes:**
    30→- Factual corrections (wrong paths, outdated names, incorrect references) → **generic update**
    31→- New procedural workflows (commit steps, CI/CD procedures, deployment flows) → **skill**
    32→- New constraints or guardrails (security rules, coding conventions) → **standard**
    33→
    34→Use the evaluator category in each issue header as a signal:

## Project Overview

**srcref** is a Kotlin web service that generates dynamic GitHub permalinks using regex patterns. Instead of linking to
fixed line numbers that break when code changes, srcref uses regex to find the target lines dynamically. Live
at https://www.srcref.com.

## Build Commands

```bash
./gradlew build -xtest        # Build without tests
./gradlew test                 # Run all tests (Kotest/JUnit5)
./gradlew check                # Full check including lint
./gradlew lintKotlin           # Lint only
./gradlew formatKotlin         # Auto-format code
./gradlew run                  # Run dev server (port 8080)
./gradlew buildFatJar          # Create fat JAR at build/libs/srcref-all.jar
./gradlew dependencyUpdates    # Check for dependency updates
```

Run a single test class:

```bash
./gradlew test --tests "FileTests"
```

Run a single named test (Kotest string spec name):

```bash
./gradlew test --tests "FileTests.calcLineNumber top-down and bottom-up"
```

Makefile shortcuts: `make build`, `make tests`, `make run`, `make uber`, `make release`.

## Architecture

**Entry point**: `Main.kt` — `object Main` with `@JvmStatic fun main()`. Starts a Ktor CIO embedded server, installs
middleware (CallLogging, DefaultHeaders, StatusPages, Compression), then calls `configureRoutes()`.

**Request flow** (e.g., `GET /github?account=X&repo=Y&...`):

1. `Routes.kt`: `readQueryParams()` builds a `Map<String, String?>` from all 12 `QueryParams` enum entries
2. `Urls.kt`: `githubRangeUrl()` validates params, constructs the raw GitHub URL
3. `ContentCache.kt`: `fetchContent()` fetches file content with ETag-based caching (304 support, LRU eviction)
4. `Urls.kt`: `calcLineNumber()` searches file lines by regex — supports occurrence selection (Nth match),
   top-down/bottom-up direction, and line offset. Has a 5-second regex timeout per search.
5. Builds `https://github.com/{account}/{repo}/blob/{branch}/{path}#L{begin}[-L{end}]` and 302-redirects the browser
6. On any error: redirects to `/problem?msg=<encoded>&<params>` instead

Core modules in `src/main/kotlin/com/pambrose/srcref/`:

- **Urls.kt** — Core logic. `calcLineNumber()` is the key algorithm; `githubRangeUrl()` orchestrates the full flow.
- **ContentCache.kt** — ETag-based HTTP cache using `ConcurrentHashMap`. Background daemon thread evicts LRU entries
  every 5 min when size exceeds `MAX_CACHE_SIZE`. HTTP client has retry logic (3 retries, exponential backoff).
- **QueryParams.kt** — Enum defining all 12 URL query parameters with defaults and validation. Begin params (`bregex`,
  `boccur`, `boffset`, `btopd`) are required; end params (`eregex`, `eoccur`, `eoffset`, `etopd`) are optional.
- **Routes.kt** — HTTP route definitions. Maps endpoints to handlers.
- **Endpoints.kt** — Enum mapping endpoint names to lowercase paths.
- **Api.kt** — Public `Api.srcrefUrl()` function for programmatic use (available as JitPack dependency).
- **pages/** — HTML pages using kotlinx.html DSL. `PageTemplate.kt` is the base template; `Edit.kt` (main form),
  `Error.kt`, `Version.kt`, `What.kt`, `Cache.kt` are individual pages. `Common.kt` has shared constants/utilities.

## Key Endpoints

| Path           | Purpose                               |
|----------------|---------------------------------------|
| `/edit`        | Main form UI                          |
| `/github`      | Redirect to computed GitHub permalink |
| `/github?edit` | Edit an existing srcref URL           |
| `/problem`     | Error display with message            |
| `/ping`        | Health check (`pong`)                 |
| `/cache`       | Cache status table                    |
| `/version`     | Version and build info                |
| `/threaddump`  | JVM thread dump (Dropwizard)          |

## Testing

Tests in `src/test/kotlin/` use Kotest `StringSpec` with JUnit5 runner:

- **FileTests.kt** — `calcLineNumber()`: top-down/bottom-up, offsets, invalid regex, occurrence out of range
- **UrlsTest.kt** — `toQueryParams()`, `srcrefToGithubUrl()`, `toInt()`, `githubRangeUrl()` with edge cases
- **ContentCacheTest.kt** — Cache CRUD, `markReferenced()`, `sortedByLastReferenced()`, volatile visibility
- **ApiTest.kt** — `Api.srcrefUrl()`: default/custom params, HTML escaping, URL encoding
- **QueryParamsTest.kt** — Enum entries, `defaultIfNull()`, `defaultIfBlank()`, `required()` validation
- **RoutesIntegrationTest.kt** — Full HTTP integration tests using `ktor-server-test-host`
- **BugFixTests.kt** — Regression tests: ETag edge cases, daemon thread, robots.txt, occurrence validation
- **EndpointsTest.kt**, **CommonTest.kt**, **MainTest.kt** — Unit tests for utilities

## Code Style

- Kotlinter (ktlint) for linting. Run `./gradlew formatKotlin` before committing.
- Disabled ktlint rules (via `.editorconfig`): `no-wildcard-imports`, `string-template-indent`, `indent`,
  `chain-method-continuation`, `import-ordering`.
- 120 char line length, 2-space indentation, UTF-8, LF line endings.

## Version Management

Version is defined in `build.gradle.kts` (`version = "2.0.1"`). Must also be updated in `Makefile` (`VERSION`) and
`README.md` when changing.

## Dependencies

Managed via `gradle/libs.versions.toml`. Key frameworks: Ktor (HTTP server/client), kotlinx.html (HTML DSL), Kotest (
testing), Dropwizard Metrics (JVM metrics), kotlin-logging + Logback. JVM toolchain: Java 17.

Build metadata (VERSION, RELEASE_DATE, BUILD_TIME) is generated at compile time by the `buildconfig` Gradle plugin into
a `BuildConfig` class.

## Environment Variables

| Variable         | Default                | Purpose                        |
|------------------|------------------------|--------------------------------|
| `PORT`           | 8080                   | HTTP server port               |
| `PREFIX`         | https://www.srcref.com | URL prefix for generated links |
| `DEFAULT_BRANCH` | master                 | Default GitHub branch          |
| `MAX_CACHE_SIZE` | 2048                   | Max cached file entries        |
| `MAX_LENGTH`     | 5MB                    | Max file size to process       |

## Deployment

Docker multi-arch build (amd64/arm64) via `make release`. Image runs on Alpine + OpenJDK 17 JRE.
Heroku supported via `system.properties` (Java 17 runtime). No CI/CD pipeline — deployment is manual.

1→# OpenFang — Claude Code Guide
     2→
     3→## What This Is
     4→
     5→A personal AI assistant framework ("OpenFang") built in Ruby. It combines a Roda web UI, ActiveRecord models (SQLite), FastMCP tool server, and a Claude Code CLI subprocess as the agent runtime.
     6→
     7→## Architecture
     8→
     9→```
    10→openfang.rb (entrypoint) → Fang::CLI (Thor)
    11→├── web/app.rb          Roda web server (port 3000)
    12→├── fang/mcp_server.rb    FastMCP tool server (port 9292)
    13→├── fang/agent.rb         Spawns `claude` CLI subprocess per conversation
    14→├── fang/bootstrap.rb     Loads everything, connects DB
    15→└── fang/scheduler.rb     Rufus-scheduler for recurring tasks
    16→```
    17→
    18→**Real-time updates**: In-memory pub/sub (`web/turbo_broadcast.rb`) → SSE → Turbo Streams in the browser. No ActionCable or Redis needed — everything runs in one process.
    19→
    20→**Agent execution**: When a user sends a message, `AgentExecutorJob` runs `Fang::Agent.execute`, which spawns a `claude` CLI subprocess with MCP tools. The subprocess uses `workspace/.mcp.json` and `workspace/CLAUDE.md` as its system prompt.
    21→
    22→## Key Conventions
    23→
    24→- **Auto-discovery via ObjectSpace**: MCP tools (`fang/tools/`) and resources (`fang/resources/`) are auto-registered by scanning for subclasses of `FastMcp::Tool` and `FastMcp::Resource`. Just create the file — no manual registration needed.
    25→- **No index pages for content types**: When the AI creates a new page/content type, add a direct link to it in the nav bar (`web/views/layout.erb`) instead of creating a separate listing page. Each page is served at `/pages/:slug`.
    26→- **Models use concerns**: Shared behavior lives in `fang/concerns/` (e.g., `HasStatus`).
    27→
    28→## Running the App
    29→
    30→```bash
    31→./openfang.rb server        # Start web UI on port 3000
    32→./openfang.rb console       # IRB with all models loaded
    33→./openfang.rb db:migrate    # Run pending migrations
    34→./openfang.rb mcp           # Start MCP server standalone
    35→```
    36→
    37→## Adding a New MCP Tool
    38→
    39→1. Create `fang/tools/my_tool.rb`:
    40→
    41→```ruby
    42→# frozen_string_literal: true
    43→
    44→module Fang
    45→  module Tools
    46→    class MyTool < FastMcp::Tool
    47→      tool_name 'my_tool'
    48→      description 'What this tool does'
    49→
    50→      arguments do
    51→        required(:name).filled(:string).description('Argument description')
    52→        optional(:option).filled(:string).description('Optional argument')
    53→      end
    54→
    55→      def call(name:, option: nil)
    56→        # Tool logic here — all Fang:: models are available
    57→        { success: true, result: 'done' }
    58→      rescue => e
    59→        { success: false, error: e.message }
    60→      end
    61→    end
    62→  end
    63→end
    64→```
    65→
    66→2. Restart the server. The tool is auto-discovered.

   101→## Design System
   102→
   103→Clean, minimal shadcn/ui-inspired design with terminal green accent. Supports light/dark mode via `prefers-color-scheme`. Inter font, rounded corners, subtle shadows.
   104→
   105→### CSS Tokens (defined in `web/public/css/style.css`)
   106→
   107→Light and dark mode tokens are defined as CSS custom properties. The `--fang-*` aliases are used by Tailwind classes.
   108→
   109→| Token | Light | Dark | Usage |
   110→|---|---|---|---|
   111→| `--background` | `#ffffff` | `#09090b` | Page background |
   112→| `--foreground` | `#0f172a` | `#fafafa` | Primary text |
   113→| `--card` | `#ffffff` | `#18181b` | Card backgrounds |
   114→| `--muted` | `#f1f5f9` | `#27272a` | Muted backgrounds |
   115→| `--muted-foreground` | `#64748b` | `#a1a1aa` | Muted text |
   116→| `--primary` | `#16a34a` | `#22c55e` | Accent (green) |
   117→| `--primary-foreground` | `#ffffff` | `#ffffff` | Text on accent |
   118→| `--border` | `#e2e8f0` | `#27272a` | Borders |
   119→| `--ring` | `#16a34a` | `#22c55e` | Focus rings |
   120→
   121→### Components
   122→- **`.card`** — rounded card with subtle border and shadow
   123→- **`.badge`** — pill label (variants: `.success`, `.error`, `.warning`, `.info`)
   124→- **`button`** — green bg, rounded. Variants: `.ghost`, `.outline`, `.sm`, `.xs`, `.icon`
   125→- **`.chat-msg.user`** / **`.chat-msg.ai`** — rounded chat bubbles
   126→- **`.prose-bubble`** — markdown content inside chat bubbles
   127→- **`.section-heading`** — card section titles
   128→- **`.msg-meta`** — chat message metadata (small, uppercase, muted)
   129→- **`.notification-unread`** — unread notification left border accent
   130→- **`.nav-trigger`** — hamburger menu button
   131→- **`.notification-badge`** — small pill badge for notification counts
   132→
   133→### Rules
   134→- **No inline styles** — all styling via Tailwind utilities or CSS classes
   135→- **No `text-transform: uppercase`** on headings — use `font-semibold tracking-tight`
   136→
   137→Tailwind CSS is loaded via CDN with custom colors: `fang-bg`, `fang-fg`, `fang-muted`, `fang-muted-fg`, `fang-accent`, `fang-accent-fg`, `fang-border`, `fang-card`, `fang-primary`, `fang-ring`.
   138→
   139→## Event System
   140→
   141→`Fang::EventBus` is a simple in-process pub/sub for decoupled automation. Call `EventBus.emit("event:name", data)` to fire an event. Triggers and workflows listen for matching events.
   142→
   143→**Emit points** are wired into:
   144→- `ScheduledTaskRunnerJob` → `task:completed:*` / `task:failed:*`
   145→- `HeartbeatRunnerJob` → `heartbeat:escalated:*` / `heartbeat:error:*`
   146→- `Notification#broadcast!` → `notification:created:*`
   147→
   148→**Triggers** (`fang/models/trigger.rb`) match events via glob patterns and fire a skill or prompt.
   149→
   150→**Workflows** (`fang/models/workflow.rb`) are multi-step pipelines with step types: `skill`, `prompt`, `condition`, `wait`, `notify`. Steps pass data via a JSON context hash with `{{context.step_name}}` interpolation. Workflows can auto-start on a `trigger_event`.
   151→
   152→## Key Files
   153→
   154→| File | Purpose |
   155→|---|---|
   156→| `openfang.rb` | CLI entrypoint |
   157→| `fang/bootstrap.rb` | Framework loader |
   158→| `fang/agent.rb` | Claude subprocess execution |
   159→| `fang/mcp_server.rb` | FastMCP tool/resource registration |
   160→| `fang/event_bus.rb` | In-process event pub/sub for triggers and workflows |
   161→| `web/app.rb` | All Roda routes |
   162→| `web/views/layout.erb` | Main layout with sidebar nav |
   163→| `web/view_helpers.rb` | HTML rendering helpers (turbo_stream, markdown, message/notification cards) |
   164→| `web/turbo_broadcast.rb` | In-memory pub/sub for SSE |
   165→| `web/public/css/style.css` | Complete design system |
   166→| `workspace/CLAUDE.md` | OpenFang's system prompt (the inner agent reads this) |
   167→| `workspace/.mcp.json` | MCP config passed to claude subprocess |
   168→
   169→## Existing MCP Tools
   170→
   171→| Tool | File | Purpose |
   172→|---|---|---|
   173→| `run_code` | `fang/tools/run_code_tool.rb` | Execute Ruby code with model access |
   174→| `run_skill` | `fang/tools/run_skill_tool.rb` | Execute saved skills by name |
   175→| `send_message` | `fang/tools/send_message_tool.rb` | Send message + broadcast via SSE |
   176→| `schedule_task` | `fang/tools/schedule_task_tool.rb` | Schedule future tasks/reminders (supports `cron:` for recurring) |

1→# CLAUDE.md
     2→
     3→This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
     4→
     5→## Commands
     6→
     7→- **Install dependencies:** `bun install`
     8→- **Run:** `bun run index.ts`
     9→- **Type check:** `bunx tsc --noEmit`
    10→
    11→## Overview
    12→
    13→CLI client for GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, Qwen Code, and Codex using the Agent Client Protocol (ACP). Features an interactive terminal UI built with Ink (React for the terminal). On launch, presents an engine selection screen, then model input, then connects and enters a chat REPL with streamed responses.
    14→
    15→## Architecture
    16→
    17→- `index.ts` — Entry point. Parses `--workdir`, renders the Ink `<App>` component.
    18→- `src/types.ts` — Shared types (`Screen`, `ChatMessage`, `ToolCallEntry`, `PlanEntry`) and `ENGINES` config dict.
    19→- `src/store.ts` — `SessionStore` typed EventEmitter bridging ACP streaming callbacks to React state.
    20→- `src/connection.ts` — Spawns the agent process, wires up ACP streams, initializes session. Emits status via `SessionStore`.
    21→- `src/agent-client.ts` — `AgentClient` implements `acp.Client`: emits session updates to `SessionStore`, auto-accepts permissions, delegates filesystem and terminal operations.
    22→- `src/terminal-manager.ts` — `TerminalManager` class encapsulating child process lifecycle (create, output, wait, kill, release) with a `Map`-based registry.
    23→- `src/hooks/useSessionStore.ts` — React hook subscribing to `SessionStore` events, manages `messages[]` + `currentMessage` state.
    24→- `src/components/` — Ink UI components: `App`, `Header`, `EngineSelect`, `ModelInput`, `Connecting`, `Chat`, `MessageBubble`, `ToolCallCard`, `ThoughtBlock`, `PlanView`, `StatusBar`, `PromptInput`.
    25→
    26→## Key Details
    27→
    28→- Runtime is **Bun** (not Node.js)
    29→- TypeScript with strict mode, `noEmit`, JSX (`react-jsx`), and bundler module resolution (`allowImportingTsExtensions` — use `.ts`/`.tsx` extensions in imports)
    30→- UI built with **Ink** (React for the terminal) — no default engine; interactive selection on startup
    31→

1→# Completeness & Balance Evaluator
     2→
     3→You are a specialized AGENTS.md evaluator focused exclusively on detecting **Completeness & Balance** issues.
     4→
     5→---
     6→
     7→## Essential Context
     8→
     9→AGENTS.md is a standardized format for providing context and instructions to AI coding agents. It should complement README.md by containing detailed, agent-specific guidance about build steps, tests, conventions, and project-specific workflows.
    10→
    11→**Evaluation Constraints**: You will ONLY receive the AGENTS.md file content itself, without access to the actual codebase, README.md, or other files. Focus on intrinsic quality signals detectable from the text alone.
    12→
    13→---
    14→
    15→## Your Focus Area: Completeness & Depth Issues
    16→
    17→You are detecting issues where the file is either too short/skeletal or too verbose/overwhelming.
    18→
    19→### 10.1 Extremely Short or Skeletal Content
    20→
    21→**Detection Signals:**
    22→- Only 1-2 sections present
    23→- Sections have only 1-2 sentences
    24→- No code blocks or command examples
    25→- Looks like a template that wasn't filled out
    26→
    27→**Example of Bad:**
    28→```markdown
    29→# AGENTS.md
    30→
    31→## Setup
    32→Install dependencies and run the project.
    33→
    34→## Testing
    35→Run tests before committing.
    36→```
    37→
    38→**Why It's Bad:** Insufficient information for agents to work effectively.
    39→
    40→**How to Detect:**
    41→- Count code blocks (0-1 suggests missing commands)
    42→- Count sections (< 3 suggests incompleteness)
    43→- Look for template-like placeholder text
    44→- Check for absence of executable commands
    45→
    46→---
    47→
    48→### 10.2 Over-Detailed or Excessive Content
    49→
    50→**Detection Signals:**
    51→- Extensive narrative explanations for every small detail
    52→- Repeated information across sections
    53→- Tutorial-style content teaching basic concepts
    54→- Over-documentation of obvious steps
    55→
    56→**Example of Bad:**
    57→```markdown
    58→## Installing Node.js
    59→First, you need to understand what Node.js is. Node.js is a JavaScript runtime
    60→built on Chrome's V8 JavaScript engine. It was created by Ryan Dahl in 2009...
    61→[500 lines about Node.js history and architecture]
    62→
    63→Now, to install Node.js, you have several options. You can download it from
    64→the official website, or you can use a version manager like nvm...
    65→[300 lines about all possible installation methods]
    66→```
    67→
    68→**Why It's Bad:** Too much information makes it hard to find relevant instructions; agents get overwhelmed.
    69→
    70→**How to Detect:**
    71→- Look for tutorial-style teaching content
    72→- Identify repeated concepts or sections
    73→- Check for basic concept explanations (what is git, what is a compiler)
    74→- Measure ratio of narrative to actionable content
    75→
    76→---
    77→
    78→### 10.3 Inappropriate Content Placement
    79→
    80→Detect when technology-specific content appears in root AGENTS.md when appropriate subdirectories exist.
    81→
    82→**What This Section Detects:**
    83→
    84→Root AGENTS.md should contain **generic, universal guidelines** applicable across the entire repository.
    85→Subdirectory AGENTS.md files should contain **context-specific rules** for that domain.
    86→
    87→**Detection Signals:**
    88→
    89→1. **Framework/Technology-Specific Content in Root:**
    90→   - Frontend frameworks: "React", "Vue", "Angular", "component", "useState", "JSX"
    91→   - UI libraries: "Chakra UI", "Material-UI", "Tailwind", "styled-components"
    92→   - Backend frameworks: "Django", "Flask", "Express", "FastAPI", "Spring Boot"
    93→   - ORMs/Databases: "Prisma", "TypeORM", "SQLAlchemy", "Hibernate", "migration"
    94→   - Mobile: "React Native", "Flutter", "SwiftUI", "Jetpack Compose"
    95→
    96→2. **Subdirectories Exist:**
    97→   - Check for section headers showing multiple files (e.g., FILE 1, FILE 2, etc.)
    98→   - Check for directory structure mentions in root (e.g., "frontend/", "backend/")
    99→   - Check for cross-references (e.g., "See frontend/AGENTS.md")
   100→
   101→3. **Subdirectory is Skeletal:**
   102→   - Subdirectory has <20 lines OR
   103→   - Subdirectory only references root ("See root AGENTS.md") OR
   104→   - Subdirectory has only generic content when specific content exists in root
   105→
   106→**Severity Calculation:**
   107→
   108→| Severity | Description |
   109→|----------|-------------|
   110→| **9** | 50+ lines of technology-specific content in root when subdirectory exists and is mostly empty |
   111→| **8** | 30-50 lines of technology-specific content in root when subdirectory exists |
   112→| **7** | 20-30 lines of technology-specific content in root with subdirectory |
   113→| **6** | Some technology-specific content in root that would fit better in subdirectory |
   114→| **≤5** | DO NOT REPORT |
   115→
   116→**Output Format:**
   117→
   118→```json
   119→{
   120→  "category": "Completeness & Balance",
   121→  "section": "10.3",
   122→  "severity": 8,
   123→  "title": "Technology-Specific Content in Root AGENTS.md",
   124→  "description": "Root AGENTS.md contains extensive React-specific guidelines that should be moved to frontend/AGENTS.md",

   126→  "impact": "Root file becomes cluttered with framework-specific details instead of universal guidelines. Agents working in non-frontend areas must parse irrelevant React content.",
   127→  "recommendation": "Move all React component guidelines, Chakra UI styling rules, and component structure patterns from root AGENTS.md to frontend/AGENTS.md. Keep only universal development rules in root.",
   128→  "affectedFiles": ["AGENTS.md", "frontend/AGENTS.md"],
   129→  "isMultiFile": true,
   130→  "location": [
   131→    {"file": "AGENTS.md", "start": 15, "end": 60},
   132→    {"file": "frontend/AGENTS.md", "start": 1, "end": 5}
   133→  ]
   134→}
   135→```
   136→
   137→**Examples:**

   410→### AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md Pair Exemption
   411→
   412→**CRITICAL**: When AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md exist in the same directory with identical or similar content, this is INTENTIONAL and should NOT be flagged.

   421→### Packmind Standards Sections (EXCLUDED FROM COMPARISON)
   422→
   423→**CRITICAL**: When comparing AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md files for consistency or missing content, **completely exclude Packmind Standards sections** from the comparison.
   424→
   425→**Why:**
   426→- Packmind tool intentionally deploys standards only to AGENTS.md files
   427→- CLAUDE.md files will not contain Packmind standards by design
   428→- This difference is intentional, not a documentation gap
   429→
   430→**Detection - Content to Skip:**
   431→
   432→1. **HTML Comment Markers:**
   433→   ```html
   434→   <!-- start: Packmind standards -->
   435→   ...content here...
   436→   <!-- end: Packmind standards -->
   437→   ```
   438→
   439→2. **Section Headings:**
   440→   - `# Packmind Standards` or `## Packmind Standards`
   441→   - All content until the next major heading or end of file
   442→
   443→**How to Handle:**
   444→
   445→- When AGENTS.md contains Packmind Standards sections but CLAUDE.md does not: **DO NOT flag as missing content**
   446→- When comparing file completeness: **Exclude Packmind content from both files before comparison**
   447→- Content differences related to Packmind standards are **NEVER an issue**

   450→
   451→```

   453→[38 lines of regular content]
   454→
   455→<!-- start: Packmind standards -->
   456→## Testing Standards
   457→[100 lines of Packmind-generated standards]
   458→<!-- end: Packmind standards -->
   459→
   460→FILE 2: apps/frontend/CLAUDE.md (38 lines)
   461→[38 lines of regular content - same as AGENTS.md]
   462→```
   463→
   464→**This is CORRECT** - CLAUDE.md has the same manual content as AGENTS.md. The missing Packmind section is intentional.
   465→

   467→- "CLAUDE.md lacks X standards present in AGENTS.md" when X is Packmind content

   472→
   473→### Cross-File Completeness Issues
   474→
   475→**CRITICAL**: Length differences alone are NOT problems. Focus on content appropriateness.
   476→
   477→#### Reversed Hierarchical Content (Severity 8-9)
   478→
   479→**Pattern**: Root has extensive technology-specific rules, subdirectories are skeletal.
   480→
   481→**Example:**
   482→- Root: 80 lines of React component guidelines
   483→- frontend/AGENTS.md: 10 lines saying "See root for React guidelines"
   484→
   485→**This is BAD** because:
   486→- Agents working in frontend need to read root file
   487→- Root file is cluttered with domain-specific details
   488→- Hierarchy is reversed (specific in root, generic in subdirectory)
   489→
   490→**Recommendation**: "Move React-specific content from root to frontend/AGENTS.md."
   491→
   492→---
   493→
   494→#### Missing Context-Specific Guidance (Severity 7-8)
   495→
   496→**Pattern**: Root is appropriately generic, but subdirectories lack context-specific content.
   497→
   498→**Example:**
   499→- Root: Generic rules about testing (appropriate)
   500→- frontend/AGENTS.md: Also generic "write tests" (missing React Testing Library details)
   501→- backend/AGENTS.md: Also generic "write tests" (missing pytest details)
   502→
   503→**This is BAD** because:
   504→- Subdirectories should provide context-specific guidance
   505→- Without specifics, agents must guess implementation details
   506→- Defeats the purpose of having separate files
   507→
   508→**Recommendation**: "Add React-specific testing guidance (React Testing Library, component patterns) to frontend/AGENTS.md."
   509→
   510→---
   511→
   512→#### Inconsistent Specialization (Severity 6-7)
   513→
   514→**Pattern**: Some subdirectories have context-specific content, similar subdirectories don't.
   515→
   516→**Example:**
   517→- frontend/AGENTS.md: 100 lines of React details (good)
   518→- backend/AGENTS.md: 15 lines of generic rules (inconsistent)
   519→
   520→**Recommendation**: "Add Python/FastAPI-specific guidance to backend/AGENTS.md to match detail level of frontend/AGENTS.md."
   521→
   522→---
   523→
   524→#### Good Hierarchical Patterns (DO NOT REPORT)
   525→
   526→These are CORRECT hierarchical documentation patterns:
   527→
   528→✅ **Root: 20 lines generic, Subdirectory: 100 lines specific**
   529→- Root has universal rules (git, testing philosophy)
   530→- Subdirectory has technology-specific details
   531→- Length difference is APPROPRIATE
   532→
   533→✅ **Root: 50 lines, Subdirectory: 30 lines**
   534→- Root has project structure, setup, workflows
   535→- Subdirectory has focused context-specific rules
   536→- Appropriate if both have right content for scope
   537→
   538→✅ **Root mentions subdirectories with cross-references**
   539→- "See frontend/AGENTS.md for React guidelines"
   540→- Clear hierarchical structure
   541→- This is GOOD design
   542→

   544→
