    42→
    43→## Improvement 2: Tool Context Groups with Pre-Classification
    44→
    45→**~4-5K tokens saved per invocation (60-70% tool schema reduction) | Medium complexity**
    46→
    47→Filter which tools are available per conversation based on context. Most conversations need only 7-13 tools, not 38. Use a cheap/fast model call to classify intent before spawning the full agent.
    48→
    49→**Tool groups:**
    50→- **core** (always loaded, 7 tools): `run_code`, `run_skill`, `send_message`, `schedule_task`, `create_page`, `create_notification`, `web_fetch`
    51→- **gmail** (6): all `gmail_*` tools
    52→- **canvas** (6): `get_canvas`, `update_canvas`, `add_canvas_component`, `update_canvas_component`, `remove_canvas_component`, `define_widget`
    53→- **data** (6): all data table CRUD tools
    54→- **documents** (3): `create_document`, `read_document`, `list_documents`
    55→- **automation** (8): triggers, workflows, heartbeats, approvals
    56→- **system** (2): `manage_python`, `start_computer_use`
    57→
    58→**Pre-classification step:**
    59→
    60→Before spawning the Claude agent subprocess, make a fast Haiku call (~200ms, ~200 tokens) to classify which tool groups the message needs:
    61→
    62→```ruby
    63→# fang/tool_classifier.rb
    64→module Fang
    65→  module ToolClassifier
    66→    GROUPS = %w[gmail canvas data documents automation system].freeze
    67→
    68→    def self.classify(message, conversation: nil)
    69→      # Include recent conversation context for better classification
    70→      context = if conversation && conversation.messages.count > 1
    71→        recent = conversation.messages.order(created_at: :desc).limit(3).map { |m| "#{m.role}: #{m.truncated_content(100)}" }.reverse.join("\n")
    72→        "Recent conversation:\n#{recent}\n\nNew message: #{message}"
    73→      else
    74→        message
    75→      end
    76→
    77→      response = Anthropic::Client.new.messages(
    78→        model: "claude-haiku-4-5-20251001",
    79→        max_tokens: 50,
    80→        system: "You classify user messages for an AI assistant. Return ONLY a comma-separated list of needed tool groups from: #{GROUPS.join(', ')}. Return 'none' if only basic tools are needed. Be conservative — only include groups clearly needed.",
    81→        messages: [{ role: "user", content: context }]
    82→      )
    83→
    84→      groups = response.dig("content", 0, "text").to_s.strip.split(",").map(&:strip)
    85→      groups = groups & GROUPS  # only allow known groups
    86→      [:core] + groups.map(&:to_sym)
    87→    rescue => e
    88→      Fang.logger.warn "Tool classification failed: #{e.message}, loading all tools"
    89→      nil  # nil = no filtering, load everything (safe fallback)
    90→    end
    91→  end
    92→end
    93→```
    94→
    95→**Implementation:**
    96→1. Add `tool_group` class-level DSL to each tool (one line per tool file)
    97→2. Create `fang/tool_classifier.rb` — Haiku-based pre-classification
    98→3. In `fang/agent.rb`, call `ToolClassifier.classify` before spawning subprocess
    99→4. Generate per-conversation `.mcp.json` with group params in the SSE URL: `http://localhost:3000/mcp/sse?groups=core,gmail`
   100→5. Add `filter_tools` block in `fang/mcp_server.rb` that reads groups from the SSE connection URL
   101→6. Store classified groups in conversation metadata so resumed sessions keep their groups (and can expand if new groups detected)
   102→
   103→**Cost of pre-classification:** ~200 tokens of Haiku input/output ≈ $0.0002 per call. Saves ~4-5K tokens of Sonnet/Opus tool schemas ≈ $0.03-0.08. ROI is ~100-400x.
   104→
   105→**Files:**
   106→- `fang/tool_classifier.rb` — new classifier module
   107→- `fang/concerns/tool_grouping.rb` — new concern with `tool_group` DSL
   108→- All `fang/tools/*.rb` — add `tool_group :group_name` (one line each)
   109→- `fang/mcp_server.rb` — add `filter_tools` block
   110→- `fang/agent.rb` — call classifier, generate per-conversation `.mcp.json`

     3→## What This Is
     4→
     5→A personal AI assistant framework ("Ned") built in Ruby. It combines a Roda web UI, ActiveRecord models (SQLite), FastMCP tool server, and a Claude Code CLI subprocess as the agent runtime.
     6→
     7→## Architecture
     8→
     9→```
    10→ai.rb (entrypoint) → Ai::CLI (Thor)
    11→├── web/app.rb          Roda web server (port 3000)
    12→├── ai/mcp_server.rb    FastMCP tool server (port 9292)
    13→├── ai/agent.rb         Spawns `claude` CLI subprocess per conversation
    14→├── ai/bootstrap.rb     Loads everything, connects DB
    15→└── ai/scheduler.rb     Rufus-scheduler for recurring tasks
    16→```
    17→
    18→**Real-time updates**: In-memory pub/sub (`web/turbo_broadcast.rb`) → SSE → Turbo Streams in the browser. No ActionCable or Redis needed — everything runs in one process.

    20→**Agent execution**: When a user sends a message, `AgentExecutorJob` runs `Ai::Agent.execute`, which spawns a `claude` CLI subprocess with MCP tools. The subprocess uses `workspace/.mcp.json` and `workspace/CLAUDE.md` as its system prompt.
    21→

> ## Documentation Index > Fetch the complete documentation index at: https://code.claude.com/docs/llms.txt > Use this file to discover all available pages before exploring further. # Manage Claude's memory > Learn how to manage Claude Code's memory across sessions with different memory locations and best practices. Claude Code has two kinds of memory that persist across sessions: * **Auto memory**: Claude automatically saves useful context like project patterns, key commands, and your preferences. This persists across sessions. * **CLAUDE.md files**: Markdown files you write and maintain with instructions, rules, and preferences for Claude to follow. Both are loaded into Claude's context at the start of every session, though auto memory loads only the first 200 lines of its main file. ## Determine memory type Claude Code offers several memory locations in a hierarchical structure, each serving a different purpose: | Memory Type | Location | Purpose | Use Case Examples | Shared With | | -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------- | | **Managed policy** | • macOS: `/Library/Application Support/ClaudeCode/CLAUDE.md`
• Linux: `/etc/claude-code/CLAUDE.md`
• Windows: `C:\Program Files\ClaudeCode\CLAUDE.md` | Organization-wide instructions managed by IT/DevOps | Company coding standards, security policies, compliance requirements | All users in organization | | **Project memory** | `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md` | Team-shared instructions for the project | Project architecture, coding standards, common workflows | Team members via source control | | **Project rules** | `./.claude/rules/*.md` | Modular, topic-specific project instructions | Language-specific guidelines, testing conventions, API standards | Team members via source control | | **User memory** | `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` | Personal preferences for all projects | Code styling preferences, personal tooling shortcuts | Just you (all projects) | | **Project memory (local)** | `./CLAUDE.local.md` | Personal project-specific preferences | Your sandbox URLs, preferred test data | Just you (current project) | | **Auto memory** | `~/.claude/projects//memory/` | Claude's automatic notes and learnings | Project patterns, debugging insights, architecture notes | Just you (per project) | CLAUDE.md files in the directory hierarchy above the working directory are loaded in full at launch. CLAUDE.md files in child directories load on demand when Claude reads files in those directories. Auto memory loads only the first 200 lines of `MEMORY.md`. More specific instructions take precedence over broader ones. CLAUDE.local.md files are automatically added to .gitignore, making them ideal for private project-specific preferences that shouldn't be checked into version control. ## Auto memory Auto memory is a persistent directory where Claude records learnings, patterns, and insights as it works. Unlike CLAUDE.md files that contain instructions you write for Claude, auto memory contains notes Claude writes for itself based on what it discovers during sessions. Auto memory is being rolled out gradually. If you aren't seeing auto memory, you can opt in by setting `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=0` in your environment. ### What Claude remembers As Claude works, it may save things like: * Project patterns: build commands, test conventions, code style preferences * Debugging insights: solutions to tricky problems, common error causes * Architecture notes: key files, module relationships, important abstractions * Your preferences: communication style, workflow habits, tool choices ### Where auto memory is stored Each project gets its own memory directory at `~/.claude/projects//memory/`. The `` path is derived from the git repository root, so all subdirectories within the same repo share one auto memory directory. Git worktrees get separate memory directories. Outside a git repo, the working directory is used instead. The directory contains a `MEMORY.md` entrypoint and optional topic files: ```text theme={null} ~/.claude/projects//memory/ ├── MEMORY.md # Concise index, loaded into every session ├── debugging.md # Detailed notes on debugging patterns ├── api-conventions.md # API design decisions └── ... # Any other topic files Claude creates ``` `MEMORY.md` acts as an index of the memory directory. Claude reads and writes files in this directory throughout your session, using `MEMORY.md` to keep track of what's stored where. ### How it works * The first 200 lines of `MEMORY.md` are loaded into Claude's system prompt at the start of every session. Content beyond 200 lines is not loaded automatically, and Claude is instructed to keep it concise by moving detailed notes into separate topic files. * Topic files like `debugging.md` or `patterns.md` are not loaded at startup. Claude reads them on demand using its standard file tools when it needs the information. * Claude reads and writes memory files during your session, so you'll see memory updates happen as you work. ### Manage auto memory Auto memory files are markdown files you can edit at any time. Use `/memory` to open the file selector, which includes your auto memory entrypoint alongside your CLAUDE.md files. To ask Claude to save something specific, tell it directly: "remember that we use pnpm, not npm" or "save to memory that the API tests require a local Redis instance". When neither variable is set, auto memory follows the gradual rollout. The variable name uses double-negative logic: `DISABLE=0` means "don't disable" and forces auto memory on. ```bash theme={null} export CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1 # Force off export CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=0 # Force on ``` ## CLAUDE.md imports CLAUDE.md files can import additional files using `@path/to/import` syntax. The following example imports 3 files: ``` See @README for project overview and @package.json for available npm commands for this project. # Additional Instructions - git workflow @docs/git-instructions.md ``` Both relative and absolute paths are allowed. Relative paths resolve relative to the file containing the import, not the working directory. For private per-project preferences that shouldn't be checked into version control, prefer `CLAUDE.local.md`: it is automatically loaded and added to `.gitignore`. If you work across multiple git worktrees, `CLAUDE.local.md` only exists in one. Use a home-directory import instead so all worktrees share the same personal instructions: ``` # Individual Preferences - @~/.claude/my-project-instructions.md ``` The first time Claude Code encounters external imports in a project, it shows an approval dialog listing the specific files. Approve to load them; decline to skip them. This is a one-time decision per project: once declined, the dialog does not resurface and the imports remain disabled. To avoid potential collisions, imports are not evaluated inside markdown code spans and code blocks. ``` This code span will not be treated as an import: `@anthropic-ai/claude-code` ``` Imported files can recursively import additional files, with a max-depth of 5 hops. You can see what memory files are loaded by running `/memory` command. ## How Claude looks up memories Claude Code reads memories recursively: starting in the cwd, Claude Code recurses up to (but not including) the root directory */* and reads any CLAUDE.md or CLAUDE.local.md files it finds. This is especially convenient when working in large repositories where you run Claude Code in *foo/bar/*, and have memories in both *foo/CLAUDE.md* and *foo/bar/CLAUDE.md*. Claude will also discover CLAUDE.md nested in subtrees under your current working directory. Instead of loading them at launch, they are only included when Claude reads files in those subtrees. ### Load memory from additional directories The `--add-dir` flag gives Claude access to additional directories outside your main working directory. By default, CLAUDE.md files from these directories are not loaded. To also load memory files (CLAUDE.md, .claude/CLAUDE.md, and .claude/rules/\*.md) from additional directories, set the `CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD` environment variable: ```bash theme={null} CLAUDE_CODE_ADDITIONAL_DIRECTORIES_CLAUDE_MD=1 claude --add-dir ../shared-config ``` ## Directly edit memories with `/memory` Use the `/memory` command during a session to open any memory file in your system editor for more extensive additions or organization. ## Set up project memory Suppose you want to set up a CLAUDE.md file to store important project information, conventions, and frequently used commands. Project memory can be stored in either `./CLAUDE.md` or `./.claude/CLAUDE.md`. Bootstrap a CLAUDE.md for your codebase with the following command: ``` > /init ``` Tips: * Include frequently used commands (build, test, lint) to avoid repeated searches * Document code style preferences and naming conventions * Add important architectural patterns specific to your project * CLAUDE.md memories can be used for both instructions shared with your team and for your individual preferences. ## Modular rules with `.claude/rules/` For larger projects, you can organize instructions into multiple files using the `.claude/rules/` directory. This allows teams to maintain focused, well-organized rule files instead of one large CLAUDE.md. ### Basic structure Place markdown files in your project's `.claude/rules/` directory: ``` your-project/ ├── .claude/ │ ├── CLAUDE.md # Main project instructions │ └── rules/ │ ├── code-style.md # Code style guidelines │ ├── testing.md # Testing conventions │ └── security.md # Security requirements ``` All `.md` files in `.claude/rules/` are automatically loaded as project memory, with the same priority as `.claude/CLAUDE.md`. ### Path-specific rules Rules can be scoped to specific files using YAML frontmatter with the `paths` field. These conditional rules only apply when Claude is working with files matching the specified patterns. ```markdown theme={null} --- paths: - "src/api/**/*.ts" --- # API Development Rules - All API endpoints must include input validation - Use the standard error response format - Include OpenAPI documentation comments ``` Rules without a `paths` field are loaded unconditionally and apply to all files. ### Glob patterns The `paths` field supports standard glob patterns: | Pattern | Matches | | ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | | `**/*.ts` | All TypeScript files in any directory | | `src/**/*` | All files under `src/` directory | | `*.md` | Markdown files in the project root | | `src/components/*.tsx` | React components in a specific directory | You can specify multiple patterns: ```markdown theme={null} --- paths: - "src/**/*.ts" - "lib/**/*.ts" - "tests/**/*.test.ts" --- ``` Brace expansion is supported for matching multiple extensions or directories: ```markdown theme={null} --- paths: - "src/**/*.{ts,tsx}" - "{src,lib}/**/*.ts" --- # TypeScript/React Rules ``` This expands `src/**/*.{ts,tsx}` to match both `.ts` and `.tsx` files. ### Subdirectories Rules can be organized into subdirectories for better structure: ``` .claude/rules/ ├── frontend/ │ ├── react.md │ └── styles.md ├── backend/ │ ├── api.md │ └── database.md └── general.md ``` All `.md` files are discovered recursively. ### Symlinks The `.claude/rules/` directory supports symlinks, allowing you to share common rules across multiple projects: ```bash theme={null} # Symlink a shared rules directory ln -s ~/shared-claude-rules .claude/rules/shared # Symlink individual rule files ln -s ~/company-standards/security.md .claude/rules/security.md ``` Symlinks are resolved and their contents are loaded normally. Circular symlinks are detected and handled gracefully. ### User-level rules You can create personal rules that apply to all your projects in `~/.claude/rules/`: ``` ~/.claude/rules/ ├── preferences.md # Your personal coding preferences └── workflows.md # Your preferred workflows ``` User-level rules are loaded before project rules, giving project rules higher priority. Best practices for `.claude/rules/`: * **Keep rules focused**: Each file should cover one topic (e.g., `testing.md`, `api-design.md`) * **Use descriptive filenames**: The filename should indicate what the rules cover * **Use conditional rules sparingly**: Only add `paths` frontmatter when rules truly apply to specific file types * **Organize with subdirectories**: Group related rules (e.g., `frontend/`, `backend/`) ## Organization-level memory management Organizations can deploy centrally managed CLAUDE.md files that apply to all users. To set up organization-level memory management: 1. Create the managed memory file at the **Managed policy** location shown in the [memory types table above](#determine-memory-type). 2. Deploy via your configuration management system (MDM, Group Policy, Ansible, etc.) to ensure consistent distribution across all developer machines. ## Memory best practices * **Be specific**: "Use 2-space indentation" is better than "Format code properly". * **Use structure to organize**: Format each individual memory as a bullet point and group related memories under descriptive markdown headings. * **Review periodically**: Update memories as your project evolves to ensure Claude is always using the most up to date information and context.

     4→
     5→## Decision: Standard vs Skill
     6→
     7→**Standard** — A short, declarative rule file always loaded into context. Defines constraints and conventions the agent must follow at all times.
     8→
     9→**Skill** — A folder with instructions, scripts, and resources loaded on-demand via progressive disclosure. Provides procedural knowledge activated when a task matches its description.
    10→
    11→### Decision Criteria
    12→
    13→Ask these four questions to decide whether a remediation should produce a standard or a skill:
    14→
    15→1. **Must the agent always know this?** If yes → standard. If it is only relevant during a specific task → skill.
    16→2. **Is it a constraint or a capability?** Constraints and guardrails → standard. Capabilities and workflows → skill.
    17→3. **Does it need bundled resources?** If it requires scripts, templates, or assets → skill. If a single file of rules suffices → standard.
    18→4. **Is it short and declarative?** Bullet-point rules → standard. Procedural paragraphs with sequenced steps → skill.
    19→
    20→### Boundary Rule
    21→
    22→Extract **rules** into a standard and **procedures** into a skill. A single remediation topic can produce both. When in doubt, prefer a standard.
    23→
    24→## Standard Creation
    25→
    26→### Generic Rules
    27→
    28→- Standards must contain a one sentence-summary describing the purpose of the rules, their intent, their rationale, as a short introduction.
    29→- Rules must be a list of bullet-points rules, starting with a verb.
    30→- Use scoped glob patterns when relevant based on the suggestions.

## Part 2 — Headless Mode (`--headless` flag)

### Why

MonoGame requires `GraphicsDevice` to initialize, so we can't fully avoid creating
a window. But we can: (1) make it tiny and invisible, (2) disable VSync and fixed
timestep so it runs at max speed, (3) skip the draw pipeline entirely.

### Changes

**`MonoDreams.Examples/Program.cs`** — pass args to Game1:
```csharp
using var game = new Game1(args);
game.Run();
```

**`MonoDreams.Examples/Game1.cs`** — accept and apply headless mode:
- Constructor: parse `args` for `--headless` flag, store in `_headless` field
- `Initialize()`: if headless, set `Window.Position` off-screen, set
  `_graphics.PreferredBackBufferWidth/Height` to 1×1, disable VSync
  (`SynchronizeWithVerticalRetrace = false`), disable fixed timestep
  (`IsFixedTimeStep = false`)
- `Draw()`: if headless, return immediately (skip `_screenController.Draw()`)
- Keep `Update()` unchanged — full logic pipeline runs

**`MonoDreams.Examples/Screens/LoadLevelExampleGameScreen.cs`** — skip screenshot
system when headless:
- Pass a `bool headless` parameter through the constructor chain (Game1 → screen registration lambda)
- In `CreateDrawSystem()`: only create `ScreenshotCaptureSystem` when `!headless`
- Actually, since `Draw()` is skipped entirely in headless mode, the draw pipeline
  never runs. So no changes needed here — the screenshot system just never fires.

**Net effect:** Only `Program.cs` and `Game1.cs` need changes for headless mode.

|------|--------|

## Part 3 — Log Assertion Helpers

### `MonoDreams.Tests/GameTestRunner.cs` (new)

A helper class that:
1. Creates a temp directory for test output
2. Writes an `input_replay.json` file from a provided `InputReplayPlan` object
   (or raw JSON string)
3. Spawns `dotnet run --project MonoDreams.Examples -- --headless` as a `Process`
   with working directory set to the repo root
4. Waits for exit with a configurable timeout (default 30s)
5. Reads the log file from the temp debug dir
6. Returns a `GameTestResult` with:
   - `ExitCode` (int)
   - `LogLines` (List<string>)
   - helper methods: `AssertLogContains(substring)`,
     `AssertLogContainsInOrder(params string[])`, `GetLogLines(LogLevel)`

### Problem: debug dir location

The game writes to `{AppDomain.BaseDirectory}/debug/`. When spawned via
`dotnet run`, that's `MonoDreams.Examples/bin/Debug/net8.0/debug/`. The test
runner knows this path and reads from it.

But multiple tests running in parallel would conflict. Solution: have the test
runner set an environment variable `MONODREAMS_DEBUG_DIR` to a unique temp path,
and have `Game1.Initialize()` prefer that over the default.

### Changes to Game1

In `Game1.Initialize()`:
```csharp

    ?? Path.Combine(AppDomain.CurrentDomain.BaseDirectory, "debug");
```

| `MonoDreams.Tests/GameTestRunner.cs` | **New** — process launcher + log reader |

   113→## Coding Conventions
   114→
   115→### Python
   116→- Line length: 100 (Black + Ruff)

   118→- Classes: PascalCase, functions: snake_case, constants: UPPER_SNAKE_CASE
   119→- Linting rules: E, F, I, W (Ruff)

   122→### TypeScript/React
   123→- Strict mode enabled

   126→- Components: PascalCase filenames
   127→
   128→### API Design
   129→- RESTful routes under `/api/v1/{resource}/{action}`
   130→- API version: v0.2.0
   131→- Auto-docs at `/docs` (Swagger) and `/redoc`
   132→
   133→## Environment Variables
   134→
   135→Key variables (see `.env.example` for full list):
   136→- `NEO4J_URI`, `NEO4J_USER`, `NEO4J_PASSWORD` - Database
   137→- `OPENROUTER_API_KEY` - LLM provider
   138→- `CONTEXT_MODEL`, `REVIEW_MODEL` - Model selection
   139→- `GITHUB_APP_ID`, `GITHUB_PRIVATE_KEY_PATH`, `GITHUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET` - GitHub App
   140→- `ENABLE_LOGFIRE`, `LOGFIRE_TOKEN` - Observability
   141→
   142→## Architecture Notes
   143→
   144→- **Layered backend**: Routers → Services → Queries → Neo4j Client
   145→- **Multi-agent reviews**: Bug-hunter + Security-auditor run in parallel, results deduplicated
   146→- **Incremental ingestion**: Push webhooks trigger partial graph updates (not full re-ingestion)
   147→- **Graph model**: 14+ node types with constraints and full-text indexes
   148→- **17 language parsers**: Each in `ingestion/languages/` with Tree-sitter queries
   149→
   150→## Graph Schema (Actual — as created by ingestion)
   151→
   152→Node types: `Function`, `Class`, `File`, `Variable`, `Module`, `Repository`
   153→
   154→Key relationships:
   155→- `(File)-[:CONTAINS]->(Function|Class|Variable)` — NOT `[:DEFINES]`
   156→- `(Class)-[:CONTAINS]->(Function)` — class methods are `Function` nodes, NOT `Method` nodes
   157→- `(Function)-[:CALLS]->(Function)` — call edges with optional `line_number` property
   158→- `(Class)-[:INHERITS]->(Class)` — inheritance
   159→- `(Repository)-[:CONTAINS]->(File)` — repo scoping
   160→- `(File)-[:IMPORTS]->(Module)` — import edges with `alias`, `imported_name`, `line_number` properties on the relationship
   161→- `(Class)-[:INCLUDES]->(Module)` — Ruby mixin includes
   162→
   163→Module nodes represent either directory paths OR external package names (e.g. `fastapi`, `react`). Properties: `name` (unique), `lang`.
   164→
   165→**Does NOT exist**: `Method` nodes, `CodeLine` nodes, `[:DEFINES]`, `[:REFERENCES]`, `[:HAS_IMPORT]`, dedicated `Import` nodes.
   166→
   167→## CodeFinder APIs (`/api/v1/query/code-finder/*`)
   168→
   169→All endpoints live in `api/routers/query.py` and delegate to `api/services/code_search.py` (`CodeFinder` class).
   170→
   171→| Endpoint | Query strategy | Notes |
   172→|---|---|---|
   173→| `/function?name=` | `MATCH (Function {name:$name})` | Exact match. Add `&fuzzy=true` for fulltext. |
   174→| `/class?name=` | `MATCH (Class {name:$name})` | Same as above. |
   175→| `/variable?name=` | `Variable.name CONTAINS $term` | Substring scan, no fulltext index. |
   176→| `/content?query=` | `code_search` fulltext → CONTAINS fallback | Searches name + docstring + source_code of Function/Class/Variable. |
   177→| `/line?query=` | `file_content_search` fulltext → File CONTAINS fallback | Arbitrary code line search across File.source_code. Returns path + line_number + match_line only (no source dump). |
   178→| `/peek?path=&line=&above=&below=` | Fetches File.source_code, slices window | Language-agnostic. Pair with `/line` or `/search` for inline browsing. |
   179→| `/module?name=` | `Module.name CONTAINS $term` | Returns module + files that import it. Module nodes = directory paths OR package names. |
   180→| `/imports?name=` | `(File)-[:IMPORTS]->(Module)` CONTAINS on module name, imported_name, alias | Substring match on all three fields. Returns module_name + imported_name + alias + file path + line. |
   181→| `/complexity?function_name=` | `MATCH (Function {name:$name})` + optional `&path=` filter | Returns score for one function. Use `&path=` when name exists in multiple files. |
   182→| `/complexity/top?limit=` | ORDER BY cyclomatic_complexity DESC, is_dependency=false | Default limit 10. Only your code, not dependencies. |
   183→
   184→## Metrics APIs (`/api/v1/query/stats`, `/metrics`, `/language/stats`)
   185→
   186→| Endpoint | What it returns |
   187→|---|---|
   188→| `GET /query/stats` | Total node counts across entire graph: functions, classes, files, variables, imports, repositories |
   189→| `GET /query/metrics` | Same as stats. Add `?repo_id=owner/repo` to scope to one repository. |
   190→| `GET /query/language/stats` | Per-language breakdown: file_count, function_count, class_count. Add `?language=Python` to filter. |
   191→
   192→## Cyclomatic Complexity
   193→
   194→Calculated at **ingestion time** by Tree-sitter parsers. Stored as `Function.cyclomatic_complexity` (integer).
   195→
   196→**Formula**: starts at 1, +1 for each: `if`, `for`, `while`, `except`, `with`, `boolean_operator` (`and`/`or`), list comprehension, `case` clause.
   197→
   198→**Language support**:
   199→- Full calculation: Python, TypeScript, C
   200→- Defaults to `1`: all other languages (C++, Java, Go, Rust, etc.)
   201→
   202→**Score interpretation**:
   203→- 1–5: Simple, easy to test
   204→- 6–10: Moderate, worth reviewing
   205→- 11–20: Complex, refactor candidate
   206→- 20+: Very high risk — bugs likely here
   207→
   208→## Full-Text Search Architecture (Two-Tier)
   209→
   210→Neo4j fulltext indexes:
   211→- `code_search` — covers `Function`, `Class`, `Method`, `Variable` nodes on `name`, `docstring`, `source_code`
   212→- `file_content_search` — covers `File` nodes on `source_code`
   213→
   214→Search strategy in `db/queries.py` `search_code()`:
   215→1. Query `code_search` index first (symbol names, docstrings)
   216→2. If empty, fall back to `file_content_search` (arbitrary code lines)
   217→3. Lucene escaping: simple identifiers → phrase search `"..."`, special-char queries → AND-keyword strategy `token1 AND token2`
   218→4. Returns lean results: `path`, `line_number`, `match_line` — no full source_code dump
   219→
   220→Peek API (`/code-finder/peek`): language-agnostic line-window fetcher. Takes `path`, `line`, `above`, `below`. Used for interactive code navigation in the frontend.
   221→
   222→## Key Endpoints
   223→
   224→| Method | Path | Description |
   225→|--------|------|-------------|
   226→| POST | `/api/v1/ingest/repository` | Ingest a repository |
   227→| POST | `/api/v1/ingest/setup` | Initialize DB schema |
   228→| GET | `/api/v1/query/search` | Full-text code search (auto-fallback symbol→file content) |
   229→| GET | `/api/v1/query/search-symbols` | Symbol-only search |
   230→| GET | `/api/v1/query/stats` | Total node counts (functions, classes, files, etc.) |
   231→| GET | `/api/v1/query/metrics` | Same as stats, supports `?repo_id=` scoping |
   232→| GET | `/api/v1/query/language/stats` | Per-language file/function/class counts |
   233→| GET | `/api/v1/query/method-usages` | Find all callers of a function |
   234→| GET | `/api/v1/query/find_callers` | Find callers of a symbol |
   235→| GET | `/api/v1/query/class_hierarchy` | Class inheritance hierarchy |
   236→| GET | `/api/v1/query/change_impact` | Change impact analysis |
   237→| GET | `/api/v1/query/code-finder/line` | Search file content (raw line search) |
   238→| GET | `/api/v1/query/code-finder/peek` | Peek lines around a file location |
   239→| GET | `/api/v1/query/code-finder/complexity` | Cyclomatic complexity for one function |
   240→| GET | `/api/v1/query/code-finder/complexity/top` | Top N most complex functions (your code only) |
   241→| GET | `/api/v1/repositories/` | List repositories |
   242→| POST | `/api/v1/webhook/onPush` | GitHub push webhook |
   243→| POST | `/api/v1/webhook/onComment` | GitHub PR comment webhook |
   244→
   245→## Cost & Token Pitfalls
   246→
   247→- NEVER use a polling/orchestrator LLM for fixed workflows — use `asyncio.gather` + direct agent calls
   248→- `pydantic_deep` pattern burned $6.33/review (700K tokens) — `check_task` returned full diff on every poll
   249→- Correct pattern: `deepagent/agent/review_pipeline.py` — 2 direct `Agent.run()` calls via `asyncio.gather`

## Graph Schema (Actual — as created by ingestion)

Node types: `Function`, `Class`, `File`, `Variable`, `Module`, `Repository`

Key relationships:
- `(File)-[:CONTAINS]->(Function|Class|Variable)` — new ingestion path
- `(File)-[:DEFINES]->(Function|Class)` — old ingestion path (both exist in graph)
- `(Class)-[:CONTAINS]->(Function)` — class methods are `Function` nodes, NOT `Method` nodes
- `(Function)-[:CALLS]->(Function)` — call edges with optional `line_number` property
- `(Class)-[:INHERITS]->(Class)` — inheritance
- `(Repository)-[:CONTAINS]->(File)` — repo scoping
- `(File)-[:IMPORTS]->(Module)` — import edges with `alias`, `imported_name`, `line_number` on the relationship
- `(Class)-[:INCLUDES]->(Module)` — Ruby mixin includes

Module nodes represent either directory paths OR external package names (e.g. `fastapi`, `react`). Properties: `name` (unique), `lang`.

**Does NOT exist**: `Method` nodes, `CodeLine` nodes, `[:REFERENCES]`, `[:HAS_IMPORT]`, dedicated `Import` nodes.

### Dual-Property Compatibility (Critical)

Different ingestion paths write different property names. Cypher queries MUST use `coalesce()`:

| Property | New ingestion | Old ingestion | Cypher pattern |
|---|---|---|---|
| Source code | `node.source_code` | `node.source` | `coalesce(n.source_code, n.source)` |
| Line number | `node.line_number` | `node.line_start` | `coalesce(n.line_number, n.line_start)` |
| File relation | `[:CONTAINS]` | `[:DEFINES]` | `OPTIONAL MATCH` both patterns |

Frontend helper in `query/page.tsx`:
```ts
function getNodeSource(item: Record<string, unknown>): string | null {
  return (item.source_code as string) || (item.source as string) || null;
}
```

## CodeFinder APIs (`/api/v1/query/code-finder/*`)

All endpoints live in `api/routers/query.py` and delegate to `ingestion/code_search.py` (`CodeFinder` class).
The `CodeFinder` class stores source under `node.source` (not `node.source_code`).

| Endpoint | Query strategy | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `/function?name=` | `MATCH (Function {name:$name})` | Exact match. Add `&fuzzy=true` for fulltext. |
| `/class?name=` | `MATCH (Class {name:$name})` | Same as above. |
| `/variable?name=` | `Variable.name CONTAINS $term` | Substring scan, no fulltext index. |
| `/content?query=` | `code_search` fulltext → CONTAINS fallback | Searches name + docstring + source_code of Function/Class/Variable. |
| `/line?query=` | `file_content_search` fulltext → File CONTAINS fallback | Arbitrary code line search across File.source_code. Returns path + line_number + match_line only (no source dump). |
| `/peek?path=&line=&above=&below=` | Fetches File.source_code, slices window | Language-agnostic. Pair with `/line` or `/search` for inline browsing. Max above/below = 200. |
| `/module?name=` | `Module.name CONTAINS $term` | Returns module + files that import it. Module nodes = directory paths OR package names. |
| `/imports?name=` | `(File)-[:IMPORTS]->(Module)` CONTAINS on module name, imported_name, alias | Substring match on all three fields. Returns module_name + imported_name + alias + file path + line. |
| `/complexity?function_name=` | `MATCH (Function {name:$name})` + optional `&path=` filter | Returns score for one function. Use `&path=` when name exists in multiple files. |
| `/complexity/top?limit=` | ORDER BY cyclomatic_complexity DESC, is_dependency=false | Default limit 10. Only your code, not dependencies. |

## Cyclomatic Complexity

Calculated at **ingestion time** by Tree-sitter parsers. Stored as `Function.cyclomatic_complexity` (integer).

**Formula**: starts at 1, +1 for each: `if`, `for`, `while`, `except`, `with`, `boolean_operator` (`and`/`or`), list comprehension, `case` clause.

**Language support**:
- Full calculation: Python, TypeScript, C
- Defaults to `1`: all other languages (C++, Java, Go, Rust, etc.)

**Score interpretation**:
- 1–5: Simple, easy to test
- 6–10: Moderate, worth reviewing
- 11–20: Complex, refactor candidate
- 20+: Very high risk — bugs likely here

## Full-Text Search Architecture (Two-Tier)

Neo4j fulltext indexes:
- `code_search` — covers `Function`, `Class`, `Variable` nodes on `name`, `docstring`, `source_code`
- `file_content_search` — covers `File` nodes on `source_code`

Search strategy in `db/queries.py` `search_code()`:
1. Query `code_search` index first (symbol names, docstrings)
2. If empty, fall back to `file_content_search` (arbitrary code lines)
3. Lucene escaping: simple identifiers → phrase search `"..."`, special-char queries → AND-keyword strategy `token1 AND token2`
4. Returns lean results: `path`, `line_number`, `match_line` — no full source_code dump

Peek API (`/code-finder/peek`): language-agnostic line-window fetcher. Takes `path`, `line`, `above`, `below`. Used for interactive code navigation in the frontend. When a node has no stored `source_code`/`source`, the frontend uses PeekViewer as a fallback (requires `file_path` + `line_number` to be known).

   103→## Architecture
   104→
   105→### Core Data Flow
   106→
   107→1. **User Input** → User adds ingredients to pantry, sets preferences (people count, meal count, diet, language)
   108→2. **Mode Selection** → User chooses Copy & Paste mode (default, secure) or API Key mode
   109→3. **API Call** → `generateRecipes()` in `src/services/llm.ts` sends structured prompt to Gemini API (or user manually copies prompt)
   110→4. **Response Parsing** → JSON response is parsed into `MealPlan` type containing recipes and shopping list
   111→5. **State Management** → SettingsContext + App.tsx manage state using React hooks (no external state library)
   112→6. **Rendering** → Components display recipes and shopping list with internationalized text
   113→
   114→### Key Technical Details
   115→
   116→**Dual Operation Modes**
   117→- **Copy & Paste Mode** (default): No API key stored. User copies prompt to external AI and pastes response back. More secure.
   118→- **API Key Mode**: Stores Gemini API key in localStorage (with security warning). Direct API calls from browser.
   119→
   120→**LLM Integration (`src/services/llm.ts`)**
   121→- Uses Google Gemini Flash 3 Preview model (`gemini-3-flash-preview`)
   122→- Base URL: `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models`
   123→- Request timeout: 60 seconds
   124→- `buildRecipePrompt()` creates structured prompt with pantry items, dietary preferences, spices
   125→- `parseRecipeResponse()` cleans markdown code blocks and parses JSON
   126→- Tracks which pantry items are used via IDs to minimize waste
   127→
   128→**Recipe Sharing (`src/utils/sharing.ts`)**
   129→- Recipes shareable via URL parameter `?recipe=<base64>`
   130→- Shopping lists via `?shoppingList=<base64>`
   131→- Uses TextEncoder for UTF-8 safe base64 encoding
   132→- No backend required for sharing functionality
   133→
   134→**State Management (`src/contexts/SettingsContext.tsx`)**
   135→- Provides global settings: `useCopyPaste`, `apiKey`, `people`, `meals`, `diet`, `styleWishes`, `language`
   136→- Auto-detects browser language
   137→- All settings persist to localStorage
   138→
   139→**ID Generation (`src/utils/idGenerator.ts`)**
   140→- Uses Web Crypto API `crypto.randomUUID()` for generating unique IDs
   141→
   142→**Internationalization (`src/constants/translations.ts`)**
   143→- Supports: English, German, Spanish, French
   144→- 200+ translation keys covering all UI text
   145→- LLM is instructed to generate recipe content in selected language
   146→- Type-safe access via translations object
   147→
   148→**Styling Architecture**
   149→- Tailwind CSS 4.x with Vite plugin
   150→- Glass-morphism effects via custom CSS classes in `src/index.css`
   151→- CSS custom properties (HSL-based) for theming
   152→- Dark mode support via `prefers-color-scheme: dark`
   153→- Framer Motion for animations
   154→

   156→
   157→```
   158→App.tsx                     # Main app, routing (normal/shared recipe/shared shopping list views)
   159→├─ Header.tsx               # Sticky header with mode toggle, API key input, language selector

   161→├─ PantryInput.tsx          # Add/remove ingredients from pantry (collapsible)

   164→│                           #   wake lock, nutrition info, JSON-LD schema, share button
   165→├─ ShoppingList.tsx         # Checkbox-based shopping list with persistence
   166→├─ WelcomeDialog.tsx        # Onboarding dialog (dismissible)
   167→├─ CopyPasteDialog.tsx      # Two-step dialog for Copy & Paste mode

   177→### Security Features
   178→

   181→  - `script-src 'self'` prevents inline scripts

   118→## Architecture
   119→
   120→### Core Data Flow
   121→
   122→1. **User Input** → User adds ingredients to pantry, sets preferences (people count, meal count, diet, language)
   123→2. **Mode Selection** → User chooses Copy & Paste mode (default, secure) or API Key mode
   124→3. **API Call** → `generateRecipes()` in `src/services/llm.ts` sends structured prompt to Gemini API (or user manually copies prompt)
   125→4. **Response Parsing** → JSON response is parsed into `MealPlan` type containing recipes and shopping list
   126→5. **State Management** → SettingsContext + App.tsx manage state using React hooks (no external state library)
   127→6. **Rendering** → Components display recipes and shopping list with internationalized text
   128→
   129→### Key Technical Details
   130→
   131→**Dual Operation Modes**
   132→- **Copy & Paste Mode** (default): No API key stored. User copies prompt to external AI and pastes response back. More secure.
   133→- **API Key Mode**: Stores Gemini API key in localStorage (with security warning). Direct API calls from browser.
   134→
   135→**LLM Integration (`src/services/llm.ts`)**
   136→- Uses Google Gemini Flash 3 Preview model (`gemini-3-flash-preview`)
   137→- Base URL: `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models`
   138→- Request timeout: 60 seconds
   139→- `buildRecipePrompt()` creates structured prompt with pantry items, dietary preferences, spices
   140→- `parseRecipeResponse()` cleans markdown code blocks and validates JSON with Zod schemas
   141→- `sanitizeUserInput()` prevents prompt injection (strips newlines, control chars, limits length)
   142→- Zod schemas (`MealPlanSchema`, `RecipeSchema`, `IngredientSchema`, `NutritionSchema`) provide runtime validation
   143→- Tracks which pantry items are used via IDs to minimize waste
   144→
   145→**Recipe Sharing (`src/utils/sharing.ts`)**
   146→- Recipes shareable via URL parameter `?recipe=<base64>`
   147→- Shopping lists via `?shoppingList=<base64>`
   148→- Uses TextEncoder for UTF-8 safe base64 encoding
   149→- No backend required for sharing functionality
   150→
   151→**State Management (`src/contexts/SettingsContext.tsx`)**
   152→- Provides global settings: `useCopyPaste`, `apiKey`, `people`, `meals`, `diet`, `styleWishes`, `language`
   153→- Auto-detects browser language
   154→- All settings persist to localStorage
   155→
   156→**ID Generation (`src/utils/idGenerator.ts`)**
   157→- Uses Web Crypto API `crypto.randomUUID()` for generating unique IDs
   158→
   159→**Internationalization (`src/constants/translations.ts`)**
   160→- Supports: English, German, Spanish, French
   161→- 200+ translation keys covering all UI text
   162→- LLM is instructed to generate recipe content in selected language
   163→- Type-safe access via translations object
   164→
   165→**Custom Hooks (`src/hooks/`)**
   166→- `useLocalStorage<T>(key, initialValue)` - Generic JSON persistence hook; also `useStringLocalStorage()` for plain strings
   167→- `useWakeLock()` - Wake Lock API wrapper (keeps screen on during cooking, auto-reacquires on visibility change)
   168→- `useFocusTrap(onClose)` - Accessibility focus trap for dialogs (Tab/Shift+Tab cycling, Escape to close, restores previous focus)
   169→
   170→**Utilities (`src/utils/`)**
   171→- `idGenerator.ts` - UUID generation via `crypto.randomUUID()`
   172→- `sharing.ts` - URL base64 encoding/decoding with Zod schema validation for shared recipes and shopping lists
   173→- `shoppingListHelpers.ts` - `getItemKey()` for unique item keys, `listsMatch()` for list comparison
   174→
   175→**Constants (`src/constants/index.ts`)**
   176→- `STORAGE_KEYS` - All localStorage key names (avoids magic strings)
   177→- `API_CONFIG` - Base URL, model name, timeout, key URL
   178→- `DEFAULTS` - Default values for people count, meals, diet, language
   179→- `VALIDATION` - Input length limits
   180→- `URL_PARAMS` - URL parameter names for sharing
   181→
   182→**Styling Architecture**
   183→- Tailwind CSS 4.x with Vite plugin
   184→- Glass-morphism effects via custom CSS classes in `src/index.css`
   185→- CSS custom properties (HSL-based) for theming
   186→- Dark mode support via `prefers-color-scheme: dark`
   187→- Framer Motion for animations

## Project Overview

AI Recipe Planner is a React-based meal planning application that uses AI (Google Gemini API) to generate personalized recipes based on available pantry ingredients. The app supports multiple languages (English, German, Spanish, French) and dietary preferences, and includes recipe sharing functionality via URL parameters.

- **Hosting**: Static site deployed on GitHub Pages at `/ai-recipe-planner/`
- **Target Audience**: Primarily for personal use
- **UX Philosophy**: Usability is key. Minimize clicks and scrolling. All settings persist to localStorage so users can jump straight to recipe generation.

**Current version**: 1.0.2

## Tech Stack

- **Framework**: React 19 + TypeScript
- **Build Tool**: Vite 7
- **Styling**: Tailwind CSS 4 (Vite plugin, CSS-based config in `src/index.css`)
- **Animations**: Framer Motion
- **Icons**: Lucide React
- **LLM Provider**: Google Gemini API (`gemini-3-flash-preview`)
- **Validation**: Zod 4 (runtime validation of LLM responses)
- **Linting**: ESLint 9 (flat config) with TypeScript-ESLint
- **Testing**: Vitest 4 + Testing Library + MSW
- **Package Manager**: npm

## Architecture

### Core Data Flow

1. **User Input** → User adds ingredients to pantry, sets preferences (people count, meal count, diet, language)
2. **Mode Selection** → User chooses Copy & Paste mode (default, secure) or API Key mode
3. **API Call** → `generateRecipes()` in `src/services/llm.ts` sends structured prompt to Gemini API (or user manually copies prompt)
4. **Response Parsing** → JSON response is validated with Zod schemas and parsed into `MealPlan` type
5. **State Management** → SettingsContext + App.tsx manage state using React hooks (no external state library)
6. **Rendering** → Components display recipes and shopping list with internationalized text

### Key Technical Details

**Dual Operation Modes**
- **Copy & Paste Mode** (default): No API key stored. User copies prompt to external AI and pastes response back. More secure.
- **API Key Mode**: Stores Gemini API key in localStorage (with security warning). Direct API calls from browser.

**LLM Integration (`src/services/llm.ts`)**
- Uses Google Gemini Flash 3 Preview model (`gemini-3-flash-preview`)
- Base URL: `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models`
- Request timeout: 60 seconds
- `buildRecipePrompt()` creates structured prompt with pantry items, dietary preferences, spices
- `parseRecipeResponse()` cleans markdown code blocks and validates JSON with Zod schemas
- `sanitizeUserInput()` prevents prompt injection (strips newlines, control chars, limits length)
- Zod schemas (`MealPlanSchema`, `RecipeSchema`, `IngredientSchema`, `NutritionSchema`) provide runtime validation
- Tracks which pantry items are used via IDs to minimize waste

**State Management (`src/contexts/SettingsContext.tsx`)**
- Provides global settings: `useCopyPaste`, `apiKey`, `people`, `meals`, `diet`, `styleWishes`, `language`
- Auto-detects browser language
- All settings persist to localStorage

**Internationalization (`src/constants/translations.ts`)**
- Supports: English, German, Spanish, French
- 200+ translation keys covering all UI text
- LLM is instructed to generate recipe content in selected language
- Type-safe access via translations object

**Custom Hooks (`src/hooks/`)**
- `useLocalStorage<T>(key, initialValue)` - Generic JSON persistence hook; also `useStringLocalStorage()` for plain strings
- `useWakeLock()` - Wake Lock API wrapper (keeps screen on during cooking, auto-reacquires on visibility change)
- `useFocusTrap(onClose)` - Accessibility focus trap for dialogs (Tab/Shift+Tab cycling, Escape to close, restores previous focus)

**Utilities (`src/utils/`)**
- `idGenerator.ts` - UUID generation via `crypto.randomUUID()`
- `sharing.ts` - URL base64 encoding/decoding with Zod schema validation for shared recipes and shopping lists
- `shoppingListHelpers.ts` - `getItemKey()` for unique item keys, `listsMatch()` for list comparison

**Constants (`src/constants/index.ts`)**
- `STORAGE_KEYS` - All localStorage key names (avoids magic strings)
- `API_CONFIG` - Base URL, model name, timeout, key URL
- `DEFAULTS` - Default values for people count, meals, diet, language
- `VALIDATION` - Input length limits
- `URL_PARAMS` - URL parameter names for sharing

**Styling**
- Tailwind CSS 4.x with Vite plugin (no `tailwind.config.js` — uses CSS-based config)
- Glass-morphism effects via custom CSS classes in `src/index.css`
- CSS custom properties (HSL-based) for theming
- Dark mode support via `prefers-color-scheme: dark`
- Framer Motion for animations

### Component Structure

```
App.tsx                     # Main app, routing (normal/shared recipe/shared shopping list views)
├─ Header.tsx               # Sticky header with mode toggle, API key input, language selector
├─ SettingsPanel.tsx        # Diet, style wishes, people/meals count (collapsible)
├─ PantryInput.tsx          # Add/remove ingredients from pantry (collapsible)
├─ SpiceRack.tsx            # Manage staples/spices always available (collapsible)
├─ RecipeCard.tsx           # Recipe display with ingredient strikethrough, step highlighting,
│                           #   wake lock, nutrition info, JSON-LD schema, share button
├─ ShoppingList.tsx         # Checkbox-based shopping list with persistence
├─ WelcomeDialog.tsx        # Onboarding dialog (dismissible)
├─ CopyPasteDialog.tsx      # Two-step dialog for Copy & Paste mode
├─ ApiKeySecurityDialog.tsx # Security warning when enabling API Key mode
├─ ClearApiKeyDialog.tsx    # Choice dialog for clearing or keeping stored API key
└─ ErrorBoundary.tsx        # Error boundary with refresh button
```

**Reusable UI Components (`src/components/ui/`)**
- `PanelHeader.tsx` - Header with icon, title, minimize button, tooltip
- `TooltipButton.tsx` - Polymorphic button/link/span with tooltip support

### Data Types

```typescript
interface PantryItem {
  id: string;
  name: string;
  amount: string;
}

interface Recipe {
  id: string;
  title: string;
  time: string;
  ingredients: Ingredient[];
  instructions: string[];
  usedIngredients: string[];        // IDs of pantry items used
  missingIngredients?: Ingredient[]; // Optional: excluded in shared recipes
  nutrition?: Nutrition;
  comments?: string;                // Optional fun fact or remark from the LLM
}

interface Ingredient {
  item: string;
  amount: string;
  unit?: string;
}

interface Nutrition {
  calories: number;
  carbs: number;    // grams
  fat: number;      // grams
  protein: number;  // grams
}

interface MealPlan {
  recipes: Recipe[];
  shoppingList: Ingredient[];
}

interface Notification {
  message: string;
  type: 'error' | 'undo';
  action?: {
    label: string;
    onClick: () => void;
    ariaLabel?: string;
  };
  timeout?: number; // Auto-dismiss after X milliseconds
}
```

### Security Features

- **Content Security Policy** in `index.html`:
  - `connect-src` allows only Gemini API
  - `script-src 'self'` prevents inline scripts
- **Input sanitization** via `sanitizeUserInput()` prevents prompt injection
- **API Key Security Dialog** warns about plain-text localStorage storage
- **XSS Protection** escapes `</script>` in JSON-LD schema output
- **Copy & Paste mode** avoids storing credentials entirely

### Advanced Features

- **Wake Lock API** - Keep screen on during cooking (button on recipe cards)
- **JSON-LD Schema** - Generates Recipe schema markup for SEO/social sharing
- **Ingredient strikethrough** - Click ingredients to mark as added
- **Active step highlighting** - Click instructions to highlight current step
- **Decoupled shopping lists** - Shared shopping lists maintain separate checkbox state

### When Writing Tests

1→# CLAUDE.md
     2→
     3→This file provides guidance to Claude Code (`claude.ai/code`) when working in this repository.
     4→
     5→## Commands
     6→
     7→```bash
     8→uv sync                                           # Install runtime + dev dependencies
     9→uv run pytest                                     # Run full test suite
    10→uv run pytest tests/test_cli.py                   # Run one test module
    11→uv run pytest -k "optimize"                       # Run tests by pattern
    12→uv run optimize-anything --help                   # CLI entry point
    13→uv run optimize-anything score FILE --evaluator-command bash eval.sh  # Score one artifact
    14→uv run python scripts/check.py                    # Unified gate: pytest + smoke + score_check
    15→uv run python scripts/check.py --skip-smoke       # Unified gate without smoke (offline)
    16→uv run python scripts/smoke_harness.py --budget 1 # CLI smoke check
    17→uv run python scripts/score_check.py              # Score regression check
    18→uv run python scripts/score_check.py --update     # Update baselines after improvement
    19→```
    20→
    21→## Architecture
    22→
    23→`optimize-anything` is a Claude Code plugin + CLI wrapper around `gepa.optimize_anything()`:
    24→
    25→- `gepa` performs propose/evaluate/reflect optimization.
    26→- This repo provides evaluator adapters, intake normalization, generation helpers, and delivery surfaces.
    27→
    28→Core evaluator protocol:
    29→
    30→```text
    31→evaluator(candidate: str) -> tuple[float, dict]
    32→```
    33→
    34→Input/output contract for external evaluators:
    35→- Input: `{"candidate": "<text>"}` (stdin for command mode, POST JSON for http mode)
    36→- Output: JSON object with required numeric `score` and optional diagnostic keys
    37→
    38→## Delivery Surfaces
    39→
    40→- `src/optimize_anything/cli.py`
    41→  - Subcommands: `optimize`, `generate-evaluator`, `intake`, `explain`, `budget`, `score`
    42→  - Supports evaluator source flags (`--evaluator-command` or `--evaluator-url`)
    43→  - Supports intake flags (`--intake-json`, `--intake-file`) and `--evaluator-cwd`
    44→
    45→- `src/optimize_anything/evaluators.py`
    46→  - `command_evaluator(...)`, `http_evaluator(...)`, strict score validation
    47→
    48→- `src/optimize_anything/intake.py`
    49→  - Normalizes intake schema and validates:
    50→    - `artifact_class`
    51→    - `quality_dimensions`
    52→    - `hard_constraints`
    53→    - `evaluation_pattern` (`verification|judge|simulation|composite`)
    54→    - `execution_mode` (`command|http`)
    55→    - `evaluator_cwd`
    56→
    57→- `src/optimize_anything/result_contract.py`
    58→  - Canonical optimize summary for CLI output
    59→
    60→## Important Distinction
    61→
    62→- `execution_mode` / runtime type: transport and execution path (`command` vs `http`)
    63→- `evaluation_pattern`: scoring strategy intent (`verification`, `judge`, `simulation`, `composite`)
    64→
    65→Do not conflate these in docs or implementation.
    66→
    67→## Plugin Structure
    68→
    69→```text
    70→.claude-plugin/plugin.json
    71→commands/optimize.md
    72→skills/generate-evaluator/
    73→skills/optimization-guide/
    74→```
    75→
    76→## Testing Notes
    77→
    78→- Use `pytest`.
    79→- CLI tests call `main(argv)`.
    80→- Evaluator tests include command, HTTP, timeout, and malformed payload cases.
    81→- Doc drift checks live in `tests/test_doc_contract.py`.
    82→
    83→## Dependencies
    84→
    85→- `gepa` (optimization engine)
    86→- `httpx` (HTTP evaluator client)
    87→- `litellm` (runtime dependency required for live optimization flows)
    88→

1→# [Unreleased]
     2→
     3→## Added
     4→
     5→- **Multi-remediation support**: Users can now run multiple independent remediations per evaluation. Each remediation runs from the current git state and produces its own downloadable patch. Past remediations are displayed in a collapsible history section above the config area, with compact cards that expand to show full diffs and action summaries. The 409 guard blocking new remediations when a completed one exists has been removed; only concurrent remediations are prevented.
     6→- **Target agent selection for remediation**: Replace 2-option file type selector (AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md) with 3 target agents (AGENTS.md, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot). Suggestion remediation now routes output to structured artifacts (standards, skills, or generic updates) with per-agent file path conventions and format templates. Error fix remediation now includes output type routing (standard, skill, or generic), matching the suggestion enrichment framework.
     7→- **Import JSON reports in Web UI**: Upload CLI-generated JSON reports (`--report json`) into the Web UI for viewing and persistence without re-running the evaluation. Available in non-cloud mode via the "Import JSON" tab on the home page. Imported evaluations are marked with an "Imported" badge in the history list.
     8→- **Re-run evaluation from summary page**: "Re-run" button in the evaluation summary header allows re-running the same repository without navigating back to the home page, with an inline provider selector in non-cloud mode
     9→- **Remediation module redesign**: Issue-level selection workflow replaces evaluator-checklist approach
    10→  - "Add to remediate" (+) button on each issue card in Errors and Suggestions tabs
    11→  - "Add all to remediation" bulk action button in each tab
    12→  - Remediate tab shows compact selected issues list grouped by type (errors/suggestions)
    13→  - Badge count on Remediate tab showing number of selected issues
    14→  - SelectionSummaryBar "Remediate" action navigates directly to the Remediate tab
    15→  - Individual issue removal from remediation queue via (X) button
    16→- **Context tab**: Move context files from Summary tab into a dedicated "Context" tab with tool-specific sections (AGENTS.md, Claude Code, GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Linked Docs). Each section groups its related items (e.g., Claude Code shows CLAUDE.md, Rules, and Skills). Uses the official Claude logo for the Claude Code section. Content browser modals now auto-select when only one item is present.
    17→- **Remediation impact evaluation**: "Evaluate Impact" button on each completed remediation card that clones the repo, applies the remediation patch, runs a full 17-evaluator analysis, and displays a before/after score comparison directly on the Remediate tab. Supports idempotent re-evaluation (returns existing result if already run), concurrent execution guard, and automatic cleanup of patched clone directories.
    18→- **Re-evaluation badges in UI**: Impact evaluations created from remediations are now visually distinguished from regular evaluations. A "Re-evaluation" badge with a link icon appears in the Latest Evaluations list, clicking it navigates to the original (parent) evaluation. The Summary tab shows a banner with the original score comparison (e.g., "7.1 → 8.4 (+1.3)").
    19→- Run suggestion evaluators when no AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md files are found, providing actionable suggestions about what documentation to create
    20→- OpenAI Codex provider (`--agent codex`)
    21→- `--concurrency` CLI option to control parallel evaluator execution
    22→- Advanced CLI options: `--timeout`, `--linked-docs-concurrency`, `--enable-assessment-features`
    23→- Remediation API route (`POST /api/remediation/generate-prompts`) accepting issues directly
    24→
    25→
    26→## Fixed
    27→
    28→- Suppress false positive severity-9 conflicts when colocated AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md contain `@` file reference annotations (e.g., `@CLAUDE.md` pointing to the companion file)
    29→- File deduplication now drops pointer files containing only `@` references, keeping only the referenced content file
    30→
    31→## Changed
    32→
    33→- Remediation API accepts `issues` array instead of `selectedEvaluators` for direct issue-to-prompt generation
    34→- Issue selection buttons and SelectionSummaryBar no longer gated behind `assessmentEnabled` feature flag
    35→- Updated evaluator filter counts in CLI help (17 total, 13 errors, 4 suggestions)

    33→
    34→# Dynasty Trading System — Startup Draft Support
    35→
    36→## Problem / Design Challenge
    37→
    38→The Dispersal Draft application was a single-tenant auction system. Supporting **Startup dynasty drafts** required a secondary market so teams can trade players with each other and re-sell won assets back to the league.
    39→
    40→Three mechanisms were needed:
    41→
    42→| Mechanism | Initiator | Flow |
    43→|-----------|-----------|------|
    44→| Commissioner Trade | Commissioner | Immediate — no approval, bypasses locks |
    45→| Direct Trade | Manager | Proposal → Accept/Reject (peer-to-peer) |
    46→| Sale Auction | Manager (seller) | Lists asset; all managers can bid |
    47→
    48→Additional challenges:
    49→- **Asset lifecycle**: prevent double-trading (one PENDING trade per asset at a time)
    50→- **Financial accuracy**: Decimal types throughout, validated against NaN/Infinity
    51→- **Concurrency safety**: TOCTOU races on SQLite with `immediate_transaction`
    52→- **Real-time coordination**: WebSocket events for all trade lifecycle changes
    53→
    54→---
    55→
    56→## Architecture Decisions
    57→
    58→### TradingService (Composition Pattern)
    59→
    60→`TradingService` wraps `DraftStateDB` rather than extending it, keeping trading logic isolated:
    61→
    62→```python
    63→class TradingService:
    64→    def __init__(self, draft_state):
    65→        self.state = draft_state
    66→        self.draft_id = draft_state.draft_id
    67→        self.db_path = draft_state.db_path
    68→```
    69→
    70→### Immediate Transaction Pattern
    71→
    72→All financial operations use `immediate_transaction(db_path)` — a context manager that opens a serializable SQLite transaction. This prevents dirty reads, lost updates, and phantom reads.
    73→
    74→### Optional Connection Parameter for Lock Checking
    75→
    76→`is_asset_locked(player_id, conn=None)` accepts an existing connection. When called inside a transaction, passing `conn` keeps the check within the same serializable boundary, closing the TOCTOU race window.
    77→
    78→### Batch Query Optimization
    79→
    80→`get_locked_asset_ids()` returns a `set` of all locked player IDs using 2 queries (all pending trades + all active sales). Replaces per-asset N+1 that would require 40 queries for 20 assets.

# Gemini CLI Context File Names

## Default Behavior
Gemini CLI looks for **`GEMINI.md`** by default as the context file name.

## Customizable File Names
You can configure alternative file names via `settings.json`. According to the documentation: *"While `GEMINI.md` is the default filename, you can configure this in your `settings.json` file."*

The example provided shows a configuration that accepts multiple file names:

```json
{
  "context": {
    "fileName": ["AGENTS.md", "CONTEXT.md", "GEMINI.md"]
  }
}
```

## Priority/Hierarchy
The CLI loads context files in a three-tier hierarchy:

1. **Global context** (`~/.gemini/GEMINI.md`)
2. **Workspace context** (in configured workspace directories and their parents)
3. **Just-in-time context** (discovered when tools access files/directories)

All files found are concatenated and sent to the model together.

## Summary
There is **no fixed list of "supported" file names**—the system uses `GEMINI.md` by default but accepts any filename you specify in your settings configuration.

# OpenCode Supported Rule File Names

Based on the documentation, OpenCode supports these filenames for project instructions, **in order of precedence**:

1. **`AGENTS.md`** (primary) - Project-specific rules in your project root
2. **`CLAUDE.md`** (fallback) - Used only if no `AGENTS.md` exists
3. **`~/.config/opencode/AGENTS.md`** (global) - Personal rules applied across all sessions
4. **`~/.claude/CLAUDE.md`** (global fallback) - Legacy Claude Code compatibility

**OpenCode does not support `OPENCODE.md`.** The documentation explicitly states: "Place an `AGENTS.md` in your project root for project-specific rules."

The precedence order is: "The first matching file wins in each category. For example, if you have both `AGENTS.md` and `CLAUDE.md`, only `AGENTS.md` is used."

You can also reference additional instruction files via the `instructions` field in `opencode.json` to load custom rules from other locations or remote URLs.

## Project Overview

Go MCP server for Todoist. Communicates via stdio (stdout = MCP protocol, stderr = logs).
Built with [go-sdk v1.3.0](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk).

## Architecture

Three-layer design, all under `internal/`:

```
main.go                → Entry point, slog setup, server bootstrap
internal/tools/        → MCP tool handlers (register.go wires all tools)
internal/todoist/      → HTTP API client (no MCP awareness)
internal/models/       → Shared data types
```

- `tools/` depends on `todoist/` and `models/`
- `todoist/` depends only on `models/`
- `models/` has zero dependencies

## Commands

```bash
make build       # Build to build/mcp-todoist
make test        # Run tests with -race
make lint        # golangci-lint
make check       # fmt + vet + lint + test
make coverage    # Tests with HTML coverage report
```

## Conventions

### Logging

Uses `log/slog` with `JSONHandler` writing to `os.Stderr`. No `log.Fatal` — use `slog.Error` + `os.Exit(1)`.
Lowercase log messages. Pass errors as structured attributes: `slog.Error("msg", "error", err)`.

### Error Handling

- API client methods return `(T, error)` — no panics
- Tool handlers return MCP error results, never crash the server

### Testing

- Tests use `net/http/httptest` for API client testing
- Test assertions use `testing.T.Fatal`/`Fatalf` — no external test libraries
- All tests run with `-race` flag

## CI

GitHub Actions runs on every push/PR to main:
- `go build`, `go test -race`, `go vet`, `staticcheck`, `go fix -diff`
- `golangci-lint v2.10.1` (separate job)

## Environment

- Requires `TODOIST_API_TOKEN` env var
- Go 1.26+

1→# Marin Architecture
     2→
     3→Marin is a framework for building reproducible language model training pipelines. At its core, Marin executes DAGs of steps using Ray for distributed processing, with automatic versioning based on code and configuration. Pipeline: data curation → transformation → tokenization → training → evaluation.
     4→
     5→## Core Architecture
     6→
     7→**Executor Pattern**: Experiments are DAGs of `ExecutorStep` objects (`lib/marin/src/marin/execution/executor.py`). Output path = `<base>/<name>-<hash>` where hash covers versioned fields and dependencies. Only changed steps re-run.
     8→
     9→**Ray Distribution**: Steps can be normal or `@ray.remote` functions. Ray ships code to workers with step-specific dependency groups from `pyproject.toml`.
    10→
    11→**Entry Point**: `executor_main()` or [`lib/marin/src/marin/run/ray_run.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/marin/src/marin/run/ray_run.py) for cluster execution.

    14→
    15→```

    17→├── pyproject.toml              # Dependencies, extras (gpu, tpu, cpu, rl, eval)

    88→### Test Parallelization
    89→
    90→**Always use `t.Parallel()` in tests.** Every top-level test function and subtest should call `t.Parallel()` unless it modifies process-global state (e.g., `os.Chdir()`).
    91→
    92→```go
    93→func TestFeature_Foo(t *testing.T) {
    94→    t.Parallel()
    95→    // ...
    96→}
    97→
    98→// Integration tests: RunForAllStrategies handles t.Parallel() for subtests internally,
    99→// but the top-level test still needs it
   100→func TestFeature_Bar(t *testing.T) {
   101→    t.Parallel()
   102→    RunForAllStrategies(t, func(t *testing.T, env *TestEnv, strategyName string) {
   103→        // ...
   104→    })
   105→}
   106→```
   107→
   108→**Exception:** Tests that modify process-global state cannot be parallelized. This includes `os.Chdir()`/`t.Chdir()` and `os.Setenv()`/`t.Setenv()` — Go's test framework will panic if these are used after `t.Parallel()`.

   132→### Code Duplication Prevention
   133→
   134→Before implementing Go code, use `/go:discover-related` to find existing utilities and patterns that might be reusable.
   135→
   136→**Check for duplication:**
   137→```bash
   138→mise run dup           # Comprehensive check (threshold 50) with summary
   139→mise run dup:staged    # Check only staged files
   140→mise run lint          # Normal lint includes dupl at threshold 75 (new issues only)
   141→mise run lint:full     # All issues at threshold 75

   145→- **75 tokens** (lint/CI) - Blocks on serious duplication (~20+ lines)
   146→- **50 tokens** (dup) - Advisory, catches smaller patterns (~10+ lines)

   148→When duplication is found:
   149→1. Check if a helper already exists in `common.go` or nearby utility files
   150→2. If not, consider extracting the duplicated logic to a shared helper
   151→3. If duplication is intentional (e.g., test setup), add a `//nolint:dupl` comment with explanation

   153→## Code Patterns
   154→
   155→### Error Handling
   156→
   157→The CLI uses a specific pattern for error output to avoid duplication between Cobra and main.go.
   158→
   159→**How it works:**
   160→- `root.go` sets `SilenceErrors: true` globally - Cobra never prints errors
   161→- `main.go` prints errors to stderr, unless the error is a `SilentError`
   162→- Commands return `NewSilentError(err)` when they've already printed a custom message
   163→
   164→**When to use `SilentError`:**
   165→Use `NewSilentError()` when you want to print a custom, user-friendly error message instead of the raw error:
   166→
   167→```go
   168→// In a command's RunE function:
   169→if _, err := paths.RepoRoot(); err != nil {
   170→    cmd.SilenceUsage = true  // Don't show usage for prerequisite errors
   171→    fmt.Fprintln(cmd.ErrOrStderr(), "Not a git repository. Please run 'entire enable' from within a git repository.")
   172→    return NewSilentError(errors.New("not a git repository"))
   173→}
   174→```
   175→
   176→**When NOT to use `SilentError`:**
   177→For normal errors where the default error message is sufficient, just return the error directly. main.go will print it:
   178→
   179→```go
   180→// Normal error - main.go will print "unknown strategy: foo"
   181→return fmt.Errorf("unknown strategy: %s", name)
   182→```
   183→
   184→**Key files:**
   185→- `errors.go` - Defines `SilentError` type and `NewSilentError()` constructor
   186→- `root.go` - Sets `SilenceErrors: true` on root command
   187→- `main.go` - Checks for `SilentError` before printing

   189→### Settings
   190→
   191→All settings access should go through the `settings` package (`cmd/entire/cli/settings/`).
   192→
   193→**Why a separate package:**
   194→The `settings` package exists to avoid import cycles. The `cli` package imports `strategy`, so `strategy` cannot import `cli`. The `settings` package provides shared settings loading that both can use.
   195→
   196→**Usage:**
   197→```go
   198→import "github.com/entireio/cli/cmd/entire/cli/settings"
   199→
   200→// Load full settings object
   201→s, err := settings.Load()
   202→if err != nil {
   203→    // handle error
   204→}
   205→if s.Enabled {
   206→    // ...
   207→}
   208→
   209→// Or use convenience functions
   210→if settings.IsSummarizeEnabled() {
   211→    // ...
   212→}
   213→```
   214→
   215→**Do NOT:**
   216→- Read `.entire/settings.json` or `.entire/settings.local.json` directly with `os.ReadFile`
   217→- Duplicate settings parsing logic in other packages
   218→- Create new settings helpers without adding them to the `settings` package
   219→
   220→**Key files:**
   221→- `settings/settings.go` - `EntireSettings` struct, `Load()`, and helper methods
   222→- `config.go` - Higher-level config functions that use settings (for `cli` package consumers)
   223→
   224→### Logging vs User Output
   225→
   226→- **Internal/debug logging**: Use `logging.Debug/Info/Warn/Error(ctx, msg, attrs...)` from `cmd/entire/cli/logging/`. Writes to `.entire/logs/`.
   227→- **User-facing output**: Use `fmt.Fprint*(cmd.OutOrStdout(), ...)` or `cmd.ErrOrStderr()`.
   228→
   229→Don't use `fmt.Print*` for operational messages (checkpoint saves, hook invocations, strategy decisions) - those should use the `logging` package.
   230→
   231→**Privacy**: Don't log user content (prompts, file contents, commit messages). Log only operational metadata (IDs, counts, paths, durations).

   233→### Git Operations
   234→
   235→We use github.com/go-git/go-git for most git operations, but with important exceptions:
   236→
   237→#### go-git v5 Bugs - Use CLI Instead
   238→
   239→**Do NOT use go-git v5 for `checkout` or `reset --hard` operations.**
   240→
   241→go-git v5 has a bug where `worktree.Reset()` with `git.HardReset` and `worktree.Checkout()` incorrectly delete untracked directories even when they're listed in `.gitignore`. This would destroy `.entire/` and `.worktrees/` directories.
   242→
   243→Use the git CLI instead:
   244→```go
   245→// WRONG - go-git deletes ignored directories
   246→worktree.Reset(&git.ResetOptions{
   247→    Commit: hash,
   248→    Mode:   git.HardReset,
   249→})
   250→
   251→// CORRECT - use git CLI
   252→cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "git", "reset", "--hard", hash.String())
   253→```
   254→
   255→See `HardResetWithProtection()` in `common.go` and `CheckoutBranch()` in `git_operations.go` for examples.
   256→
   257→Regression tests in `hard_reset_test.go` verify this behavior - if go-git v6 fixes this issue, those tests can be used to validate switching back.
   258→
   259→#### Repo Root vs Current Working Directory
   260→
   261→**Always use repo root (not `os.Getwd()`) when working with git-relative paths.**
   262→
   263→Git commands like `git status` and `worktree.Status()` return paths relative to the **repository root**, not the current working directory. When an agent runs from a subdirectory (e.g., `/repo/frontend`), using `os.Getwd()` to construct absolute paths will produce incorrect results for files in sibling directories.
   264→
   265→```go
   266→// WRONG - breaks when running from subdirectory
   267→cwd, _ := os.Getwd()  // e.g., /repo/frontend
   268→absPath := filepath.Join(cwd, file)  // file="api/src/types.ts" → /repo/frontend/api/src/types.ts (WRONG)
   269→
   270→// CORRECT - use repo root
   271→repoRoot, _ := paths.RepoRoot()  // or strategy.GetWorktreePath()
   272→absPath := filepath.Join(repoRoot, file)  // → /repo/api/src/types.ts (CORRECT)
   273→```
   274→
   275→This also affects path filtering. The `paths.ToRelativePath()` function rejects paths starting with `..`, so computing relative paths from cwd instead of repo root will filter out files in sibling directories:
   276→
   277→```go
   278→// WRONG - filters out sibling directory files
   279→cwd, _ := os.Getwd()  // /repo/frontend
   280→relPath := paths.ToRelativePath("/repo/api/file.ts", cwd)  // returns "" (filtered out as "../api/file.ts")
   281→
   282→// CORRECT - keeps all repo files
   283→repoRoot, _ := paths.RepoRoot()
   284→relPath := paths.ToRelativePath("/repo/api/file.ts", repoRoot)  // returns "api/file.ts"
   285→```
   286→
   287→**When to use `os.Getwd()`:** Only when you actually need the current directory (e.g., finding agent session directories that are cwd-relative).
   288→
   289→**When to use repo root:** Any time you're working with paths from git status, git diff, or any git-relative file list.
   290→
   291→Test case in `state_test.go`: `TestFilterAndNormalizePaths_SiblingDirectories` documents this bug pattern.

   293→### Session Strategies (`cmd/entire/cli/strategy/`)
   294→
   295→The CLI uses a strategy pattern for managing session data and checkpoints. Each strategy implements the `Strategy` interface defined in `strategy.go`.
   296→
   297→#### Core Interface
   298→All strategies implement:
   299→- `SaveStep()` - Save session step checkpoint (code + metadata)
   300→- `SaveTaskStep()` - Save subagent task step checkpoint
   301→- `GetRewindPoints()` / `Rewind()` - List and restore to checkpoints
   302→- `GetSessionLog()` / `GetSessionInfo()` - Retrieve session data
   303→- `ListSessions()` / `GetSession()` - Session discovery
   304→
   305→#### Available Strategies
   306→
   307→| Strategy | Main Branch | Metadata Storage | Use Case |
   308→|----------|-------------|------------------|----------|
   309→| **manual-commit** (default) | Unchanged (no commits) | `entire/<HEAD-hash>-<worktreeHash>` branches + `entire/checkpoints/v1` | Recommended for most workflows |
   310→| **auto-commit** | Creates clean commits | Orphan `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch | Teams that want code commits from sessions |
   311→
   312→#### Strategy Details
   313→
   314→**Manual-Commit Strategy** (`manual_commit*.go`) - Default
   315→- **Does not modify** the active branch - no commits created on the working branch
   316→- Creates shadow branch `entire/<HEAD-commit-hash[:7]>-<worktreeHash[:6]>` per base commit + worktree
   317→- **Worktree-specific branches** - each git worktree gets its own shadow branch namespace, preventing conflicts
   318→- **Supports multiple concurrent sessions** - checkpoints from different sessions in the same directory interleave on the same shadow branch
   319→- Session logs are condensed to permanent `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch on user commits
   320→- Builds git trees in-memory using go-git plumbing APIs
   321→- Rewind restores files from shadow branch commit tree (does not use `git reset`)
   322→- **Location-independent transcript resolution** - transcript paths are always computed dynamically from the current repo location (via `agent.GetSessionDir` + `agent.ResolveSessionFile`), never stored in checkpoint metadata. This ensures restore/rewind works after repo relocation or across machines.
   323→- Tracks session state in `.git/entire-sessions/` (shared across worktrees)
   324→- **Shadow branch migration** - if user does stash/pull/rebase (HEAD changes without commit), shadow branch is automatically moved to new base commit
   325→- **Orphaned branch cleanup** - if a shadow branch exists without a corresponding session state file, it is automatically reset when a new session starts
   326→- PrePush hook can push `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch alongside user pushes
   327→- `AllowsMainBranch() = true` - safe to use on main/master since it never modifies commit history
   328→
   329→**Auto-Commit Strategy** (`auto_commit.go`)
   330→- Code commits to active branch with **clean history** (commits have `Entire-Checkpoint` trailer only)
   331→- Metadata stored on orphan `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch at sharded paths: `<id[:2]>/<id[2:]>/`
   332→- Uses `checkpoint.WriteCommitted()` for metadata storage
   333→- Checkpoint ID (12-hex-char) links code commits to metadata on `entire/checkpoints/v1`
   334→- Full rewind allowed if commit is only on current branch (not in main); otherwise logs-only
   335→- Rewind via `git reset --hard`
   336→- PrePush hook can push `entire/checkpoints/v1` branch alongside user pushes
   337→- `AllowsMainBranch() = true` - creates commits on active branch, safe to use on main/master
   338→
