1→# JTBD Analysis: Agent Learnings
     2→
     3→## Feature Overview
     4→
     5→Agent Learnings is the "Synaptic Plasticity" of Brain -- persistent behavioral modifications that convert short-term agent failures into long-term wisdom. Two sources: human-created (immediately active) and agent-suggested (pending human approval). Injected into agent system prompts at runtime (JIT prompting).
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Job 1: Persistent Agent Correction
    10→
    11→### Job Story
    12→
    13→**When** I have corrected the same agent mistake for the third time in a week,
    14→**I want to** record a permanent behavioral rule that the agent must follow,
    15→**so I can** stop wasting time repeating corrections that the agent forgets between sessions.
    16→
    17→### Job Dimensions
    18→
    19→| Dimension | Description |
    20→|-----------|-------------|
    21→| **Functional** | Persist a behavioral correction so the agent applies it in all future sessions without being re-told |
    22→| **Emotional** | Feel heard and in control -- "the system actually learns from me" instead of "talking to a wall" |
    23→| **Social** | Be seen as someone whose corrections matter -- the team benefits from one person's correction |
    24→
    25→### Four Forces Analysis
    26→
    27→| Force | Description |
    28→|-------|-------------|
    29→| **Push** | Repeating "don't use null, use undefined" every session. Agent apologizes, then does it again next session. Frustration compounds -- "I've told you this five times." |
    30→| **Pull** | One correction, applied forever. Say it once, never repeat it. Agent becomes smarter over time. |
    31→| **Anxiety** | "What if my correction was wrong and now it's baked in permanently?" -- fear of irreversible bad rules. "What if I create so many rules they conflict?" |
    32→| **Habit** | Copy-pasting correction text into CLAUDE.md files. Manually maintaining agent instructions. "At least I know what's in the prompt." |
    33→
    34→### Assessment
    35→- Switch likelihood: **High** -- push is extremely strong (daily frustration)
    36→- Key blocker: Anxiety about permanence and conflict
    37→- Key enabler: Push of repeated corrections
    38→- Design implication: Make learnings editable, deactivatable, and conflict-visible. Show what is active so users feel in control.
    39→
    40→---
    41→
    42→## Job 2: Agent Self-Improvement
    43→
    44→### Job Story
    45→
    46→**When** an agent notices it has been corrected on the same pattern three times or detects a recurring failure mode,
    47→**I want to** suggest a behavioral learning for itself or another agent,
    48→**so I can** prevent future failures without requiring human intervention for every correction.
    49→
    50→### Job Dimensions
    51→
    52→| Dimension | Description |
    53→|-----------|-------------|
    54→| **Functional** | Detect patterns in agent behavior and propose persistent corrections that prevent recurrence |
    55→| **Emotional** | (Agent perspective) Operate with increasing competence; (Human perspective) Feel that agents are getting smarter autonomously |
    56→| **Social** | Demonstrate that the system self-improves -- stakeholders see an organization that learns, not just executes |
    57→
    58→### Four Forces Analysis
    59→
    60→| Force | Description |
    61→|-------|-------------|
    62→| **Push** | Agents repeat the same mistakes. Observer detects the pattern but has no mechanism to fix it permanently. Coding agent violates conventions that are documented but not in its prompt. |
    63→| **Pull** | Cross-agent coaching: Observer notices PM agent's weakness and suggests a learning. System develops institutional memory. |
    64→| **Anxiety** | "What if the agent suggests bad rules that make things worse?" -- fear of autonomous degradation. "What if agents flood me with low-quality suggestions?" |
    65→| **Habit** | Manually updating agent prompts after noticing patterns. Relying on static CLAUDE.md files that grow without curation. |
    66→
    67→### Assessment
    68→- Switch likelihood: **Medium-High** -- strong pull, but anxiety about autonomous rule creation is real
    69→- Key blocker: Anxiety about quality and volume of agent-suggested learnings
    70→- Key enabler: Pull of a self-improving system
    71→- Design implication: Agent suggestions always require human approval. Surface with evidence (what triggered the suggestion). Rate-limit suggestions per agent.
    72→
    73→---
    74→
    75→## Job 3: Runtime Learning Consumption
    76→
    77→### Job Story
    78→
    79→**When** an agent starts a new session in a workspace that has accumulated behavioral learnings,
    80→**I want to** have the right learnings injected into my system prompt without bloating it,
    81→**so I can** operate with the accumulated wisdom of the workspace while keeping my context window efficient.
    82→
    83→### Job Dimensions
    84→
    85→| Dimension | Description |
    86→|-----------|-------------|
    87→| **Functional** | Select and inject relevant learnings into agent prompts at session start without exceeding token budgets |
    88→| **Emotional** | (Agent perspective) Competence from first interaction; (Human perspective) Confidence that agents remember past corrections |
    89→| **Social** | Team members see consistent agent behavior across sessions -- "the agent remembers what we taught it" |
    90→
    91→### Four Forces Analysis
    92→
    93→| Force | Description |
    94→|-------|-------------|
    95→| **Push** | Agent prompts are static -- same base prompt regardless of workspace history. Corrections from last week are forgotten. New sessions start from zero. |
    96→| **Pull** | JIT prompting: only relevant learnings injected, keeping prompts lean. Agent immediately applies accumulated wisdom. Context-aware selection. |
    97→| **Anxiety** | "What if too many learnings bloat the prompt and degrade performance?" -- token budget concerns. "What if conflicting learnings confuse the agent?" |
    98→| **Habit** | Hardcoded rules in base system prompts. Static CLAUDE.md files. Manual prompt engineering. |
    99→
   100→### Assessment
   101→- Switch likelihood: **High** -- technical improvement with clear benefits
   102→- Key blocker: Anxiety about prompt bloat and conflict
   103→- Key enabler: JIT selection keeping prompts lean
   104→- Design implication: Token budget for learnings section. Priority ordering (human > agent). Conflict detection before injection. Show which learnings are active in session context.
   105→
   106→---
   107→
   108→## Job 4: Learning Governance and Curation
   109→
   110→### Job Story
   111→
   112→**When** my workspace has accumulated 30+ learnings over several months and some may be outdated or conflicting,
   113→**I want to** review, curate, and resolve conflicts in the learning library,
   114→**so I can** maintain a healthy set of behavioral rules that improve agent performance rather than degrading it through accumulation.
   115→
   116→### Job Dimensions
   117→
   118→| Dimension | Description |
   119→|-----------|-------------|
   120→| **Functional** | View all learnings, detect conflicts, supersede outdated ones, and verify that the active set is coherent |
   121→| **Emotional** | Feel in control of the system's accumulated knowledge -- "I understand what the agents know" rather than "who knows what rules are in there" |
   122→| **Social** | Be a responsible steward of organizational knowledge -- demonstrate governance to stakeholders |
   123→
   124→### Four Forces Analysis
   125→
   126→| Force | Description |
   127→|-------|-------------|
   128→| **Push** | Learning library grows without curation. Contradictory rules accumulate. Agent behavior becomes unpredictable. Nobody knows what rules are active. |
   129→| **Pull** | Clean, curated library with conflict detection. Visual overview of what agents know. Supersession chain showing evolution. |
   130→| **Anxiety** | "If I deactivate a learning, will something break?" -- fear of removing useful rules. "I don't remember why this learning was created." |
   131→| **Habit** | Ignoring accumulated rules. Adding new rules without reviewing old ones. "It works, don't touch it." |
   132→
   133→### Assessment
   134→- Switch likelihood: **Medium** -- need emerges over time, not immediately
   135→- Key blocker: Anxiety about deactivating learnings + habit of ignoring accumulation
   136→- Key enabler: Conflict detection making curation necessary
   137→- Design implication: Show learning provenance (who created it, when, why). Conflict detection surfaces problems proactively. Deactivation is soft (can reactivate). Supersession preserves history.
   138→
   139→---
   140→
   141→## Opportunity Scoring
   142→
   143→| # | Outcome Statement | Imp. (%) | Sat. (%) | Score | Priority |
   144→|---|-------------------|----------|----------|-------|----------|
   145→| 1 | Minimize the number of times a human must repeat the same correction to an agent | 95 | 10 | 18.0 | Extremely Underserved |
   146→| 2 | Minimize the likelihood of an agent repeating a previously corrected mistake | 92 | 12 | 17.2 | Extremely Underserved |
   147→| 3 | Minimize the time for an agent to apply workspace-specific behavioral rules at session start | 85 | 20 | 14.5 | Extremely Underserved |
   148→| 4 | Minimize the likelihood of conflicting learnings degrading agent performance | 80 | 15 | 14.5 | Extremely Underserved |
   149→| 5 | Minimize the time to review and approve agent-suggested learnings | 75 | 10 | 14.0 | Underserved |
   150→| 6 | Minimize the likelihood of prompt bloat from accumulated learnings | 78 | 25 | 13.1 | Underserved |
   151→| 7 | Minimize the time to identify and resolve conflicting learnings | 70 | 15 | 12.5 | Underserved |
   152→| 8 | Maximize the likelihood that agent-suggested learnings are high quality | 72 | 18 | 12.6 | Underserved |
   153→| 9 | Minimize the time to understand why a learning was created (provenance) | 65 | 20 | 11.0 | Appropriately Served |
   154→| 10 | Minimize the effort to curate the learning library over time | 60 | 25 | 9.5 | Overserved |
   155→
   156→### Scoring Method
   157→- Importance: estimated % rating 4+ on 5-point scale (team estimate based on feature description and user pain analysis)
   158→- Satisfaction: estimated % rating 4+ with current workarounds
   159→- Score: Importance + max(0, Importance - Satisfaction)
   160→- Data quality: team estimate, not user survey. Confidence: Medium.
   161→
   162→### Top Opportunities (Score >= 12)
   163→1. Persistent correction (18.0) -- core feature, highest priority
   164→2. Mistake non-recurrence (17.2) -- directly tied to #1
   165→3. Runtime injection (14.5) -- enables correction persistence
   166→4. Conflict prevention (14.5) -- safety net for accumulated learnings
   167→5. Approval efficiency (14.0) -- governance flow
   168→6. Prompt bloat prevention (13.1) -- technical enabler
   169→7. Quality of agent suggestions (12.6) -- trust building
   170→8. Conflict resolution (12.5) -- curation support

1→# Observer Learning Proposals — Architecture Design
     2→
     3→## Problem Statement
     4→
     5→The Observer agent currently detects contradictions, anomalies, and patterns in the knowledge graph — but can only express findings as **observations** (signals). It cannot propose **learnings** (persistent behavioral rules). The `suggestLearning()` function exists in `learning/detector.ts` with rate limiting and dismissed similarity gates, but nothing calls it.
     6→
     7→The user's vision adds a **diagnostic reasoning layer**: the Observer doesn't just count pattern frequency — it diagnoses *why* the gap between intent and reality exists and proposes a categorized fix.
     8→
     9→## Scope
    10→
    11→This feature extends the existing agent-learnings architecture (ADR-026 through ADR-030) with:
    12→1. A `suggest_learning` tool for the Observer agent
    13→2. Diagnostic reasoning ("Root Cause Trace") in the graph scan pipeline
    14→3. Observation cluster → learning escalation in the graph scan
    15→
    16→**Out of scope**: Chat agent correction detection (US-AL-002 source 1), new schema tables, UI changes beyond existing governance feed cards.
    17→
    18→## Quality Attribute Priorities
    19→
    20→| Attribute | Priority | Rationale |
    21→|-----------|----------|-----------|
    22→| **Auditability** | Highest | Every learning proposal must trace back to evidence nodes. The graph edge that failed must be identifiable. |
    23→| **Safety** | High | Agent-suggested learnings are always `pending_approval`. Rate limiting prevents spam. Dismissed similarity prevents re-suggestion. |
    24→| **Maintainability** | High | Extends existing Observer pipeline patterns. No new infrastructure. |
    25→| **Testability** | High | Diagnostic reasoning uses `generateObject` (mockable). Pure functions for classification. |
    26→| **Performance** | Medium | Runs during graph scan (background, not user-facing). LLM calls are bounded. |
    27→
    28→## Constraints
    29→
    30→- Functional paradigm (per CLAUDE.md)
    31→- No `null` in domain data
    32→- No module-level mutable singletons
    33→- `suggestLearning()` already handles rate limiting + dismissed similarity — reuse, don't duplicate
    34→- Observer model is optional — graceful degradation when unavailable (ADR-025)
    35→- Two-step KNN for all vector similarity queries (SurrealDB HNSW+WHERE bug)
    36→- Background DB work tracked via `deps.inflight.track()`
    37→
    38→## C4 System Context (L1)
    39→
    40→Unchanged from agent-learnings architecture. The Observer is already shown as a container that interacts with the Learning Domain.
    41→
    42→## C4 Container (L2) — Observer Learning Proposal Flow
    43→
    44→```mermaid
    45→C4Container
    46→    title Observer Learning Proposals - Container View
    47→
    48→    Container_Boundary(brain, "Brain Platform") {

1→# Observer Learning Proposals — Architecture Design
     2→
     3→## Problem Statement
     4→
     5→The Observer agent currently detects contradictions, anomalies, and patterns in the knowledge graph — but can only express findings as **observations** (signals). It cannot propose **learnings** (persistent behavioral rules). The `suggestLearning()` function exists in `learning/detector.ts` with rate limiting and dismissed similarity gates, but nothing calls it.
     6→
     7→The user's vision adds a **diagnostic reasoning layer**: the Observer doesn't just count pattern frequency — it diagnoses *why* the gap between intent and reality exists and proposes a categorized fix.
     8→
     9→## Scope
    10→
    11→This feature extends the existing agent-learnings architecture (ADR-026 through ADR-030) with:
    12→1. A `suggest_learning` tool for the Observer agent
    13→2. Diagnostic reasoning ("Root Cause Trace") in the graph scan pipeline
    14→3. Observation cluster → learning escalation in the graph scan
    15→
    16→**Out of scope**: Chat agent correction detection (US-AL-002 source 1), new schema tables, UI changes beyond existing governance feed cards.
    17→
    18→## Quality Attribute Priorities
    19→
    20→| Attribute | Priority | Rationale |
    21→|-----------|----------|-----------|
    22→| **Auditability** | Highest | Every learning proposal must trace back to evidence nodes. The graph edge that failed must be identifiable. |
    23→| **Safety** | High | Agent-suggested learnings are always `pending_approval`. Rate limiting prevents spam. Dismissed similarity prevents re-suggestion. |
    24→| **Maintainability** | High | Extends existing Observer pipeline patterns. No new infrastructure. |
    25→| **Testability** | High | Diagnostic reasoning uses `generateObject` (mockable). Pure functions for classification. |
    26→| **Performance** | Medium | Runs during graph scan (background, not user-facing). LLM calls are bounded. |

    93→## Architecture Decision: Root Cause Trace
    94→
    95→### The Three-Question Framework
    96→
    97→When the Observer detects a pattern (observation cluster, repeated contradiction, or anomaly pattern), it performs a **Root Cause Trace** — an LLM-based diagnostic that classifies the failure into one of three categories:
    98→
    99→| Category | Question | Example | Learning Type | Target |
   100→|----------|----------|---------|---------------|--------|
   101→| **Policy Failure** | "Did the rules allow something they shouldn't have?" | Policy permitted $500 spend but should cap at $200 for this agent role | `constraint` | Policy owner / affected agents |
   102→| **Context Failure** | "Did the agent lack information it needed?" | Agent didn't know the API was in maintenance mode | `instruction` | Affected agent type(s) |
   103→| **Behavioral Drift** | "Did the agent ignore a rule it already had?" | Agent kept retrying a broken endpoint despite a "fail fast" learning | `constraint` | Drifting agent type |
   104→
   105→### Mapping to Existing Learning Types
   106→
   107→The three root cause categories map directly to the existing `learning_type` enum:
   108→
   109→| Root Cause | `learning_type` | Rationale |
   110→|------------|-----------------|-----------|
   111→| Policy failure | `constraint` | Must-follow rule that tightens boundaries |
   112→| Context failure | `instruction` | Conditional guidance — "when X, inject Y into context" |
   113→| Behavioral drift | `constraint` | Reinforcement of existing rule (may supersede weak version) |
   114→
   115→No schema changes needed. The existing `learning` table already supports all three categories.
   116→
   117→## Component Design
   118→
   119→### 1. Observation Clusterer (`observer/learning-diagnosis.ts`)
   120→
   121→Groups open observations by embedding similarity to find recurring patterns.
   122→
   123→**Input**: Workspace record, minimum cluster size (default: 3), time window (default: 14 days)
   124→
   125→**Algorithm**:
   126→1. Query open/acknowledged observations from the past 14 days with embeddings
   127→2. For each observation, find neighbors via KNN (two-step pattern)
   128→3. Group into clusters where pairwise similarity > 0.75
   129→4. Filter clusters with size >= threshold
   130→5. Deduplicate: check if any active learning already covers the cluster (KNN on active learnings, similarity > 0.80 → skip)
   131→
   132→**Output**: `Array<ObservationCluster>` where each cluster contains observation records and a representative text.
   133→
   134→```typescript
   135→type ObservationCluster = {
   136→  observations: Array<{ id: string; text: string; severity: string; entityRefs: string[] }>;
   137→  representativeText: string;
   138→  clusterSize: number;
   139→};
   140→```
   141→
   142→### 2. Root Cause Classifier (`observer/learning-diagnosis.ts`)
   143→
   144→LLM-based classification using `generateObject` with structured output.
   145→
   146→**Input**: Observation cluster + related entity context (decisions, tasks, policies linked via `observes` edges)
   147→
   148→**Schema** (Zod):
   149→```typescript
   150→const rootCauseSchema = z.object({
   151→  category: z.enum(["policy_failure", "context_failure", "behavioral_drift"]),
   152→  should_propose_learning: z.boolean().describe("True ONLY if confidence >= 0.70 AND high conviction in category and proposed text. False if root cause is ambiguous or learning too generic."),
   153→  proposed_learning_type: z.enum(["constraint", "instruction"]).describe("constraint for must-follow rules (policy/behavioral fixes), instruction for conditional guidance (context fixes)"),
   154→  reasoning: z.string().describe("Why this category was chosen, referencing specific evidence"),
   155→  proposed_learning_text: z.string().describe("The behavioral rule that would prevent recurrence"),
   156→  target_agents: z.array(z.string()).describe("Which agent types should receive this learning"),
   157→  evidence_refs: z.array(z.string()).describe("table:id references to supporting evidence"),
   158→  confidence: z.number().min(0).max(1),
   159→});
   160→```
   161→
   162→**Prompt structure**:
   163→```
   164→You are the Observer agent performing root cause analysis.
   165→
   166→## Pattern Detected
   167→{cluster representative text with observation quotes}
   168→
   169→## Related Entities
   170→{decisions, tasks, policies linked to the observations}
   171→
   172→## Existing Active Learnings
   173→{learnings already active for the target agent types}
   174→
   175→## Classification Instructions
   176→Determine WHY this pattern keeps recurring:
   177→
   178→1. Policy Failure: The governance rules allowed something they shouldn't.
   179→   → Propose a constraint that tightens the boundary.
   180→
   181→2. Context Failure: The agent lacked information it needed to act correctly.
   182→   → Propose an instruction that injects the missing context.
   183→
   184→3. Behavioral Drift: The agent had the information but didn't apply it.
   185→   → Propose a constraint that reinforces the expected behavior.
   186→
   187→Set should_propose_learning to true ONLY if:
   188→- confidence >= 0.70
   189→- You have high conviction in both the category AND the proposed text
   190→- The proposed learning is specific enough to be actionable
   191→
   192→Set should_propose_learning to false if:
   193→- The root cause is ambiguous or could fit multiple categories
   194→- The proposed learning text is too generic ("be more careful")
   195→- The evidence is insufficient to justify a permanent behavioral rule
   196→
   197→For proposed_learning_type, choose based on the fix needed:
   198→- "constraint" for must-follow rules (policy fixes, behavioral reinforcement)
   199→- "instruction" for conditional guidance (context injection, situational awareness)
   200→```
   201→
   202→**Proposal gate** (two-check): The LLM outputs `should_propose_learning` (its own assessment) AND `confidence` (numeric). The code gates on both:
   203→- If `should_propose_learning === false` OR `confidence < 0.70`: create an observation instead of a learning proposal: "Emerging pattern detected but root cause unclear. Monitoring."
   204→- This dual gate prevents the LLM from proposing low-confidence learnings while still allowing it to decline even when confidence is technically high (e.g., "I'm confident this is a policy failure, but the proposed fix is too vague").
   205→
   206→### 3. Learning Proposer (`observer/learning-diagnosis.ts`)
   207→
   208→Composes the classified root cause into a `CreateLearningInput` and delegates to `suggestLearning()`.
   209→
   210→**Mapping**:
   211→```typescript
   212→function rootCauseToLearningInput(
   213→  rootCause: RootCauseResult,
   214→  cluster: ObservationCluster,
   215→): CreateLearningInput {
   216→  return {
   217→    text: rootCause.proposed_learning_text,
   218→    learningType: rootCause.proposed_learning_type, // LLM determines type directly
   219→    source: "agent",
   220→    suggestedBy: "observer",
   221→    patternConfidence: rootCause.confidence,
   222→    targetAgents: rootCause.target_agents,
   223→    evidenceIds: cluster.observations.map(obs => ({ table: "observation", id: obs.id })),
   224→  };
   225→}
   226→```
   227→
   228→**Existing gates** (handled by `suggestLearning()`):
   229→1. Rate limit: max 5 per agent per workspace per 7 days
   230→2. Dismissed similarity: KNN on dismissed learnings, skip if similarity > 0.85
   231→
   232→### 4. Coverage Checker (embedded in proposer)
   233→
   234→Before calling `suggestLearning()`, checks if an active learning already covers the pattern:
   235→
   236→1. Generate embedding for proposed learning text
   237→2. KNN query against active learnings (two-step pattern)
   238→3. If any match with similarity > 0.80: skip and log `observer.learning.coverage_skip` with matched learning text. No observation created — this is a dedup signal, not a user-facing finding.
   239→
   240→This is distinct from the dismissed similarity check (which checks *dismissed* learnings). Both run: coverage check first, then `suggestLearning()` handles rate limit + dismissed check.
   241→
   242→## Integration Points
   243→
   244→### Graph Scan Extension
   245→
   246→The diagnostic pipeline plugs into the **end** of `runGraphScan()`, after pattern synthesis:

   251→  ├── 2. Stale blocked tasks (existing)

   265→
   266→For the event-driven path (`POST /api/observe/:table/:id`), the Observer can also suggest learnings when it detects a repeated pattern during single-entity verification. This is lighter weight than graph scan:
   267→

   269→- If threshold met, run the diagnostic pipeline on the entity-scoped cluster

If a pending learning exists with embedding similarity > 0.80 to the proposed text, skip (graph scan already proposed it).
   271→- This catches patterns faster than waiting for the next scheduled scan while avoiding duplicate proposals

   334→## ADR
   335→
   336→### ADR-031: Root Cause Trace for Observer Learning Proposals
   337→
   338→**Status**: Proposed
   339→
   340→**Context**: The Observer detects patterns (repeated contradictions, observation clusters, anomalies) but can only express them as observations. US-AL-002 specifies three data sources for learning suggestions, with the Observer responsible for trace-based detection and observation escalation. The question is whether the Observer should suggest learnings based on **frequency alone** (3 occurrences = suggest) or **diagnostic reasoning** (classify the root cause, propose a categorized fix).
   341→
   342→**Decision**: Diagnostic reasoning via LLM-based root cause classification. The Observer runs a "Root Cause Trace" that classifies patterns into policy failure / context failure / behavioral drift, then proposes a learning with the appropriate `learning_type`.
   343→
   344→**Alternatives Considered**:
   345→
   346→1. **Frequency-only**: Suggest a learning whenever 3+ observations cluster on the same topic. Text extracted from observation representative. No classification.
   347→   - Rejected: Produces generic learnings ("stop doing X") without diagnosing why. Doesn't distinguish between "the rules are wrong" and "the agent isn't following existing rules." The human reviewer gets a suggestion without the reasoning trace.
   348→
   349→2. **Human-triggered only**: Observer creates a special "pattern detected" observation. Human reads it and manually creates a learning.
   350→   - Rejected: Adds friction. Human must diagnose the root cause themselves. Doesn't leverage the graph traversal the Observer already does.
   351→
   352→3. **Rule-based classification**: Hardcoded heuristics (e.g., "if observation mentions policy → policy_failure").
   353→   - Rejected: Too brittle. Real patterns often span multiple categories. LLM classification with structured output gives reasoning traces.
   354→
   355→**Consequences**:
   356→- Positive: Learning proposals include diagnosis and evidence trail. Human reviewer sees *why* the Observer thinks this fix is needed, not just *what* to fix. Category mapping ensures the learning is the right type (constraint vs instruction).
   357→- Positive: Reuses existing `suggestLearning()` gates — no new rate limiting or dismissed check infrastructure.
   358→- Negative: Adds one LLM call per observation cluster during graph scan. Bounded by cluster count (typically 0-5 per scan). Cost: ~$0.01-0.05 per scan cycle.
   359→- Negative: Requires observer model to be configured. When unavailable, diagnostic pipeline is skipped entirely (observations still created, just not escalated to learnings).
   360→

    93→## Architecture Decision: Root Cause Trace
    94→
    95→### The Three-Question Framework
    96→
    97→When the Observer detects a pattern (observation cluster, repeated contradiction, or anomaly pattern), it performs a **Root Cause Trace** — an LLM-based diagnostic that classifies the failure into one of three categories:
    98→
    99→| Category | Question | Example | Learning Type | Target |
   100→|----------|----------|---------|---------------|--------|
   101→| **Policy Failure** | "Did the rules allow something they shouldn't have?" | Policy permitted $500 spend but should cap at $200 for this agent role | `constraint` | Policy owner / affected agents |
   102→| **Context Failure** | "Did the agent lack information it needed?" | Agent didn't know the API was in maintenance mode | `instruction` | Affected agent type(s) |
   103→| **Behavioral Drift** | "Did the agent ignore a rule it already had?" | Agent kept retrying a broken endpoint despite a "fail fast" learning | `constraint` | Drifting agent type |
   104→
   105→### Mapping to Existing Learning Types
   106→
   107→The three root cause categories map directly to the existing `learning_type` enum:
   108→
   109→| Root Cause | `learning_type` | Rationale |
   110→|------------|-----------------|-----------|
   111→| Policy failure | `constraint` | Must-follow rule that tightens boundaries |
   112→| Context failure | `instruction` | Conditional guidance — "when X, inject Y into context" |
   113→| Behavioral drift | `constraint` | Reinforcement of existing rule (may supersede weak version) |
   114→
   115→No schema changes needed. The existing `learning` table already supports all three categories.
   116→
   117→## Component Design
   118→
   119→### 1. Observation Clusterer (`observer/learning-diagnosis.ts`)
   120→
   121→Groups open observations by embedding similarity to find recurring patterns.
   122→
   123→**Input**: Workspace record, minimum cluster size (default: 3), time window (default: 14 days)
   124→
   125→**Algorithm**:
   126→1. Query open/acknowledged observations from the past 14 days with embeddings
   127→2. For each observation, find neighbors via KNN (two-step pattern)
   128→3. Group into clusters where pairwise similarity > 0.75
   129→4. Filter clusters with size >= threshold
   130→5. Deduplicate: check if any active learning already covers the cluster (KNN on active learnings, similarity > 0.80 → skip)
   131→
   132→**Output**: `Array<ObservationCluster>` where each cluster contains observation records and a representative text.
   133→
   134→```typescript
   135→type ObservationCluster = {
   136→  observations: Array<{ id: string; text: string; severity: string; entityRefs: string[] }>;
   137→  representativeText: string;
   138→  clusterSize: number;
   139→};
   140→```
   141→
   142→### 2. Root Cause Classifier (`observer/learning-diagnosis.ts`)
   143→
   144→LLM-based classification using `generateObject` with structured output.
   145→
   146→**Input**: Observation cluster + related entity context (decisions, tasks, policies linked via `observes` edges)
   147→
   148→**Schema** (Zod):
   149→```typescript
   150→const rootCauseSchema = z.object({
   151→  category: z.enum(["policy_failure", "context_failure", "behavioral_drift"]),
   152→  should_propose_learning: z.boolean().describe("True ONLY if confidence >= 0.70 AND high conviction in category and proposed text. False if root cause is ambiguous or learning too generic."),
   153→  proposed_learning_type: z.enum(["constraint", "instruction"]).describe("constraint for must-follow rules (policy/behavioral fixes), instruction for conditional guidance (context fixes)"),
   154→  reasoning: z.string().describe("Why this category was chosen, referencing specific evidence"),
   155→  proposed_learning_text: z.string().describe("The behavioral rule that would prevent recurrence"),
   156→  target_agents: z.array(z.string()).describe("Which agent types should receive this learning"),
   157→  evidence_refs: z.array(z.string()).describe("table:id references to supporting evidence"),
   158→  confidence: z.number().min(0).max(1),
   159→});
   160→```
   161→
   162→**Prompt structure**:
   163→```
   164→You are the Observer agent performing root cause analysis.
   165→
   166→## Pattern Detected
   167→{cluster representative text with observation quotes}
   168→
   169→## Related Entities
   170→{decisions, tasks, policies linked to the observations}
   171→
   172→## Existing Active Learnings
   173→{learnings already active for the target agent types}
   174→
   175→## Classification Instructions
   176→Determine WHY this pattern keeps recurring:
   177→
   178→1. Policy Failure: The governance rules allowed something they shouldn't.
   179→   → Propose a constraint that tightens the boundary.
   180→
   181→2. Context Failure: The agent lacked information it needed to act correctly.
   182→   → Propose an instruction that injects the missing context.
   183→
   184→3. Behavioral Drift: The agent had the information but didn't apply it.
   185→   → Propose a constraint that reinforces the expected behavior.
   186→
   187→Set should_propose_learning to true ONLY if:
   188→- confidence >= 0.70
   189→- You have high conviction in both the category AND the proposed text
   190→- The proposed learning is specific enough to be actionable
   191→
   192→Set should_propose_learning to false if:
   193→- The root cause is ambiguous or could fit multiple categories
   194→- The proposed learning text is too generic ("be more careful")
   195→- The evidence is insufficient to justify a permanent behavioral rule
   196→
   197→For proposed_learning_type, choose based on the fix needed:
   198→- "constraint" for must-follow rules (policy fixes, behavioral reinforcement)
   199→- "instruction" for conditional guidance (context injection, situational awareness)
   200→```
   201→
   202→**Proposal gate** (two-check): The LLM outputs `should_propose_learning` (its own assessment) AND `confidence` (numeric). The code gates on both:
   203→- If `should_propose_learning === false` OR `confidence < 0.70`: create an observation instead of a learning proposal: "Emerging pattern detected but root cause unclear. Monitoring."
   204→- This dual gate prevents the LLM from proposing low-confidence learnings while still allowing it to decline even when confidence is technically high (e.g., "I'm confident this is a policy failure, but the proposed fix is too vague").
   205→
   206→### 3. Learning Proposer (`observer/learning-diagnosis.ts`)
   207→
   208→Composes the classified root cause into a `CreateLearningInput` and delegates to `suggestLearning()`.
   209→
   210→**Mapping**:
   211→```typescript
   212→function rootCauseToLearningInput(
   213→  rootCause: RootCauseResult,
   214→  cluster: ObservationCluster,
   215→): CreateLearningInput {
   216→  return {
   217→    text: rootCause.proposed_learning_text,
   218→    learningType: rootCause.proposed_learning_type, // LLM determines type directly
   219→    source: "agent",
   220→    suggestedBy: "observer",
   221→    patternConfidence: rootCause.confidence,
   222→    targetAgents: rootCause.target_agents,
   223→    evidenceIds: cluster.observations.map(obs => ({ table: "observation", id: obs.id })),
   224→  };
   225→}
   226→```
   227→
   228→**Existing gates** (handled by `suggestLearning()`):
   229→1. Rate limit: max 5 per agent per workspace per 7 days
   230→2. Dismissed similarity: KNN on dismissed learnings, skip if similarity > 0.85
   231→
   232→### 4. Coverage Checker (embedded in proposer)
   233→
   234→Before calling `suggestLearning()`, checks if an active learning already covers the pattern:
   235→
   236→1. Generate embedding for proposed learning text
   237→2. KNN query against active learnings (two-step pattern)
   238→3. If any match with similarity > 0.80: skip and log `observer.learning.coverage_skip` with matched learning text. No observation created — this is a dedup signal, not a user-facing finding.
   239→
   240→This is distinct from the dismissed similarity check (which checks *dismissed* learnings). Both run: coverage check first, then `suggestLearning()` handles rate limit + dismissed check.
   241→

   334→## ADR
   335→
   336→### ADR-031: Root Cause Trace for Observer Learning Proposals
   337→
   338→**Status**: Proposed
   339→
   340→**Context**: The Observer detects patterns (repeated contradictions, observation clusters, anomalies) but can only express them as observations. US-AL-002 specifies three data sources for learning suggestions, with the Observer responsible for trace-based detection and observation escalation. The question is whether the Observer should suggest learnings based on **frequency alone** (3 occurrences = suggest) or **diagnostic reasoning** (classify the root cause, propose a categorized fix).
   341→
   342→**Decision**: Diagnostic reasoning via LLM-based root cause classification. The Observer runs a "Root Cause Trace" that classifies patterns into policy failure / context failure / behavioral drift, then proposes a learning with the appropriate `learning_type`.
   343→
   344→**Alternatives Considered**:
   345→
   346→1. **Frequency-only**: Suggest a learning whenever 3+ observations cluster on the same topic. Text extracted from observation representative. No classification.
   347→   - Rejected: Produces generic learnings ("stop doing X") without diagnosing why. Doesn't distinguish between "the rules are wrong" and "the agent isn't following existing rules." The human reviewer gets a suggestion without the reasoning trace.
   348→
   349→2. **Human-triggered only**: Observer creates a special "pattern detected" observation. Human reads it and manually creates a learning.
   350→   - Rejected: Adds friction. Human must diagnose the root cause themselves. Doesn't leverage the graph traversal the Observer already does.
   351→
   352→3. **Rule-based classification**: Hardcoded heuristics (e.g., "if observation mentions policy → policy_failure").
   353→   - Rejected: Too brittle. Real patterns often span multiple categories. LLM classification with structured output gives reasoning traces.
   354→
   355→**Consequences**:
   356→- Positive: Learning proposals include diagnosis and evidence trail. Human reviewer sees *why* the Observer thinks this fix is needed, not just *what* to fix. Category mapping ensures the learning is the right type (constraint vs instruction).
   357→- Positive: Reuses existing `suggestLearning()` gates — no new rate limiting or dismissed check infrastructure.
   358→- Negative: Adds one LLM call per observation cluster during graph scan. Bounded by cluster count (typically 0-5 per scan). Cost: ~$0.01-0.05 per scan cycle.
   359→- Negative: Requires observer model to be configured. When unavailable, diagnostic pipeline is skipped entirely (observations still created, just not escalated to learnings).

   331→## SCIM 2.0 Provisioning API
   332→
   333→Header-based API versioning via Spring Framework 7 (`API-Version: 1.0`). See [scim/README.md](scim/README.md) for full documentation.
   334→
   335→**Key packages:** `com.keeplearning.auth.scim`
   336→
   337→| Class | Purpose |
   338→|-------|---------|
   339→| `ScimUserController` | SCIM User CRUD (`/api/scim/v2/realms/{realm}/Users`) |
   340→| `ScimBulkController` | Bulk create/update (`/api/scim/v2/realms/{realm}/Bulk`) |
   341→| `ScimChecksumController` | User checksum (`/api/scim/v2/realms/{realm}/Users/checksum`) |
   342→| `ScimDiscoveryController` | ServiceProviderConfig, Schemas, ResourceTypes |
   343→| `ScimUserService` | Business logic wrapping UserRepository |
   344→| `ScimBulkService` | Processes bulk POST/PUT operations (per-operation error handling) |
   345→| `ScimChecksumService` | Computes deterministic SHA-256 user checksum via `ScimChecksumUtil` |
   346→| `ScimUserMapper` | User entity ↔ SCIM resource mapping |
   347→| `ScimFilterTranslator` | SCIM filter → R2DBC SQL translation |
   348→| `ScimExceptionHandler` | RFC 7644 §3.12 error responses |

   350→### Forge SDK (`forge/`)
   351→
   352→Client SDK for SCIM 2.0 user provisioning. Uses Spring WebFlux + OAuth2 client credentials.
   353→
   354→**Key Types (all renamed from `Forge*` to `Auth*` — old names kept as `@Deprecated` typealiases):**
   355→
   356→| Class | Purpose |
   357→|-------|---------|
   358→| `AuthUser` | Abstract base class for user domain entities (extend to add custom fields) |
   359→| `AuthRepository<T>` | Generic repository interface with CRUD + `createAll`/`updateAll` bulk ops |
   360→| `DefaultAuthRepository<T>` | Default implementation mapping `AuthUser` ↔ `ScimUserResource` |
   361→| `ScimClient` | Low-level SCIM HTTP client (`listUsers`, `getUser`, `createUser`, `replaceUser`, `patchUser`, `deleteUser`, `bulkRequest`, `getChecksum`) |
   362→| `AuthProperties` | Configuration: `forge.base-url`, `forge.realm-name`, `forge.client-registration-id`, `forge.api-version`, `forge.startup-sync.enabled` |
   363→| `AuthAutoConfiguration` | Auto-configures `forgeWebClient`, `scimClient`, and conditionally `startupSyncRunner` |
   364→| `AuthException` | Exception thrown on SCIM API errors (wraps HTTP status + `ScimErrorResponse`) |
   365→| `EnableAuth` | Optional annotation for explicit SDK opt-in |
   366→
   367→**Startup Sync (`forge/src/main/kotlin/.../sync/`):**
   368→
   369→| Class | Purpose |
   370→|-------|---------|
   371→| `AuthStartupSync<T>` | Abstract class clients extend — provides `fetchAllLocalUsers()` and `mapToAuthUser()` |
   372→| `StartupSyncRunner<T>` | `ApplicationRunner` that checksums local vs remote users and bulk-syncs differences on startup |
   373→
   374→Sync algorithm: compute local checksum → compare with `GET /Users/checksum` → if different, fetch all remote, diff by email → bulk POST creates + bulk PUT updates. Remote-only users ignored. Failures non-fatal.
   375→
   376→`StartupSyncRunner` is registered only when an `AuthStartupSync` bean exists AND `forge.startup-sync.enabled=true` (default).
   377→
   378→### ParadeDB Setup (Required for V2+ migrations)
   379→
   380→PostgreSQL must have ParadeDB extensions installed:
   381→
   382→1. Install ParadeDB binaries: https://docs.paradedb.com/deploy/self-hosted/extension
   383→2. **Postgres 17+**: No config changes needed, extensions load dynamically
   384→3. **Postgres 16 and earlier**: Add to `postgresql.conf` and restart:
   385→   ```ini
   386→   shared_preload_libraries = 'pg_search'
   387→   ```
   388→4. Extensions created by migration: `pg_search` (BM25), `vector` (pgvector)

It parses session history from multiple AI coding tools (Claude Code, Cursor, Codex CLI, Copilot CLI), stores structured data in a local SQLite database, and provides both terminal analytics and a browser-based dashboard with LLM-powered insights.

    11→**Architecture:** Single-repo pnpm workspace monorepo with three packages: CLI, dashboard (Vite + React SPA), and server (Hono API).
    12→
    13→**Privacy model:** Fully local-first. No cloud accounts, no sign-ups, no data leaves the machine. SQLite database at `~/.code-insights/data.db`.
    14→
    15→**Purpose:** A free, open-source tool helping developers who use multiple AI coding tools analyze their sessions, collect insights, track decisions and learnings, and build knowledge over time.

    19→## Development Philosophy (CRITICAL)
    20→
    21→**No MVPs, no prototypes, no half-measures.** This product is LIVE with real users. Every feature ships as a full, complete implementation. We do not build "minimum viable" anything — we build the real thing, iterate based on feedback, and revert or update if it doesn't work out.
    22→
    23→This principle applies to planning, designing, AND implementation:
    24→- **Planning:** Don't scope down to "MVP facet set" vs "ideal set." Design the complete solution.
    25→- **Designing:** Don't propose phased rollouts with "ship phase 1, add phase 2 later." Design it right the first time.
    26→- **Implementing:** Don't cut corners with "we can add this later." Build it now or explicitly decide not to build it.
    27→
    28→If something needs to change after shipping, we change it. That's cheaper than shipping incomplete work that creates technical debt and confuses users.

   135→## Architecture
   136→
   137→### Data Flow
   138→
   139→```
   140→Source tool session files -> Provider (discover + parse) -> SQLite -> Dashboard (localhost)
   141→                                                         -> CLI stats commands
   142→```
   143→
   144→### SQLite Database
   145→
   146→- Location: `~/.code-insights/data.db`
   147→- WAL mode enabled for concurrent reads during CLI sync
   148→- Uses better-sqlite3 (synchronous, fast, no async overhead)
   149→- Schema managed via versioned migrations applied on startup
   150→- All timestamps stored as ISO 8601 strings
   151→
   152→### Provider Architecture
   153→
   154→All source tools are integrated via the `SessionProvider` interface (`providers/types.ts`):
   155→
   156→```typescript
   157→interface SessionProvider {
   158→  getProviderName(): string;                                    // e.g. 'claude-code', 'cursor'
   159→  discover(options?: { projectFilter?: string }): Promise<string[]>;  // Find session files
   160→  parse(filePath: string): Promise<ParsedSession | null>;       // Parse into common format
   161→}
   162→```
   163→
   164→Providers are registered in `providers/registry.ts`. To add a new source tool:
   165→1. Create `providers/<name>.ts` implementing `SessionProvider`
   166→2. Register it in `providers/registry.ts`
   167→3. Add color entry to dashboard `SOURCE_TOOL_COLORS`
   168→4. Add avatar case to dashboard `getAssistantConfig()`
   169→5. Add tool name aliases if tool names differ
   170→6. Add option to source filter dropdown
   171→
   172→### Directory Structure (`/cli/src/`)
   173→- `commands/` - CLI commands (init, sync, status, dashboard, reset, install-hook, config)
   174→- `commands/stats/` - Stats command suite (4-layer architecture):
   175→  - `data/types.ts` - `StatsDataSource` interface, `SessionRow`, error classes
   176→  - `data/source.ts` - Data source factory
   177→  - `data/local.ts` - SQLite data source implementation
   178→  - `data/aggregation.ts` - Pure compute functions (overview, cost, projects, today, models)
   179→  - `data/fuzzy-match.ts` - Levenshtein distance for `--project` name matching
   180→  - `render/` - Terminal rendering (colors, format, charts, layout)
   181→  - `actions/` - Action handlers for each subcommand + shared error handler
   182→  - `index.ts` - Command tree with lazy imports
   183→  - `shared.ts` - Shared CLI flags
   184→- `providers/` - Source tool providers (claude-code, cursor, codex, copilot-cli)
   185→- `providers/types.ts` - `SessionProvider` interface
   186→- `providers/registry.ts` - Provider registration and lookup
   187→- `parser/jsonl.ts` - JSONL file parsing (used by ClaudeCodeProvider)
   188→- `parser/titles.ts` - Smart session title generation (5-tier fallback strategy)
   189→- `db/` - SQLite schema, migrations, query functions
   190→- `utils/config.ts` - Configuration management (~/.code-insights/config.json)
   191→- `utils/device.ts` - Device ID generation, git remote detection, stable project IDs
   192→- `utils/paths.ts` - Virtual path handling (shared by sync and stats)
   193→- `types.ts` - TypeScript type definitions (SINGLE SOURCE OF TRUTH)
   194→- `index.ts` - CLI entry point (Commander.js)
   195→
   196→### SQLite Tables
   197→- `projects` - Project metadata (id is hash of git remote URL or path)
   198→- `sessions` - Session metadata with generated titles, character classification, device info
   199→- `insights` - LLM-generated insights (types: summary, decision, learning, technique, prompt_quality)
   200→- `messages` - Full message content (stored during sync)

   204→## Type Architecture (CRITICAL)
   205→
   206→Types are defined **once** in `cli/src/types.ts`. This is the single source of truth for the entire monorepo.
   207→
   208→```
   209→CLI (cli/src/types.ts)       -> Writes to SQLite
   210→Server (server/src/)         -> Reads from SQLite, exposes via API
   211→Dashboard (dashboard/src/)   -> Reads from Server API

   214→**Rules:**
   215→- New SQLite columns MUST have defaults or be nullable (backward compatible)
   216→- Type changes in `types.ts` must be reflected in SQLite migrations
   217→- TA owns this contract — flag all type changes to `technical-architect`

   219→### Key Types (`cli/src/types.ts`)

   222→- `Insight` - Types: summary | decision | learning | technique | prompt_quality; source: 'llm'
   223→- `SessionCharacter` - 7 session classifications: deep_focus | bug_hunt | feature_build | exploration | refactor | learning | quick_task
   224→- `ClaudeInsightConfig` - Config format
   225→- `SyncState` - File modification tracking for incremental sync

   243→
   244→### Orchestrator Role (Main Claude)
   245→
   246→The orchestrator (you, the main Claude session) coordinates agents. Rules:
   247→
   248→**You CAN:**
   249→- Edit `CLAUDE.md` directly (you own it)
   250→- Delegate implementation to the appropriate agent
   251→- Run agents in parallel IF no dependencies exist
   252→- Make final decisions when agents disagree
   253→
   254→**You MUST NOT:**
   255→- Implement code directly when an agent should do it
   256→- Skip the ceremony steps
   257→- Merge PRs (only the founder does this)

   259→### Pre-Spawn Dependency Check (MANDATORY)
   260→
   261→Before parallelizing agents, verify:
   262→
   263→1. List each agent's **inputs** — What does it need?
   264→2. List each agent's **outputs** — What does it produce?
   265→3. Map **dependencies** — Does B need A's output?
   266→4. Decide: **Sequential or Parallel**
   267→
   268→**Safe to Parallelize:**
   269→- Independent domains with no shared types or schema changes
   270→- Read-only research tasks
   271→- CLI bug fix + Dashboard UI fix (if no shared state)
   272→
   273→**Must Run Sequentially:**
   274→- TA (type decision) -> Engineer (implement types)
   275→- TA (schema decision) -> Engineer (implement)
   276→- Any change touching `types.ts`

   284→```
   285→Step 1:  Founder assigns task or identifies work

   287→Step 3:  Dev agent reviews context (source files, types, existing patterns)

   297→### Step-by-Step Ownership

   300→|------|-------|---------------|
   301→| 1-2 | Orchestrator | Correct agent identified |
   302→| 3 | Dev agent | Files reviewed, understanding confirmed |
   303→| 4 | Dev agent -> TA | Questions resolved, no assumptions |
   304→| 5 | TA | Explicit approval or changes requested |
   305→| 6 | TA + Dev agent | Both confirm ready to implement |
   306→| 7 | Dev agent | Clean repo, feature branch created |
   307→| 8 | Dev agent | Code implemented, CI passes locally |
   308→| 9 | TA + Outsider + Dev agent | All review comments addressed |
   309→| 10 | **Founder only** | PR merged to main |

   311→### When to Engage TA (Steps 4-5)
   312→
   313→**Required (schema/contract impact):**
   314→- Adding/modifying SQLite columns or tables
   315→- Changing type definitions in `types.ts`
   316→- Modifying data contract (what providers write vs what dashboard reads)
   317→- Changing configuration format
   318→- Adding new server API endpoints
   319→
   320→**Not required (domain-internal):**
   321→- New command flags
   322→- Parser improvements
   323→- Terminal UI changes
   324→- Dashboard component styling
   325→- LLM provider additions

   327→### CI Simulation Gate (Step 8 — BLOCKING)

   329→Before creating ANY PR:

   335→**If ANY check fails:** Fix before creating PR. Never rely on CI.

   389→## Triple-Layer Code Review (MANDATORY)
   390→
   391→All PRs go through multi-layer review:
   392→
   393→### Phase 1: Parallel Independent Reviews (No Cross-Contamination)
   394→
   395→| Role | Reviewer | Focus |
   396→|------|----------|-------|
   397→| **INSIDER** | `technical-architect` | Type alignment, schema contract, architecture patterns |
   398→| **OUTSIDER** | `code-review:code-review` skill | Security, best practices, logic bugs, fresh perspective |
   399→
   400→**CRITICAL:** Phase 1 reviews run in parallel. TA must NOT read outsider comments during initial review.
   401→
   402→### Phase 2: TA Synthesis (After Both Reviews Complete)
   403→
   404→TA reads outsider comments, does 2nd pass, and creates consolidated list:
   405→
   406→```markdown
   407→## TA Synthesis: [PR Title]
   408→
   409→**Must Fix:**
   410→1. [issue and required fix]
   411→
   412→**Won't Fix (With Rationale):**
   413→1. [outsider comment] - Reason: [domain-specific justification]
   414→
   415→**Final Verdict:** Ready / Changes Required / Escalate to Founder
   416→```
   417→
   418→### Phase 3: Dev Agent Implements Fixes
   419→
   420→Dev agent receives consolidated list, implements fixes, re-runs CI gate, updates PR.
   421→
   422→### CRITICAL: Agents NEVER Merge PRs
   423→
   424→```
   425→FORBIDDEN: gh pr merge (or any merge command)
   426→CORRECT: Report "PR #XX is ready for merge" and STOP
   427→```
   428→
   429→**Only the founder merges PRs.** This is enforced by hookify rule `block-pr-merge`.

   483→## Key Patterns
   484→
   485→### Session Character Classification
   486→Sessions are classified into one of 7 types based on tool call patterns:
   487→- `deep_focus`, `bug_hunt`, `feature_build`, `exploration`, `refactor`, `learning`, `quick_task`
   488→
   489→### Title Generation
   490→Multi-tier fallback: Claude summary -> user message (scored) -> character-based -> generic fallback.
   491→
   492→### SQLite Integration
   493→- Uses better-sqlite3 with WAL mode for concurrent access
   494→- Schema versioned via migrations applied on startup
   495→- Incremental sync tracks file modification times in `~/.code-insights/sync-state.json`
   496→- Project IDs derived from git remote URLs (stable across devices) with path-hash fallback
   497→
   498→### Configuration
   499→- Config stored at `~/.code-insights/config.json` (mode 0o600)
   500→- Sync state at `~/.code-insights/sync-state.json`
   501→- Device ID at `~/.code-insights/device-id`
   502→- SQLite database at `~/.code-insights/data.db`
   503→
   504→### Hook Integration
   505→- `install-hook` modifies `~/.claude/settings.json` to add a Stop hook
   506→- Hook runs `code-insights sync -q` automatically when Claude Code sessions end
   507→
   508→### Multi-Source Support
   509→
   510→The CLI and dashboard support sessions from multiple AI coding tools via the `sourceTool` field.
   511→
   512→**Supported sources:** `'claude-code'` (default), `'cursor'`, `'codex-cli'`, `'copilot-cli'`
   513→
   514→**Adding a new source tool:**
   515→1. CLI: Create a new provider in `cli/src/providers/` implementing `SessionProvider`
   516→2. Register in `cli/src/providers/registry.ts`
   517→3. Dashboard: Add color entry to `SOURCE_TOOL_COLORS`
   518→4. Dashboard: Add avatar case to `getAssistantConfig()`
   519→5. Dashboard: Add tool name aliases (if tool names differ)
   520→6. Dashboard: Add option to source filter dropdown

1→# Research: OpenClaw Gateway Protocol Integration for Brain
     2→
     3→**Date**: 2026-03-15
     4→**Research Question**: Are people running multiple OpenClaw instances? Would it make sense for Brain to support the OpenClaw Gateway Protocol to control and manage them?
     5→
     6→---
     7→
     8→## 1. Are People Running Multiple OpenClaw Instances?
     9→
    10→**Yes — and it's a growing pattern with real pain points.**
    11→
    12→### Evidence
    13→
    14→**Single Gateway, Multiple Agents (common)**: OpenClaw's Gateway natively supports hosting multiple agents side-by-side within one process. Each agent gets its own workspace, session isolation, and personality (`AGENTS.md`, `SOUL.md`). Routing is deterministic via channel bindings — e.g., WhatsApp DMs go to Agent A, Telegram goes to Agent B. This is the default multi-agent setup.
    15→
    16→**Multiple Gateways (emerging power-user pattern)**: A growing subset of users runs *multiple Gateway processes* on the same host or across hosts. OpenClaw officially documents this via `--profile` flags and isolation checklists (`OPENCLAW_CONFIG_PATH`, `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, unique ports).
    17→
    18→Key drivers for multi-gateway:
    19→
    20→| Driver | Description | Source |
    21→|--------|-------------|--------|
    22→| **Credential isolation** | Microsoft's security research flagged "credential bleed" — all agents in a single gateway share the same secrets pool. A compromised plugin can harvest credentials meant for a different agent. | [Microsoft Defender Security Research](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/security/blog/2026/02/19/running-openclaw-safely-identity-isolation-runtime-risk/) |
    23→| **Trust tier separation** | Users split gateways by trust level: personal, work, dev tools, client-facing. Each tier gets its own secrets, API keys, and blast radius. | [Multi-Gateway Need Analysis (Trilogy AI)](https://trilogyai.substack.com/p/the-need-for-a-multi-gateway-openclaw) |
    24→| **Managed fleet deployments** | DigitalOcean App Platform offers elastic scaling for multi-agent OpenClaw with zero-downtime Git-driven upgrades. | [DigitalOcean Blog](https://www.digitalocean.com/blog/openclaw-digitalocean-app-platform) |
    25→| **Rescue bots** | A second gateway as a "rescue bot" that can debug/reconfigure the primary gateway if it breaks. | [OpenClaw Multiple Gateways docs](https://docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/multiple-gateways) |
    26→
    27→**Community tooling confirms demand**: [openclaw-mission-control](https://github.com/abhi1693/openclaw-mission-control) (2.4k stars, 532 forks, 1,071 commits) is a full orchestration dashboard built on the Gateway Protocol for managing agents, assigning tasks, and coordinating multi-agent collaboration.
    28→
    29→### Scale of the Pattern
    30→
    31→- Users routinely run 5-15+ agents per gateway
    32→- Power users run 3-5 gateway tiers (personal/work/dev/client/rescue)
    33→- Enterprise/team deployments use DigitalOcean or self-hosted fleet infrastructure
    34→- The multi-gateway pattern is ~6 months old but growing rapidly due to security concerns
    35→
    36→---
    37→
    38→## 2. OpenClaw Gateway Protocol — Technical Summary
    39→
    40→The Gateway Protocol is a **WebSocket-based control plane** that serves as the single transport for all OpenClaw clients (CLI, web UI, macOS app, iOS/Android nodes, headless nodes).
    41→
    42→### Transport & Framing
    43→
    44→- WebSocket with text frames containing JSON payloads
    45→- First frame must be a `connect` request
    46→- Protocol version negotiation via `minProtocol`/`maxProtocol` (currently v3)
    47→- Heartbeat via configurable `tickIntervalMs` (default 15s)
    48→
    49→### Authentication & Device Identity
    50→
    51→- Challenge-response handshake: server sends `connect.challenge` with nonce, client signs and responds
    52→- Signature payloads v2/v3 (v3 binds platform + device family)
    53→- Device tokens issued after pairing, scoped to connection role + scopes
    54→- Token rotation/revocation via `device.token.rotate` / `device.token.revoke`
    55→- Optional TLS with cert fingerprint pinning
    56→- Gateway token auth via `OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_TOKEN`
    57→
    58→### Roles & Scopes
    59→
    60→| Role | Purpose | Scopes |
    61→|------|---------|--------|
    62→| **operator** | Full control plane access (CLI, web UI) | `operator.read`, `operator.write`, `operator.pairing` |
    63→| **node** | Device/sensor nodes (iOS, headless) | Capabilities + commands (e.g., `camera.snap`, `screen.record`) |
    64→
    65→### API Surface
    66→
    67→The protocol exposes the **full gateway API**: status, channels, models, chat, agent management, sessions, nodes, exec approvals. Schemas are defined in TypeBox (`src/gateway/protocol/schema.ts`) and auto-generated for TypeScript and Swift.
    68→
    69→### Key Methods
    70→
    71→- `connect` — handshake with role/scope declaration
    72→- Agent/session management (create, list, status, history)
    73→- Chat (send messages, stream responses)
    74→- Tool invocation and exec approvals
    75→- Node commands (camera, canvas, screen, location, voice)
    76→- Presence (online/offline status of connected clients)
    77→
    78→---
    79→
    80→## 3. Would Brain Integration Make Sense?
    81→
    82→### What Brain Could Offer OpenClaw Users
    83→
    84→Brain's value proposition for OpenClaw users maps directly to their pain points:
    85→
    86→| OpenClaw Pain Point | Brain Solution |
    87→|---------------------|----------------|
    88→| **Agents have no shared memory** — each agent's workspace is isolated, sessions don't cross-talk | Brain's knowledge graph gives all agents shared context without session coupling |
    89→| **No cross-agent coordination** — routing is deterministic (binding rules), not intelligent | Brain's observation/suggestion system enables emergent coordination through shared state |
    90→| **No decision governance** — agents act within sandbox rules but there's no decision audit trail | Brain tracks every decision with provenance, author, reasoning, and approval chain |
    91→| **Multi-gateway management is manual** — tier configs, port allocation, secret rotation are all hand-managed | Brain could serve as the control plane that orchestrates multiple gateways |
    92→| **Context drift across sessions** — compaction and session pruning lose long-term continuity | Brain's persistent graph preserves decisions and learnings across all sessions |
    93→
    94→### Integration Architecture Options
    95→
    96→#### Option A: Brain as Gateway Protocol Client (Operator)
    97→
    98→Brain connects to one or more OpenClaw Gateways as an `operator` role client via WebSocket. This gives Brain:
    99→
   100→- Real-time visibility into agent sessions, status, and chat
   101→- Ability to send messages/instructions to agents
   102→- Access to exec approvals (Brain becomes the approval authority)
   103→- Session history for graph extraction
   104→
   105→```
   106→Brain Server
   107→  ├─ WS → OpenClaw Gateway 1 (personal tier)
   108→  ├─ WS → OpenClaw Gateway 2 (work tier)
   109→  └─ WS → OpenClaw Gateway 3 (dev tier)
   110→      │
   111→      └─ Gateway Protocol (operator.read + operator.write)
   112→           ├─ Monitor agent sessions
   113→           ├─ Extract decisions/observations from chat
   114→           ├─ Inject context from knowledge graph
   115→           └─ Approve/deny exec requests via policy graph
   116→```
   117→
   118→**Pros**: Full bidirectional control. Brain becomes the "brain" for OpenClaw agents — exactly what it's designed for. Exec approvals map perfectly to Brain's intent/authority scope model.
   119→
   120→**Cons**: Requires maintaining a WebSocket client for a moving protocol (v3 today). Tight coupling to OpenClaw's protocol evolution.
   121→
   122→#### Option B: Brain as MCP Server for OpenClaw Agents
   123→
   124→OpenClaw already supports MCP. Brain already has an MCP server. OpenClaw agents could connect to Brain's MCP server for context injection — no Gateway Protocol needed.
   125→
   126→```
   127→OpenClaw Agent
   128→  └─ MCP Client → Brain MCP Server
   129→       ├─ get_context (decisions, constraints, tasks)
   130→       ├─ create_observation
   131→       ├─ resolve_decision
   132→       └─ ask_question
   133→```
   134→
   135→**Pros**: Already works today. No new protocol to implement. Each OpenClaw agent independently connects to Brain.
   136→
   137→**Cons**: No centralized control. Brain can't proactively inject context or approve exec requests. Each agent must be configured individually.
   138→
   139→#### Option C: Hybrid — MCP for Context + Gateway Protocol for Control
   140→
   141→Use MCP for the data plane (context injection, decision logging) and the Gateway Protocol for the control plane (monitoring, approvals, orchestration).
   142→
   143→**This is the recommended approach** — it plays to each protocol's strength.
   144→
   145→### Alignment with Brain's Architecture
   146→
   147→| Brain Concept | OpenClaw Mapping | Fit |
   148→|---------------|-----------------|-----|
   149→| **Authority Scopes** | Gateway `scopes` + `permissions` | Direct — Brain's tiered authority maps to OpenClaw's operator scopes |
   150→| **Intent Authorization** | `exec approvals` | Direct — OpenClaw's approval flow is Brain's intent pattern |
   151→| **Agent Sessions** | Gateway sessions + presence | Direct — session tracking already exists in both |
   152→| **Observations** | Chat history extraction | Good — Brain's extraction pipeline can process OpenClaw chat |
   153→| **Policy Graph** | Sandbox/tool policy | Strong — Brain policies could drive OpenClaw sandbox config |
   154→| **Traces** | Session history + tool calls | Good — OpenClaw logs map to Brain's hierarchical traces |
   155→
   156→---
   157→
   158→## 4. Recommendation
   159→
   160→**Yes, supporting the OpenClaw Gateway Protocol is strategically valuable**, but prioritize in phases:
   161→
   162→### Phase 1: MCP Integration (low effort, immediate value)
   163→- Document how to connect OpenClaw agents to Brain's existing MCP server
   164→- This works today with `brain init` — just point OpenClaw's MCP config at Brain
   165→- Zero new code needed in Brain
   166→
   167→### Phase 2: Gateway Protocol Observer (medium effort, high value)
   168→- Implement a read-only Gateway Protocol client (`operator.read` scope)
   169→- Connect to one or more OpenClaw Gateways
   170→- Extract decisions, observations, and context from agent chat sessions
   171→- Feed into Brain's extraction pipeline
   172→- Surface cross-agent contradictions via the Observer
   173→
   174→### Phase 3: Gateway Protocol Controller (higher effort, differentiation)
   175→- Add `operator.write` scope
   176→- Implement exec approval integration — Brain's policy graph becomes the approval authority
   177→- Enable proactive context injection into agent sessions
   178→- Manage multi-gateway fleet configuration from Brain's UI
   179→
   180→### Why This Matters
   181→
   182→OpenClaw has 302k+ GitHub stars and is the fastest-growing AI agent framework. The community is actively building orchestration tooling (Mission Control has 2.4k stars in months). The pain points — no shared memory, no decision governance, manual multi-gateway management — are exactly what Brain solves.
   183→
   184→Brain positioning as **"the brain for your OpenClaw agents"** is a natural GTM narrative that doesn't require replacing anything — just adding the missing coordination layer.
   185→

   134→
   135→## 5. Component Architecture
   136→
   137→### 5.1 Request Pipeline (Synchronous Hot Path)
   138→
   139→```
   140→Agent Request
   141→  |
   142→  +-> [1] Parse request body (extract model, stream flag, metadata)
   143→  +-> [2] Identity Resolution (parse metadata.user_id + X-Brain-* headers)
   144→  +-> [3] Policy Evaluation (model access + budget + rate limit)
   145→  |     |-- DENY -> Return 403/429 with policy_ref + remediation
   146→  |     |-- ALLOW -> continue
   147→  +-> [4] Forward to upstream provider (raw byte relay)
   148→  +-> [5] Return Response to agent (SSE stream or JSON)
   149→```
   150→
   151→**Latency budget**: Steps 1-3 must complete within 10ms p99. Step 4 adds zero overhead (raw byte pipe). Step 5 is the upstream's response time.
   152→
   153→### 5.2 Post-Response Pipeline (Asynchronous, Non-Blocking)
   154→
   155→```
   156→Stream Complete / Response Received
   157→  |
   158→  +-> [6] Extract usage (from SSE buffer or JSON response body)
   159→  +-> [7] Compute cost (pricing table lookup + token math)
   160→  +-> [8] Write llm_call trace node to SurrealDB
   161→  +-> [9] Create RELATE edges (invoked, scoped_to, attributed_to, governed_by)
   162→  +-> [10] On write failure: retry 3x exponential backoff -> stderr JSON fallback
   163→```
   164→
   165→All post-response work runs via `deps.inflight.track()` consistent with Brain's existing async pattern.
   166→
   167→### 5.3 Component Boundaries
   168→
   169→| Component | Responsibility | Driven Port (Input) | Driving Port (Output) |
   170→|-----------|---------------|--------------------|--------------------|
   171→| Anthropic Route | HTTP handling, pipeline orchestration for Anthropic format | `POST /proxy/llm/anthropic/v1/messages` | Forward request, trigger trace |
   172→| OpenAI Route | HTTP handling, pipeline orchestration for OpenAI format | `POST /proxy/llm/openai/v1/chat/completions` | Forward request, trigger trace |
   173→| Identity Resolver | Parse and validate identity signals | Request headers + body metadata | Resolved identity (workspace, session, task) |
   174→| Policy Evaluator | Pre-request authorization | Resolved identity + model | Allow/deny decision with policy trace |
   175→| Request Forwarder | Transparent SSE/JSON relay | Upstream URL + headers + body | Raw byte stream to client |
   176→| SSE Usage Extractor | Parse SSE events for usage data | Raw byte buffer from stream | Token counts + stop reason |
   177→| Cost Calculator | Compute per-request cost | Model + token counts | Cost in USD |
   178→| Trace Writer | Persist trace + edges to graph | Trace data (identity, usage, cost) | llm_call trace node + RELATE edges |
   179→| Pricing Table | Model-to-rate lookup | Model ID | Per-token rates |
   180→| Rate Limiter | Sliding window rate enforcement | Workspace ID | Allow/deny + current count |
   181→| Spend API | Aggregation queries for dashboard | HTTP GET with filters | Spend breakdown JSON |

   185→## 6. Data Model
   186→
   187→### 6.1 Extended `trace` Table (per ADR-042)
   188→
   189→The existing `trace` table is extended with `"llm_call"` as a new type value and LLM-specific optional fields. No new table is created.
   190→
   191→**New fields on `trace`** (optional, populated when `type = "llm_call"`):
   192→```
   193→  - model: option<string>                  -- model ID from response
   194→  - provider: option<string>               -- "anthropic" | "openai"
   195→  - input_tokens: option<int>
   196→  - output_tokens: option<int>
   197→  - cache_creation_tokens: option<int>
   198→  - cache_read_tokens: option<int>
   199→  - cost_usd: option<float>
   200→  - stop_reason: option<string>
   201→  - request_id: option<string>             -- Anthropic's request-id header
   202→```
   203→
   204→**Existing fields reused**: `session` (record<agent_session>), `workspace` (record<workspace>), `duration_ms`, `input`/`output` (FLEXIBLE), `parent_trace`, `actor`, `created_at`.
   205→
   206→**`agent_session` rename**: `opencode_session_id` → `external_session_id` to store Claude Code session UUID (or any external agent session ID).
   207→
   208→Indexes already exist on `trace` for `session`, `workspace`, `created_at`.
   209→
   210→### 6.2 Graph Topology
   211→
   212→```
   213→agent_session --[session]--> llm_call trace --[workspace]--> workspace
   214→                                                      --[parent_trace]--> trace (parent)
   215→```
   216→
   217→Attribution to task/project flows through the `agent_session` which already links to `task_id` and `project`.
   218→
   219→### 6.3 Key Queries
   220→
   221→**Per-workspace spend (today)**:
   222→```sql
   223→SELECT math::sum(cost_usd) AS total, count() AS calls
   224→FROM trace
   225→WHERE type = "llm_call" AND workspace = $ws AND created_at >= $today_start;
   226→```
   227→
   228→**Per-session breakdown**:
   229→```sql
   230→SELECT session, model, math::sum(cost_usd) AS spend, count() AS calls
   231→FROM trace
   232→WHERE type = "llm_call" AND workspace = $ws AND created_at >= $start
   233→GROUP BY session, model;
   234→```
   235→
   236→**Per-project via agent_session**:
   237→```sql
   238→SELECT session.project AS project, math::sum(cost_usd) AS spend, count() AS calls
   239→FROM trace
   240→WHERE type = "llm_call" AND workspace = $ws AND created_at >= $start
   241→FETCH session
   242→GROUP BY project;
   243→```
   244→
   245→**Full session timeline (agent traces + LLM calls interleaved)**:
   246→```sql
   247→SELECT type, model, tool_name, cost_usd, duration_ms, created_at
   248→FROM trace
   249→WHERE session = $session_id
   250→ORDER BY created_at ASC;
   251→```

   269→## 8. Integration Patterns
   270→
   271→### 8.1 Policy Engine Integration
   272→
   273→The proxy reuses `evaluatePolicyGate()` from `policy-gate.ts` with an adapted context. For LLM proxy policy evaluation, the intent context maps:
   274→
   275→| Policy Field | Proxy Value |
   276→|-------------|-------------|
   277→| `action` | `"llm_call"` |
   278→| `resource` | Model ID (e.g., `"claude-sonnet-4"`) |
   279→| `agent_role` | Agent type from `X-Brain-Agent-Type` header or inferred |
   280→
   281→Budget and rate limit checks are separate from the policy gate:
   282→- **Budget**: Read spend counter from llm_call trace aggregation, compare against workspace-configured limit
   283→- **Rate limit**: In-memory sliding window counter per workspace (too frequent for DB queries)
   284→
   285→### 8.2 Observation System Integration
   286→
   287→Warning observations created for:
   288→- Unresolved workspace (request forwarded but unattributed)
   289→- Missing LLM proxy policies (permissive default)
   290→- Graph write failure after retry exhaustion
   291→- Anomalous spending patterns (2x average rate)
   292→
   293→### 8.3 Inflight Tracker Integration
   294→
   295→All async post-response work tracked via `deps.inflight.track()`:
   296→- Trace node creation
   297→- Edge creation
   298→- Retry attempts
   299→- Observation creation on failure
   300→
   301→This ensures acceptance tests can `drain()` pending work before asserting.
   302→
   303→### 8.4 Multi-Provider Abstraction
   304→
   305→Two route handlers, one shared pipeline:
   306→
   307→| Route | Provider | Wire Format | Usage Extraction |
   308→|-------|----------|-------------|-----------------|
   309→| `/proxy/llm/anthropic/v1/messages` | Anthropic | Anthropic Messages API | `message_start` + `message_delta` SSE events |
   310→| `/proxy/llm/openai/v1/chat/completions` | OpenRouter/Ollama | OpenAI Chat Completions | `usage` field in final SSE chunk or JSON response |
   311→
   312→Both routes share: identity resolver, policy evaluator, cost calculator, trace writer. Only the SSE usage extraction and request forwarding URL differ.
   313→

   315→
   316→| Method | Path | Purpose | Story |
   317→|--------|------|---------|-------|
   318→| POST | `/proxy/llm/anthropic/v1/messages` | Anthropic proxy passthrough | US-LP-001 |
   319→| POST | `/proxy/llm/anthropic/v1/messages/count_tokens` | Token counting (no trace) | US-LP-001 |
   320→| POST | `/proxy/llm/openai/v1/chat/completions` | OpenAI-compatible proxy | US-LP-001 |

   330→## 9. Quality Attribute Strategies
   331→
   332→| Attribute | Strategy | Measure |
   333→|-----------|----------|---------|
   334→| **Performance** | Raw byte SSE forwarding; no decode/re-encode on hot path; async post-processing | < 50ms p95 TTFT overhead |
   335→| **Reliability** | 3x retry with exponential backoff on graph writes; stderr JSON fallback; inflight tracker for drain | 100% trace capture (with fallback) |
   336→| **Security** | Client API key forwarded (never stored); workspace validation; policy enforcement | No credential storage in proxy |
   337→| **Maintainability** | Functional pipeline (pure functions for identity, cost, policy); shared components across providers | Single responsibility per component |
   338→| **Auditability** | Every trace linked to session/workspace/task/policy via RELATE edges; provenance chain queryable | Full graph traversal from trace to intent |
   339→| **Scalability** | In-memory rate limiting; cached policy lookups (60s TTL); spend aggregation with short-TTL cache | < 10ms p99 policy check |

   522→## 13. Rejected Simple Alternatives
   523→
   524→### Alternative 1: Log-only proxy (no graph writes)
   525→- **What**: Forward requests transparently, log usage to stdout/file
   526→- **Expected impact**: Solves ~30% (visibility into calls, but no cost attribution, no policy enforcement, no graph-traversable audit)
   527→- **Why insufficient**: Does not address JS-1 (cost visibility), JS-3 (governed autonomy), or JS-4 (auditable provenance). The existing walking skeleton already does log-only.
   528→
   529→### Alternative 2: Anthropic Usage API polling
   530→- **What**: Periodically poll Anthropic's Usage/Cost API for billing data, import into graph
   531→- **Expected impact**: Solves ~40% (cost visibility at workspace level, but no per-task attribution, no policy enforcement, no real-time data)
   532→- **Why insufficient**: Anthropic's Usage API provides aggregate billing, not per-call attribution. Cannot link costs to tasks/sessions. No pre-request policy enforcement. Polling latency means data is always stale.
   533→
   534→### Why the full proxy is necessary
   535→Both alternatives fail because they cannot: (1) attribute costs to individual tasks/sessions, (2) enforce policies before forwarding requests, or (3) build graph-traversable provenance chains. The proxy intercepts at the right point to capture all three.

    19→- Real-time cost computation from model-specific pricing tables
    20→- Policy enforcement (model access, budget limits, rate limiting)
    21→- Spend monitoring API for dashboard consumption
    22→- Audit provenance chain traversal and export
