   135→## 5. Component Architecture
   136→
   137→### 5.1 Request Pipeline (Synchronous Hot Path)
   138→
   139→```
   140→Agent Request
   141→  |
   142→  +-> [1] Parse request body (extract model, stream flag, metadata)
   143→  +-> [2] Identity Resolution (parse metadata.user_id + X-Brain-* headers)
   144→  +-> [3] Policy Evaluation (model access + budget + rate limit)
   145→  |     |-- DENY -> Return 403/429 with policy_ref + remediation
   146→  |     |-- ALLOW -> continue
   147→  +-> [4] Forward to upstream provider (raw byte relay)
   148→  +-> [5] Return Response to agent (SSE stream or JSON)
   149→```
   150→
   151→**Latency budget**: Steps 1-3 must complete within 10ms p99. Step 4 adds zero overhead (raw byte pipe). Step 5 is the upstream's response time.
   152→
   153→### 5.2 Post-Response Pipeline (Asynchronous, Non-Blocking)
   154→
   155→```
   156→Stream Complete / Response Received
   157→  |
   158→  +-> [6] Extract usage (from SSE buffer or JSON response body)
   159→  +-> [7] Compute cost (pricing table lookup + token math)
   160→  +-> [8] Write llm_call trace node to SurrealDB
   161→  +-> [9] Create RELATE edges (invoked, scoped_to, attributed_to, governed_by)
   162→  +-> [10] On write failure: retry 3x exponential backoff -> stderr JSON fallback
   163→```
   164→
   165→All post-response work runs via `deps.inflight.track()` consistent with Brain's existing async pattern.
   166→
   167→### 5.3 Component Boundaries
   168→
   169→| Component | Responsibility | Driven Port (Input) | Driving Port (Output) |
   170→|-----------|---------------|--------------------|--------------------|
   171→| Anthropic Route | HTTP handling, pipeline orchestration for Anthropic format | `POST /proxy/llm/anthropic/v1/messages` | Forward request, trigger trace |
   172→| OpenAI Route | HTTP handling, pipeline orchestration for OpenAI format | `POST /proxy/llm/openai/v1/chat/completions` | Forward request, trigger trace |
   173→| Identity Resolver | Parse and validate identity signals | Request headers + body metadata | Resolved identity (workspace, session, task) |
   174→| Policy Evaluator | Pre-request authorization | Resolved identity + model | Allow/deny decision with policy trace |
   175→| Request Forwarder | Transparent SSE/JSON relay | Upstream URL + headers + body | Raw byte stream to client |
   176→| SSE Usage Extractor | Parse SSE events for usage data | Raw byte buffer from stream | Token counts + stop reason |
   177→| Cost Calculator | Compute per-request cost | Model + token counts | Cost in USD |
   178→| Trace Writer | Persist trace + edges to graph | Trace data (identity, usage, cost) | llm_call trace node + RELATE edges |
   179→| Pricing Table | Model-to-rate lookup | Model ID | Per-token rates |
   180→| Rate Limiter | Sliding window rate enforcement | Workspace ID | Allow/deny + current count |
   181→| Spend API | Aggregation queries for dashboard | HTTP GET with filters | Spend breakdown JSON |

   185→## 6. Data Model
   186→
   187→### 6.1 Extended `trace` Table (per ADR-042)
   188→
   189→The existing `trace` table is extended with `"llm_call"` as a new type value and LLM-specific optional fields. No new table is created.
   190→
   191→**New fields on `trace`** (optional, populated when `type = "llm_call"`):
   192→```
   193→  - model: option<string>                  -- model ID from response
   194→  - provider: option<string>               -- "anthropic" | "openai"
   195→  - input_tokens: option<int>
   196→  - output_tokens: option<int>
   197→  - cache_creation_tokens: option<int>
   198→  - cache_read_tokens: option<int>
   199→  - cost_usd: option<float>
   200→  - stop_reason: option<string>
   201→  - request_id: option<string>             -- Anthropic's request-id header
   202→```
   203→
   204→**Existing fields reused**: `session` (record<agent_session>), `workspace` (record<workspace>), `duration_ms`, `input`/`output` (FLEXIBLE), `parent_trace`, `actor`, `created_at`.
   205→
   206→**`agent_session` rename**: `opencode_session_id` → `external_session_id` to store Claude Code session UUID (or any external agent session ID).
   207→
   208→Indexes already exist on `trace` for `session`, `workspace`, `created_at`.
   209→
   210→### 6.2 Graph Topology
   211→
   212→```
   213→agent_session --[session]--> llm_call trace --[workspace]--> workspace
   214→                                                      --[parent_trace]--> trace (parent)
   215→```
   216→
   217→Attribution to task/project flows through the `agent_session` which already links to `task_id` and `project`.
   218→
   219→### 6.3 Key Queries
   220→
   221→**Per-workspace spend (today)**:
   222→```sql
   223→SELECT math::sum(cost_usd) AS total, count() AS calls
   224→FROM trace
   225→WHERE type = "llm_call" AND workspace = $ws AND created_at >= $today_start;
   226→```
   227→
   228→**Per-session breakdown**:
   229→```sql
   230→SELECT session, model, math::sum(cost_usd) AS spend, count() AS calls
   231→FROM trace
   232→WHERE type = "llm_call" AND workspace = $ws AND created_at >= $start
   233→GROUP BY session, model;
   234→```
   235→
   236→**Per-project via agent_session**:
   237→```sql
   238→SELECT session.project AS project, math::sum(cost_usd) AS spend, count() AS calls
   239→FROM trace
   240→WHERE type = "llm_call" AND workspace = $ws AND created_at >= $start
   241→FETCH session
   242→GROUP BY project;
   243→```
   244→
   245→**Full session timeline (agent traces + LLM calls interleaved)**:
   246→```sql
   247→SELECT type, model, tool_name, cost_usd, duration_ms, created_at
   248→FROM trace
   249→WHERE session = $session_id
   250→ORDER BY created_at ASC;
   251→```

   269→## 8. Integration Patterns
   270→
   271→### 8.1 Policy Engine Integration
   272→
   273→The proxy reuses `evaluatePolicyGate()` from `policy-gate.ts` with an adapted context. For LLM proxy policy evaluation, the intent context maps:
   274→
   275→| Policy Field | Proxy Value |
   276→|-------------|-------------|
   277→| `action` | `"llm_call"` |
   278→| `resource` | Model ID (e.g., `"claude-sonnet-4"`) |
   279→| `agent_role` | Agent type from `X-Brain-Agent-Type` header or inferred |
   280→
   281→Budget and rate limit checks are separate from the policy gate:
   282→- **Budget**: Read spend counter from llm_call trace aggregation, compare against workspace-configured limit
   283→- **Rate limit**: In-memory sliding window counter per workspace (too frequent for DB queries)
   284→
   285→### 8.2 Observation System Integration
   286→
   287→Warning observations created for:
   288→- Unresolved workspace (request forwarded but unattributed)
   289→- Missing LLM proxy policies (permissive default)
   290→- Graph write failure after retry exhaustion
   291→- Anomalous spending patterns (2x average rate)
   292→
   293→### 8.3 Inflight Tracker Integration
   294→
   295→All async post-response work tracked via `deps.inflight.track()`:
   296→- Trace node creation
   297→- Edge creation
   298→- Retry attempts
   299→- Observation creation on failure
   300→
   301→This ensures acceptance tests can `drain()` pending work before asserting.
   302→
   303→### 8.4 Multi-Provider Abstraction
   304→
   305→Two route handlers, one shared pipeline:
   306→
   307→| Route | Provider | Wire Format | Usage Extraction |

   309→| `/proxy/llm/anthropic/v1/messages` | Anthropic | Anthropic Messages API | `message_start` + `message_delta` SSE events |
   310→| `/proxy/llm/openai/v1/chat/completions` | OpenRouter/Ollama | OpenAI Chat Completions | `usage` field in final SSE chunk or JSON response |
   311→
   312→Both routes share: identity resolver, policy evaluator, cost calculator, trace writer. Only the SSE usage extraction and request forwarding URL differ.

   330→## 9. Quality Attribute Strategies
   331→
   332→| Attribute | Strategy | Measure |
   333→|-----------|----------|---------|
   334→| **Performance** | Raw byte SSE forwarding; no decode/re-encode on hot path; async post-processing | < 50ms p95 TTFT overhead |
   335→| **Reliability** | 3x retry with exponential backoff on graph writes; stderr JSON fallback; inflight tracker for drain | 100% trace capture (with fallback) |
   336→| **Security** | Client API key forwarded (never stored); workspace validation; policy enforcement | No credential storage in proxy |
   337→| **Maintainability** | Functional pipeline (pure functions for identity, cost, policy); shared components across providers | Single responsibility per component |
   338→| **Auditability** | Every trace linked to session/workspace/task/policy via RELATE edges; provenance chain queryable | Full graph traversal from trace to intent |
   339→| **Scalability** | In-memory rate limiting; cached policy lookups (60s TTL); spend aggregation with short-TTL cache | < 10ms p99 policy check |

   522→## 13. Rejected Simple Alternatives
   523→
   524→### Alternative 1: Log-only proxy (no graph writes)
   525→- **What**: Forward requests transparently, log usage to stdout/file
   526→- **Expected impact**: Solves ~30% (visibility into calls, but no cost attribution, no policy enforcement, no graph-traversable audit)
   527→- **Why insufficient**: Does not address JS-1 (cost visibility), JS-3 (governed autonomy), or JS-4 (auditable provenance). The existing walking skeleton already does log-only.
   528→
   529→### Alternative 2: Anthropic Usage API polling
   530→- **What**: Periodically poll Anthropic's Usage/Cost API for billing data, import into graph
   531→- **Expected impact**: Solves ~40% (cost visibility at workspace level, but no per-task attribution, no policy enforcement, no real-time data)
   532→- **Why insufficient**: Anthropic's Usage API provides aggregate billing, not per-call attribution. Cannot link costs to tasks/sessions. No pre-request policy enforcement. Polling latency means data is always stale.
   533→
   534→### Why the full proxy is necessary
   535→Both alternatives fail because they cannot: (1) attribute costs to individual tasks/sessions, (2) enforce policies before forwarding requests, or (3) build graph-traversable provenance chains. The proxy intercepts at the right point to capture all three.

## Project Summary
Hickory is a modern, full-stack help desk ticket management system. Built with .NET 9 backend and Next.js 15 frontend, using PostgreSQL and Redis.

| Frontend | Next.js 15, React, TypeScript, Tailwind CSS |
| Database | PostgreSQL 16 (Npgsql) |
| Cache/Messaging | Redis (MassTransit) |
| Auth | JWT Bearer tokens |
| Real-time | SignalR |
| Observability | OpenTelemetry, Serilog |
| Monorepo | Nx |

## Directory Structure

hickory/
├── apps/
│   ├── api/              # .NET 9 ASP.NET Core API
│   │   ├── Controllers/  # REST endpoints
│   │   ├── src/          # Business logic

├── tests/                # Integration/performance tests
├── scripts/              # Build/dev scripts
└── hickory.sln           # .NET solution file

| Command | Purpose |
|---------|---------|
| `dotnet run` | Run API (from apps/api) |
| `dotnet test` | Run .NET tests |
| `dotnet ef database update` | Apply EF migrations |
| `npm run dev` | Start Next.js dev server |
| `npm test` | Run Jest tests |
| `npm run test:performance` | Run perf tests |

## Code Conventions
1. **CQRS Pattern**: Use MediatR for commands and queries
2. **Validation**: FluentValidation for all request DTOs
3. **API**: RESTful design with NSwag/Swagger documentation
4. **Dependency Injection**: Use .NET built-in DI container
5. **Logging**: Serilog with structured logging
6. **Frontend**: Tailwind for styling, TypeScript strict mode

# 1. Start fresh from main
git checkout main && git pull origin main

# 2. Create feature branch
git checkout -b feature/short-description   # or fix/short-description

# 3. Work on changes, commit with conventional commits
git add . && git commit -m "feat: add ticket search"

# 4. Push and create PR
git push -u origin feature/short-description
```

## Code Style

Follow existing patterns in the codebase:
- Check similar files before creating new ones
- Match naming conventions, file organization, and code structure
- When in doubt, look at neighboring files for guidance

## Security

- Never commit secrets, API keys, or credentials
- Use environment variables for sensitive configuration
- Validate all user input
- Follow existing auth/authorization patterns in the codebase

## Setup Options
1. **Dev Container** (recommended): Open in VS Code → "Reopen in Container"
2. **Docker Compose**: `docker compose -f docker/docker-compose.yml up -d`
3. **Local**: Install .NET 9, Node.js 20+, PostgreSQL 16, Redis 7

    73→- **Project**: a named initiative with status, description.
    74→- **Feature**: a capability or deliverable within a project.
    75→- **Task**: an actionable work item. Status: open/todo/ready/in_progress/blocked/done/completed.
    76→
    77→**Cross-cutting entities** (attach to any level):
    78→- **Decision**: a choice that was made. Lifecycle: extracted → proposed → provisional → confirmed → superseded.
    79→- **Question**: an open question requiring a choice. Only for pending decisions, not informational queries.
    80→- **Observation**: a lightweight signal (info/warning/conflict). Lifecycle: open → acknowledged → resolved.
    81→- **Suggestion**: a proactive agent-to-human proposal. Categories: optimization, risk, opportunity, conflict, missing, pivot.
    82→
    83→**Entity ID format:** MCP tools use \`table:id\` for polymorphic references (e.g. \`task:abc123\`, \`decision:def456\`).
    84→
    85→## Decision Governance
    86→
    87→- **Your decisions are always \`provisional\` or \`inferred\`** — only humans confirm.
    88→- This means you can move fast without blocking, while humans retain authority.
    89→
    90→## Best Practices
    91→
    92→1. **Check before deciding.** Call \`resolve_decision\` first — the answer may already exist from another agent or human.
    93→2. **Ask, don't guess.** If uncertain, \`ask_question\` is better than \`create_provisional_decision\`.
    94→3. **Log as you go.** Don't batch decisions for the end. Log each significant choice when you make it.
    95→4. **Decompose tasks.** Use \`create_subtask\` to break work into pieces, then update status as each completes.
    96→5. **Check constraints.** Before adding a dependency or changing an approach, call \`check_constraints\`.
    97→6. **Include task IDs in commit messages.** Use \`task:<raw-task-id>\` (or \`tasks: <id1>, <id2>\`). Describe *what* changed and *why*.`;
    98→
    99→// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   100→// Commands (slash commands installed to .claude/commands/)
   101→// ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
   102→
   103→export const BRAIN_COMMANDS: Record<string, string> = {
   104→  "brain-start-task.md": `---
   105→name: brain-start-task
   106→description: Start working on a specific task from the Brain knowledge graph
   107→user_invocable: true
   108→args: task_id
   109→---
   110→
   111→# /brain-start-task <task_id>
   112→
   113→Start a task-scoped session focused on a specific task.
   114→
   115→## Instructions
   116→
   117→1. Call \`get_task_context\` with the task_id to get task-scoped context
   118→2. Display the task details: title, description, status, dependencies
   119→3. Show existing subtasks (if a previous agent already decomposed this task — do NOT re-decompose)
   120→4. Show sibling tasks (for awareness of parallel work)
   121→5. Show related decisions and constraints
   122→6. Call \`update_task_status\` to set the task to "in_progress" if it's currently "todo" or "ready"
   123→7. If the task has no subtasks, analyze what needs to be done and offer to create subtasks via \`create_subtask\`
   124→8. Begin implementation, using Brain MCP tools throughout:
   125→   - \`resolve_decision\` when hitting implementation choices
   126→   - \`check_constraints\` before adding dependencies or changing approaches
   127→   - \`create_provisional_decision\` when making choices the graph doesn't cover
   128→   - \`ask_question\` when genuinely uncertain
   129→   - \`update_task_status\` as subtasks complete`,
   130→
   131→  "brain-status.md": `---
   132→name: brain-status
   133→description: Show current Brain knowledge graph context for this project
   134→user_invocable: true
   135→---
   136→
   137→# /brain-status

   144→2. Display the results in a readable format:

   147→   - Provisional decisions (follow but note for review)
   148→   - Active tasks with status
   149→   - Open questions
   150→   - Recent changes
   151→3. If there are contested decisions, highlight them prominently
   152→4. Suggest next actions based on the context (e.g., "Task X is blocked by question Y")`,

     9→# Brain Knowledge Graph Integration
    10→
    11→This project is connected to the Brain knowledge graph via MCP tools. The graph contains decisions, constraints, tasks, questions, and observations from all agents and humans working on this workspace.
    12→
    13→## Getting Context
    14→
    15→Use `get_context` with a description of what you're working on. The server automatically finds the right project, tasks, decisions, and constraints — no need to pass project IDs manually.
    16→
    17→Example: `get_context({ intent: "implementing OAuth flow for the auth service" })`
    18→
    19→You can include task IDs (`task:abc123`), project names, file paths, or just a plain description.
    20→
    21→## Hooks
    22→
    23→- **SessionStart** loads workspace/project context automatically
    24→- **PreToolUse** injects brain context when dispatching subagents
    25→- **UserPromptSubmit** checks for workspace-level graph updates
    26→- **Stop** catches unlogged decisions before the session ends
    27→- **SessionEnd** logs session summary to the graph

   106→- **Telemetry migrated from Supabase to PostHog** — Replaces the custom Supabase Edge Function with PostHog for product analytics. Provides retention charts, feature funnels, and a real analytics dashboard instead of raw event storage.
   107→- **Stable machine identity** — Machine IDs no longer rotate monthly, enabling accurate unique user counts and retention analysis. IDs remain anonymous (SHA-256 hash, no PII).
   108→- **Expanded event schema** — All CLI commands now include `duration_ms` for performance tracking. Sync events include exact session counts and per-provider breakdowns. Analysis events capture LLM provider and model.
   109→- **Dashboard telemetry** — Page views and load timing tracked via `posthog-js` (client-side). Configured with `autocapture: false`, `persistence: 'memory'`, `ip: false` for privacy.
   110→- **`trackEvent` signature change** — Now accepts `(event: TelemetryEventName, properties?)` instead of `(command, success, subcommand?)`. Typed event names for autocomplete and typo prevention.
   111→
   112→### Added
   113→
   114→- **`GET /api/telemetry/identity`** — New server endpoint returns shared `distinct_id` for dashboard SPA initialization.
   115→- **`shutdownTelemetry()`** — Graceful PostHog flush on server shutdown with 3-second timeout guard.
   116→- **`posthog-node`** dependency in CLI (~20KB, lazy-initialized)
   117→- **`posthog-js`** dependency in dashboard (~45KB, memory-only persistence)
   118→- **Analysis failure tracking** — `analysis_run` events now fire on both success and failure for observability.
   119→
   120→### Removed
   121→
   122→- Supabase Edge Function endpoint, HMAC signing key, and `signPayload()`
   123→- Monthly-rotating machine ID (`getMachineId()` with date salt)
   124→- `getSessionCountBucket()` — replaced by exact `total_sessions` person property
   125→- `getDataSource()` — always 'local', provided no value
   126→
   127→### Fixed
   128→
   129→- **`RecurringInsightResult.groups`** — Fixed type error using `.insights` instead of `.groups` for recurring insight count.
   130→
   131→## [3.1.1] - 2026-03-02
   132→
   133→### Fixed
   134→
   135→- **Sync now updates existing sessions** — Previously, modified session files (e.g., active sessions gaining new messages) were skipped during sync because the session ID already existed in SQLite. Message counts, token usage, costs, and end times would remain stale after the initial sync. The sync now upserts session data and recalculates usage stats when existing sessions are updated.
   136→- **Cursor virtual-path sessions re-sync on DB change** — When the backing `state.vscdb` file was modified (new messages in an existing composer), virtual-path sessions were incorrectly skipped. Now re-syncs all sessions from a multi-session DB when the file changes.
   137→- **Improved sync summary** — Reports "new" vs "updated" session counts instead of a single "synced" number.
   138→

   140→
   141→### Fixed
   142→
   143→- **`--version` now reads from package.json** — Previously hardcoded as `3.0.0`, causing `code-insights --version` to always report `3.0.0` regardless of installed version.

   152→
   153→See [MIGRATION.md](../MIGRATION.md) for the full upgrade guide from v2.

   155→### Breaking Changes
   156→
   157→- **Firebase removed** — No Firestore sync, no Firebase credentials, no service account required. All data is stored locally in SQLite at `~/.code-insights/data.db`.
   158→- **`connect` command removed** — Generated Firebase connection URLs. No longer needed.
   159→- **`init` config format changed** — v2 config had Firebase credentials fields. v3 config has only sync settings and optional LLM config. Re-run `code-insights init` after upgrading.
   160→- **Data source changed to SQLite** — v2 wrote to Firestore. v3 writes to local SQLite. Existing Firestore data is not migrated. Re-sync with `code-insights sync --force`.
   161→- **Hosted dashboard removed** — The dashboard at code-insights.app is no longer maintained.
   162→
   163→### Added

   165→- **`dashboard` command** — Starts a local Hono server and opens the built-in React SPA at `localhost:7890`. Replaces the hosted dashboard.
   166→- **Embedded Vite + React SPA** — Full browser dashboard for session browsing, analytics, and insights. No external URL required.
   167→- **Server-side LLM analysis** — API keys are stored and used server-side. No key exposure to the browser.
   168→- **Multi-tool support** — Session providers for Cursor, Codex CLI, and Copilot CLI (in addition to Claude Code).
   169→- **`config llm` command** — Interactive and non-interactive LLM provider configuration (Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Ollama).

   171→- **`--verbose` flag on `sync`** — Show diagnostic warnings from providers.
   172→- **`--regenerate-titles` flag on `sync`** — Regenerate session titles from content.

   178→- **`open`** — Now opens `localhost:7890` (local dashboard server) instead of code-insights.app.

1→# Reflect & Patterns — Landing Page Section Design
     2→
     3→**Status:** Draft
     4→**Author:** UX Engineer
     5→**Date:** 2026-03-16
     6→
     7→---
     8→
     9→## Placement Recommendation
    10→
    11→**Position: After FeaturesSection, before MultiSourceSection.**
    12→
    13→```
    14→Hero
    15→ProofSection          (what the LLM extracts — session-level)
    16→ProblemSection        (before/after)
    17→HowItWorksSection     (install steps)
    18→FeaturesSection       (3 pillars)
    19→>>> ReflectSection    (NEW — cross-session patterns & growth) <<<
    20→MultiSourceSection    (5 tools)
    21→PrivacySection        (local-first)
    22→FinalCTASection       (install CTA)
    23→```
    24→
    25→**Rationale:** The page currently flows from "what you get per session" (Proof) through "how it works" (HowItWorks) to "what the tool covers" (Features). Reflect is the *next logical escalation* — it answers "what happens when you have *many* sessions?" It belongs after the three pillars (which mention knowledge, prompts, analytics) because Reflect synthesizes across all three. Placing it before MultiSource keeps the "social proof" sections (multi-tool, privacy, open source) grouped at the bottom as trust-builders.
    26→
    27→---
    28→
    29→## Purpose
    30→
    31→Convince the developer that Code Insights is not just a session viewer — it is a *feedback loop* that helps them improve over time. The Reflect feature is the headline differentiator for v4. This section must communicate:
    32→
    33→1. Sessions are analyzed for friction points and effective patterns (the "what")
    34→2. Weekly synthesis turns raw data into rules and skills (the "so what")
    35→3. You can generate CLAUDE.md / .cursorrules from your own patterns (the "now what")
    36→
    37→---
    38→
    39→## Narrative Arc
    40→
    41→The section uses a **three-beat structure** that mirrors the developer's journey:
    42→
    43→- Beat 1: "Every session teaches you something" (analysis)
    44→- Beat 2: "Patterns emerge across sessions" (synthesis)
    45→- Beat 3: "Turn patterns into rules" (action)

547→def _smoke_test_prompt(issue_url: str) -> str:
   548→    issue_number = extract_issue_number(issue_url)
   549→    return (
   550→        f"Run a smoke test to verify the implementation actually works.\n\n"
   551→        f"1. Fetch the implementation plan from GitHub issue {issue_url} using:\n"
   552→        f"   gh issue view {issue_number} --json body --jq .body\n\n"
   553→        "2. Look for a 'Validation' section (## Validation header) in the plan.\n\n"
   554→        "3. If a Validation section exists, execute those validation instructions exactly:\n"
   555→        "   - Start any long-running processes (servers, etc.) in the background\n"
   556→        "   - Use a non-standard port (e.g., 8099) to avoid conflicts\n"
   557→        "   - Wait up to 30 seconds for the service to be ready (poll with curl or similar)\n"
   558→        "   - Run each specified check\n"
   559→        "   - ALWAYS kill all background processes before exiting, even on failure\n"
   560→        "   - Report pass/fail for each check\n\n"
   561→        "4. If NO Validation section exists, fall back to convention-based discovery:\n"
   562→        "   - Read README.md, CLAUDE.md, pyproject.toml, package.json, Makefile, docker-compose.yml\n"
   563→        "   - Figure out how to run the application locally\n"
   564→        "   - Perform a basic sanity check: does it start? Does --help work? "
   565→        "Does a health endpoint respond?\n"
   566→        "   - ALWAYS kill all background processes before exiting\n\n"
   567→        "5. End your response with EXACTLY one of these lines (no extra text after it):\n"
   568→        "   SMOKE_TEST_PASS\n"
   569→        "   SMOKE_TEST_FAIL: <brief summary of what failed>\n\n"
   570→        "IMPORTANT: You MUST clean up all background processes before finishing. "
   571→        "Use 'kill %1' or 'kill $PID' to stop any servers you started."

   594→    ci_failures: str = "",

   596→    parts = [

   606→    if issue_url:

   612→            "Look for the Validation section. Execute the validation checks. "

   615→            "run the checks, and kill them before finishing. "

1→## Code Review Instructions
     2→
     3→1. Launch a haiku agent to return a list of file paths (not their contents) for all relevant CLAUDE.md files including:
     4→
     5→    - The root CLAUDE.md file, if it exists
     6→    - Any CLAUDE.md files in directories containing files modified by the workspace diff (use mcp__conductor__GetWorkspaceDiff with stat option)
     7→
     8→2. If this workspace has an associated PR, read the title and description (but not the changes). This will be helpful context.
     9→
    10→3. In parallel with step 2, launch a sonnet agent to view the changes, using mcp__conductor__GetWorkspaceDiff, and return a summary of the changes
    11→
    12→4. Launch 4 agents in parallel to independently review the changes using mcp__conductor__GetWorkspaceDiff. Each agent should return the list of issues, where each issue includes a description and the reason it was flagged (e.g. "CLAUDE.md adherence", "bug"). The agents should do the following:
    13→
    14→    Agents 1 + 2: CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md compliance sonnet agents
    15→    Audit changes for CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md compliance in parallel. Note: When evaluating CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md compliance for a file, you should only consider CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md files that share a file path with the file or parents.
    16→
    17→    Agent 3: Opus bug agent
    18→    Scan for obvious bugs. Focus only on the diff itself without reading extra context. Flag only significant bugs; ignore nitpicks and likely false positives. Do not flag issues that you cannot validate without looking at context outside of the git diff.
    19→
    20→    Agent 4: Opus bug agent
    21→    Look for problems that exist in the introduced code. This could be security issues, incorrect logic, etc. Only look for issues that fall within the changed code.
    22→
    23→    **CRITICAL: We only want HIGH SIGNAL issues.** This means:
    24→
    25→    - Objective bugs that will cause incorrect behavior at runtime
    26→    - Clear, unambiguous CLAUDE.md violations where you can quote the exact rule being broken
    27→
    28→    We do NOT want:
    29→
    30→    - Subjective concerns or "suggestions"
    31→    - Style preferences not explicitly required by CLAUDE.md
    32→    - Potential issues that "might" be problems
    33→    - Anything requiring interpretation or judgment calls
    34→
    35→    If you are not certain an issue is real, do not flag it. False positives erode trust and waste reviewer time.
    36→
    37→    In addition to the above, each subagent should be told the PR title and description. This will help provide context regarding the author's intent.
    38→
    39→5. For each issue found in the previous step, launch parallel subagents to validate the issue. These subagents should get the PR title and description along with a description of the issue. The agent's job is to review the issue to validate that the stated issue is truly an issue with high confidence. For example, if an issue such as "variable is not defined" was flagged, the subagent's job would be to validate that is actually true in the code. Another example would be CLAUDE.md issues. The agent should validate that the CLAUDE.md rule that was violated is scoped for this file and is actually violated. Use Opus subagents for bugs and logic issues, and sonnet agents for CLAUDE.md violations.
    40→
    41→6. Filter out any issues that were not validated in step 5. This step will give us our list of high signal issues for our review.
    42→
    43→7. Post inline comments for each issue using mcp__conductor__DiffComment:
    44→
    45→    **IMPORTANT: Only post ONE comment per unique issue.**
    46→
    47→8. Write out a list of issues found, along with the location of the comment. For example:
    48→
    49→    <example>
    50→    ### **#1 Empty input causes crash**
    51→
    52→    If the input field is empty when page loads, the app will crash.
    53→
    54→    File: src/ui/Input.tsx
    55→
    56→    ### **#2 Dead code**
    57→
    58→    The getUserData function is now unused. It should be deleted.
    59→
    60→    File: src/core/UserData.ts
    61→    </example>
    62→
    63→Use this list when evaluating issues in Steps 5 and 6 (these are false positives, do NOT flag):
    64→
    65→-   Pre-existing issues
    66→-   Something that appears to be a bug but is actually correct
    67→-   Pedantic nitpicks that a senior engineer would not flag
    68→-   Issues that a linter will catch (do not run the linter to verify)
    69→-   General code quality concerns (e.g., lack of test coverage, general security issues) unless explicitly required in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md
    70→-   Issues mentioned in CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md but explicitly silenced in the code (e.g., via a lint ignore comment)
    71→
    72→Notes:
    73→
    74→-   All subagents should be explicitly instructed not to post comments themselves. Only you, the main agent, should post comments.
    75→-   Do not use the AskUserQuestion tool. Your goal should be to complete the entire review without user intervention.
    76→-   Use gh CLI to interact with GitHub (e.g., fetch pull requests, create comments). Do not use web fetch.
    77→-   You must cite and link each issue in inline comments (e.g., if referring to a CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md rule, include a link to it).
    78→
    79→## Fallback: if you don't have access to subagents
    80→
    81→If you don't have subagents, perform all the steps above yourself sequentially instead of launching agents. Do each review axis (CLAUDE.md compliance, bug scan, introduced problems) yourself, and validate each issue yourself.
    82→
    83→## Fallback: if you don't have access to the workspace diff tool
    84→
    85→If you don't have access to the mcp__conductor__GetWorkspaceDiff tool, use the following git commands to get the diff:
    86→
    87→```bash
    88→# Get the merge base between this branch and the target
    89→MERGE_BASE=$(git merge-base origin/main HEAD)
    90→
    91→# Get the committed diff against the merge base
    92→git diff $MERGE_BASE HEAD
    93→
    94→# Get any uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged)
    95→git diff HEAD
    96→```
    97→
    98→Review the combination of both outputs: the first shows all committed changes on this branch relative to the target, and the second shows any uncommitted work in progress.
    99→
   100→No need to mention in your report whether or not you used one of the fallback strategies; it's usually irrelevant.

# opensrc Project Overview

## What Is This Project?

**opensrc** is a CLI tool that automates fetching source code for npm packages and GitHub repositories, enabling AI coding agents to access implementation details beyond type definitions and documentation.

## Tools/Templates & Purpose

The project provides a single command-line tool with these capabilities:

- **Package Source Fetching**: "Fetch source for a package (auto-detects version from lockfile)"
- **Repository Cloning**: Supports npm packages, GitHub repos via multiple formats (shorthand, URLs, prefixes)
- **Source Management**: List and remove fetched sources
- **Project Integration**: Optional file modifications (.gitignore, tsconfig.json, AGENTS.md)

## Tech Stack

- **Language**: TypeScript (97.5%), JavaScript (2.5%)
- **Runtime**: Node.js
- **Package Manager**: pnpm
- **Testing**: Vitest
- **Distribution**: Published as global npm package

## Directory Structure (Visible)

```
opensrc/
├── src/                    # Source code
├── .gitignore
├── .prettierignore
├── AGENTS.md
├── LICENSE                 # Apache-2.0
├── README.md
├── package.json
├── pnpm-lock.yaml
├── tsconfig.json
└── vitest.config.ts
```

## Important Note

**This is not a Rust project**—it's TypeScript/JavaScript. There is no scaffolding functionality for creating new Rust CLI projects. The tool is specifically designed for fetching and managing source code contexts for AI agents working with JavaScript/Node.js ecosystems.

1→# Workflow Generation Eval Framework
     2→
     3→## Problem
     4→
     5→The `/workflow` skill generates Python workflow scripts via LLM. When iterating on the skill's prompt, there's no way to systematically verify that the generated workflows make good decisions — right graph topology, appropriate model selection, correct use of parallel execution, sensitivity to repo context (CLAUDE.md instructions).
     6→
     7→## Goal
     8→
     9→A scenario-based eval framework that:
    10→
    11→1. Presents a natural language task + a scaffolded repo to headless Claude
    12→2. Claude generates a workflow.py using the `/workflow` skill
    13→3. The generated graph is imported and inspected with Python assertions
    14→4. No workflow execution — only structural inspection
    15→
    16→This enables prompt iteration: change the skill, re-run evals, check if the LLM still makes good decisions.
    17→
    18→## Design
    19→
    20→### Engine changes
    21→
    22→#### 1. Expose prompt templates on node functions
    23→
    24→Add a `_prompt_template` attribute to `claude_node`, `codex_node`, `gemini_node`, and `shell_node` — same pattern as the existing `_diagram_label`. This lets assertions inspect what prompt or command each node uses.
    25→
    26→```python
    27→# In claude_node:
    28→_node._prompt_template = prompt_template
    29→
    30→# In shell_node:
    31→_node._prompt_template = command_template
    32→```
    33→
    34→#### 2. Require `build_graph()` in generated scripts
    35→
    36→Update the `/workflow` skill (commands/workflow.md) to require that generated scripts put graph construction in a `build_graph()` function. The `if __name__ == "__main__"` block calls `build_graph()` and then runs it. This makes the graph importable for inspection without execution.

    44→if __name__ == "__main__":

    76→### GraphInspector (`helpers.py`)
    77→
    78→A query interface over the StateGraph internals. All methods operate on the graph's internal data structures (`_nodes`, `_node_meta`, `_edges`, `_conditional_edges`, `_parallel_edges`).
    79→
    80→```python
    81→class GraphInspector:
    82→    """Pattern-matching query interface for StateGraph inspection.
    83→
    84→    All query methods use substring/pattern matching to be resilient
    85→    to LLM-chosen node names varying between runs.
    86→    """
    87→
    88→    def __init__(self, graph: StateGraph):
    89→        self.graph = graph
    90→
    91→    def has_node_with_meta(self, *patterns: str) -> bool:
    92→        """True if any node's _node_meta value contains one of the patterns.
    93→
    94→        Example: has_node_with_meta("shell") — checks for a shell node.
    95→        Example: has_node_with_meta("claude", "codex") — checks for either.
    96→        """
    97→
    98→    def get_nodes_with_meta(self, pattern: str) -> list[str]:
    99→        """Return node names whose _node_meta value contains pattern."""
   100→
   101→    def has_node_with_prompt_containing(self, keyword: str) -> bool:
   102→        """True if any node's _prompt_template contains keyword (case-insensitive).
   103→
   104→        Uses the _prompt_template attribute added to node functions.
   105→        """
   106→
   107→    def get_nodes_with_prompt_containing(self, keyword: str) -> list[str]:
   108→        """Return node names whose _prompt_template contains keyword."""
   109→
   110→    def has_parallel_group(self) -> bool:
   111→        """True if the graph uses add_parallel_edges."""
   112→
   113→    def has_parallel_group_containing(self, *meta_patterns: str) -> bool:
   114→        """True if any parallel group's targets include nodes matching the patterns."""
   115→
   116→    def has_conditional_loop(self, meta_contains: str | None = None) -> bool:
   117→        """True if a conditional edge routes back to a previously-seen node (cycle).
   118→
   119→        If meta_contains is provided, only considers loops where the source node's
   120→        meta contains the pattern (e.g., meta_contains='shell' for test-fix loops).
   121→        """
   122→
   123→    def node_count(self) -> int:
   124→        """Total number of nodes in the graph."""
   125→
   126→    def get_edge_targets(self, source_pattern: str) -> list[str]:
   127→        """All targets reachable from nodes whose name contains source_pattern.
   128→
   129→        Checks unconditional, conditional, and parallel edges.
   130→        """
   131→
   132→    def has_edge_to_end(self) -> bool:
   133→        """True if the graph has at least one edge to END."""
   134→
   135→    def get_model_for_node(self, node_name_pattern: str) -> str | None:
   136→        """Return the _node_meta (model info) for the first node matching pattern."""

1→# Workflow Generation Eval Framework
     2→
     3→## Problem
     4→
     5→The `/workflow` skill generates Python workflow scripts via LLM. When iterating on the skill's prompt, there's no way to systematically verify that the generated workflows make good decisions — right graph topology, appropriate model selection, correct use of parallel execution, sensitivity to repo context (CLAUDE.md instructions).
     6→
     7→## Goal
     8→
     9→A scenario-based eval framework that:
    10→
    11→1. Presents a natural language task + a scaffolded repo to headless Claude
    12→2. Claude generates a workflow.py using the `/workflow` skill
    13→3. The generated graph is imported and inspected with Python assertions
    14→4. No workflow execution — only structural inspection
    15→
    16→This enables prompt iteration: change the skill, re-run evals, check if the LLM still makes good decisions.
    17→
    18→## Design
    19→
    20→### Engine changes
    21→
    22→#### 1. Expose prompt templates on node functions
    23→
    24→Add a `_prompt_template` attribute to `claude_node`, `codex_node`, `gemini_node`, `shell_node`, and `template_node` — same pattern as the existing `_diagram_label`. This lets assertions inspect what prompt or command each node uses.
    25→
    26→```python
    27→# In claude_node:
    28→_node._prompt_template = prompt_template
    29→
    30→# In shell_node:
    31→_node._prompt_template = command_template
    32→
    33→# In template_node:
    34→_node._prompt_template = template
    35→```
    36→
    37→`python_node` does not get `_prompt_template` since it wraps arbitrary functions with no template string.
    38→
    39→#### 2. Require `build_graph()` in generated scripts
    40→
    41→Update the `/workflow` skill (commands/workflow.md) to require that generated scripts put graph construction in a `build_graph()` function. This makes the graph importable for inspection without execution.
    42→
    43→`build_graph()` accepts an optional `models` parameter (defaulting to `detect_available_models()`) so that callers can control model availability for deterministic graph topology:
    44→
    45→```python
    46→def build_graph(models: dict[str, bool] | None = None) -> StateGraph:
    47→    if models is None:
    48→        models = detect_available_models()
    49→    HAS_CODEX = models["codex"]
    50→    HAS_GEMINI = models["gemini"]
    51→
    52→    graph = StateGraph(max_iterations=5)
    53→    # ... add nodes, edges, using HAS_CODEX/HAS_GEMINI for node selection ...
    54→    return graph
    55→
    56→if __name__ == "__main__":
    57→    graph = build_graph()
    58→    if "--diagram" in sys.argv:
    59→        print(graph.to_ascii())
    60→        sys.exit(0)
    61→    initial_state = {"work_dir": os.getcwd(), ...}
    62→    asyncio.run(graph.run(initial_state))
    63→```
    64→
    65→All graph topology decisions (node types, edges, parallel groups) must happen inside `build_graph()`. The `if __name__` block only handles `initial_state` construction and execution.
    66→

   129→### GraphInspector (`helpers.py`)
   130→
   131→A query interface over the StateGraph internals. All methods operate on the graph's internal data structures (`_nodes`, `_node_meta`, `_edges`, `_conditional_edges`, `_parallel_edges`).
   132→
   133→**Meta pattern matching:** All `*_meta` methods use **substring matching** against the `_diagram_label` values stored in `_node_meta`. For example, `"claude"` matches `"claude opus/high"`, `"shell"` matches `"shell"`, `"codex"` matches `"codex default"`. This makes assertions resilient to model/effort variations.
   134→
   135→**Prompt pattern matching:** All `*_prompt_containing` methods use **case-insensitive substring matching** against the `_prompt_template` attribute set on node functions by the engine's node helpers.
   136→
   137→```python
   138→class GraphInspector:
   139→    """Pattern-matching query interface for StateGraph inspection."""
   140→
   141→    def __init__(self, graph: StateGraph):
   142→        self.graph = graph
   143→
   144→    def has_node_with_meta(self, *patterns: str) -> bool:
   145→        """True if any node's _node_meta value contains one of the patterns.
   146→
   147→        Example: has_node_with_meta("shell") — checks for a shell node.
   148→        Example: has_node_with_meta("claude", "codex") — checks for either.
   149→        """
   150→
   151→    def get_nodes_with_meta(self, pattern: str) -> list[str]:
   152→        """Return node names whose _node_meta value contains pattern."""
   153→
   154→    def has_node_with_prompt_containing(self, keyword: str) -> bool:
   155→        """True if any node's _prompt_template contains keyword (case-insensitive)."""
   156→
   157→    def get_nodes_with_prompt_containing(self, keyword: str) -> list[str]:
   158→        """Return node names whose _prompt_template contains keyword."""
   159→
   160→    def has_parallel_group(self) -> bool:
   161→        """True if the graph uses add_parallel_edges."""
   162→
   163→    def has_parallel_group_containing(self, *meta_patterns: str) -> bool:
   164→        """True if any parallel group's targets include nodes matching the patterns."""
   165→
   166→    def has_conditional_loop(self, meta_contains: str | None = None) -> bool:
   167→        """True if a conditional edge creates a cycle in the graph.
   168→
   169→        Algorithm: for each conditional edge, check if any of its route_map
   170→        targets is an ancestor of its source — i.e., the target appears as a
   171→        source in any edge chain that leads to the conditional edge's source.
   172→        Simplified approach: check if any route_map target also appears as a
   173→        source of an edge (unconditional or parallel) earlier in the graph,
   174→        creating a back-edge.
   175→
   176→        If meta_contains is provided, only considers conditional edges where
   177→        the source node's meta contains the pattern.
   178→        """
   179→
   180→    def node_count(self) -> int:
   181→        """Total number of nodes in the graph."""
   182→
   183→    def get_edge_targets(self, source_pattern: str) -> list[str]:
   184→        """All targets reachable from nodes whose name contains source_pattern.
   185→
   186→        Checks unconditional, conditional, and parallel edges.
   187→        """
   188→
   189→    def has_edge_to_end(self) -> bool:
   190→        """True if the graph has at least one edge to END."""
   191→
   192→    def get_model_for_node(self, node_name_pattern: str) -> str | None:
   193→        """Return the _node_meta (model info) for the first node matching pattern."""
   194→```

Here is a complete list of issues found in PR #16 where the code violates, ignores, or contradicts comments and spec-documented expectations:

---

**Issue 1: `bugfix_bare/assertions.py` omits the negative assertion specified in the spec's example**

The spec's `assertions.py` example for `bugfix_bare` (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-03-17-workflow-eval-framework-design.md`, lines 120-126) explicitly includes:
```python
# Bare repo — should NOT have doc update or lint steps
assert not h.has_node_with_prompt_containing("doc"), "no doc step expected on bare repo"
```

The PR's `dev-loop/tests/workflow_eval/scenarios/bugfix_bare/assertions.py` omits this negative assertion entirely. The comment in the spec table (line 257) also lists "minimal nodes, no unnecessary steps" as a key assertion for this scenario. The spec's commentary on this is explicit and is the whole point of a "bare repo" scenario — verifying that the workflow doesn't hallucinate quality gates that weren't asked for.

---

**Issue 2: `generate_workflow` uses regex-based path extraction instead of glob/mtime approach described in the spec**

The spec (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-03-17-workflow-eval-framework-design.md`, lines 210-211) says:
> "The generated script is written to `/tmp/workflow_*.py`. The test locates it by globbing for the most recently modified match (and cleans up stale files before each run to avoid collisions)."

The implementation in `test_scenarios.py` (`_extract_workflow_path`, lines 73-87) instead parses the path from Claude's text output with a regex. It has no pre-run cleanup of stale `/tmp/workflow_*.py` files and no fallback glob. This means:
- If Claude does not print the path in its output (which can happen with LLM variance), the test fails even if the file was written correctly.
- Stale files from previous runs are never cleaned up, which can cause confusion when inspecting results.

The plan doc (`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-03-17-workflow-eval-framework.md`, lines 2711-2769) even includes `_cleanup_stale_workflows()` and glob-based detection as part of the plan, but neither made it into the implementation.

---

**Issue 3: `bugfix_backend_instructions/assertions.py` omits the "update docs" assertion listed in the spec**

The spec scenario table (line 258) says the key assertion for `bugfix_backend_instructions` is "Same loop + lint/typecheck/**doc nodes from instructions**". The repo's `CLAUDE.md` says "Update documentation in docs/ when changing public APIs". The assertions file does check for lint and typecheck but never checks for a documentation-related node or prompt keyword, despite the spec table calling this out and the comment in the assertions file itself saying `# CLAUDE.md says to run lint and typecheck — should appear somewhere`.

---

**Issue 4: `helpers.py` docstring describes `get_edge_targets` as returning "All non-END targets", but method name and inline comment say "Excludes END sentinels"**

In `helpers.py`, lines 125-128:
```python
def get_edge_targets(self, source_pattern: str) -> list[str]:
    """All non-END targets reachable from nodes whose name contains source_pattern.

    Excludes END sentinels — use has_edge_to_end() to check termination.
    """
```

The docstring is consistent. However, the spec (`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-03-17-workflow-eval-framework-design.md`, line 183) describes this method as:
```
def get_edge_targets(self, source_pattern: str) -> list[str]:
    """All targets reachable from nodes whose name contains source_pattern.
    Checks unconditional, conditional, and parallel edges.
    """
```

The spec does not mention the END-exclusion behavior. This is a docstring discrepancy between spec and implementation — the behavior (excluding END) is undocumented in the spec, which could confuse future scenario authors who expect to use this to verify termination.

---

**Issue 5: `python_node` sets `_diagram_label = "python"` but the spec explicitly says it should NOT get `_prompt_template`**

The spec (line 37) says:
> "`python_node` does not get `_prompt_template` since it wraps arbitrary functions with no template string."

The implementation correctly omits `_prompt_template` from `python_node`. However, `python_node` does set `_diagram_label = "python"` on the inner function (in `engine.py`, lines 491 and 497). The module-level docstring for `helpers.py` says:
> "All meta methods use substring matching against `_diagram_label` values in `_node_meta`."

But `_node_meta` is only populated in `add_node` when `fn._diagram_label` is set. For `python_node`, the label is set on the returned closure (line 497) but not on the original function (line 491 sets it on `fn` directly when it's already async). This means that when a sync function is wrapped, `_diagram_label` ends up on `_node` (the inner async wrapper), but when an async function is passed, it's set on `fn` (the original function). This is inconsistent, though the behavior happens to be correct in both cases since `add_node` checks `getattr(fn, "_diagram_label", None)` on whatever callable is passed in.

---

**Issue 6: `refactoring_bare/assertions.py` omits the "review step" assertion listed in the spec**

The spec scenario table (line 263) lists "Runs existing tests, **review step**, no new test creation step" as the key assertions for `refactoring_bare`. The PR's `dev-loop/tests/workflow_eval/scenarios/refactoring_bare/assertions.py` only checks for LLM node, shell node, and edge to END. It does not assert that a review step (code review or security review) is present, and it does not assert the negative: that no new test-creation step was added (which would be wrong for a pure refactoring).      3→This section provides practical examples for using SKF: Skill Forge.
     4→
     5→---
     6→
     7→## Example Workflows
     8→
     9→### Quick Skill — 47 Seconds
    10→
    11→Developer adds `spacetimedb` to a Next.js project. Agent keeps hallucinating methods.
    12→
    13→```
    14→@Ferris QS spacetimedb
    15→```
    16→
    17→Ferris resolves to GitHub, extracts 14 public functions via source reading, validates against spec. Skill appears in `skills/spacetimedb/`. Agent stops hallucinating. Forty-seven seconds. Done.
    18→
    19→### Brownfield Platform — 8 Minutes
    20→
    21→Alex's team adopts BMAD for 10 microservices (TypeScript, Go, Rust).
    22→
    23→```
    24→@Ferris SF          # Setup — Deep mode detected
    25→@Ferris AN          # Analyze — 10 services mapped
    26→@Ferris CS --batch  # Create — batch generation
    27→```
    28→
    29→10 individual skills + 1 platform stack skill. BMM architect navigates cross-service flows with verified knowledge.
    30→
    31→### Release Prep — Trust Builder
    32→
    33→Sarah prepares v3.0.0 with breaking changes.
    34→
    35→```
    36→@Ferris AS    # Audit — finds 3 renames, 1 removal, 1 addition
    37→@Ferris US    # Update — preserves [MANUAL] sections, adds annotations
    38→@Ferris TS    # Test — verify completeness
    39→@Ferris EX    # Export — package for npm release
    40→```
    41→
    42→Ships with npm release. Consumers upgrade — their agents use the correct function names. Zero hallucination tickets.
    43→
    44→### Stack Skill — Integration Intelligence
    45→
    46→Armel's full-stack project: Next.js + Serwist + SpacetimeDB + better-auth.
    47→
    48→```
    49→@Ferris SS
    50→```
    51→
    52→Ferris detects 8 significant dependencies, finds 5 co-import integration points. Generates a consolidated stack skill. The agent now knows: "When you modify the auth flow, update the Serwist cache exclusion at `src/sw.ts:L23`." Integration intelligence no other tool provides.
    53→
    54→---
    55→
    56→## Common Scenarios
    57→
    58→### Scenario A: Greenfield + BMM Integration
    59→
    60→BMAD user starts a new project. BMM architect suggests skill generation after retrospective.
    61→
    62→```
    63→@Ferris BS    # Brief — scope the skill
    64→@Ferris CS    # Create — compile from brief
    65→@Ferris TS    # Test — verify completeness
    66→@Ferris EX    # Export — inject into CLAUDE.md
    67→```
    68→
    69→Skills accumulate over sprints. Agent gets smarter every iteration.
    70→
    71→### Scenario B: Multi-Repo Platform
    72→
    73→Alex needs cross-service knowledge for 10 microservices.
    74→
    75→One forge project, multiple QMD collections, hub-and-spoke skills with integration patterns.
    76→
    77→### Scenario C: External Dependency
    78→
    79→Developer needs skills for a library that doesn't have official skills.
    80→
    81→```
    82→@Ferris QS better-auth
    83→```
    84→
    85→Checks ecosystem first. If no official skill exists: generates from source. `source_authority: community`.
    86→
    87→### Scenario D: Docs-Only (SaaS/Closed Source)
    88→
    89→No source code available — only documentation.
    90→
    91→Generate from docs + QMD-indexed content. T2/T3 confidence only. `source_authority: community`.
    92→
    93→---
    94→
    95→## Tips & Tricks
    96→
    97→### Progressive Capability
    98→
    99→Start with Quick mode (no setup required), upgrade to Forge (install ast-grep), then Deep (QMD already included). Each tier builds on the previous — you never lose capability.
   100→
   101→### Batch Operations
   102→
   103→Use `--batch` with `create-skill` and `test-skill` to process multiple skills at once. Progress is checkpointed — use `--continue` to resume if interrupted.
   104→
   105→### Stack Skills + Individual Skills
   106→
   107→Stack skills focus on integration patterns. Individual skills focus on API surface. Use both together for maximum coverage.
   108→
   109→### The Loop
   110→
   111→After each sprint's refactor, run `@Ferris US` to regenerate changed components. Export updates CLAUDE.md automatically. Skill generation becomes routine — like running tests.
   112→
   113→---
   114→
   115→## Troubleshooting
   116→
   117→### Common Issues
   118→
   119→**"Forge halted: ast-grep not found"**
   120→Install ast-grep to unlock Forge mode: https://ast-grep.github.io
   121→
   122→**"No brief found"**
   123→Run `@Ferris BS` first to create a skill brief, or use `@Ferris QS` for brief-less generation.
   124→
   125→**"Ecosystem check: official skill exists"**
   126→An official skill already exists for this package. Consider installing it with `npx skills add` instead of generating your own.
   127→
   128→**Quick mode skills have lower confidence**
   129→Quick mode reads source without AST analysis. Install ast-grep to upgrade to Forge mode for structural truth (T1 confidence).
   130→
   131→---
   132→
   133→## Getting More Help
   134→
   135→- Run `@Ferris SF` to check your current tier and tool availability
   136→- Review `forge-config.yaml` for runtime configuration
   137→- Check module configuration in your BMAD settings
   138→- Consult the broader BMAD documentation

1→# SKF Workflows
     2→
     3→Ten workflows covering the full skill compilation lifecycle — from source discovery through verified export.
     4→
     5→All workflows are triggered via Ferris (`@Ferris <code>`) and execute as step-by-step sequences with just-in-time step loading.
     6→
     7→## Workflow Index
     8→
     9→| Code | Workflow | Steps | Mode | Purpose |
    10→| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    11→| SF | [setup-forge](setup-forge/workflow.md) | 4 | Architect | Initialize environment, detect tools, set capability tier |
    12→| AN | [analyze-source](analyze-source/workflow.md) | 7 | Architect | Discover skillable units in a repo, produce recommended briefs |
    13→| BS | [brief-skill](brief-skill/workflow.md) | 5 | Architect | Design a skill scope through guided discovery |
    14→| CS | [create-skill](create-skill/workflow.md) | 8 | Surgeon | Compile a skill from brief with provenance (supports --batch) |
    15→| QS | [quick-skill](quick-skill/workflow.md) | 6 | Surgeon | Fast skill from package name or GitHub URL — no brief needed |
    16→| SS | [create-stack-skill](create-stack-skill/workflow.md) | 9 | Surgeon | Consolidated project stack skill with integration patterns |
    17→| US | [update-skill](update-skill/workflow.md) | 7 | Surgeon | Regenerate after source changes, preserving \[MANUAL\] sections |
    18→| AS | [audit-skill](audit-skill/workflow.md) | 6 | Audit | Drift detection between skill and current source code |
    19→| TS | [test-skill](test-skill/workflow.md) | 6 | Audit | Cognitive completeness verification — quality gate before export |
    20→| EX | [export-skill](export-skill/workflow.md) | 6 | Delivery | Package for distribution, inject into CLAUDE.md/AGENTS.md |
    21→
    22→## Typical Flows
    23→
    24→**First-time setup:**
    25→
    26→```
    27→SF → AN → CS (batch) → TS → EX
    28→```
    29→
    30→**Single skill (full quality):**
    31→
    32→```
    33→SF → BS → CS → TS → EX
    34→```
    35→
    36→**Single skill (fast):**
    37→
    38→```
    39→SF → QS → EX
    40→```
    41→
    42→**Maintenance:**
    43→
    44→```
    45→AS → US → TS → EX
    46→```
    47→
    48→## Directory Structure
    49→
    50→Each workflow follows a consistent structure:
    51→
    52→```
    53→{workflow}/
    54→├── workflow.md              # Entry point — goals, mode routing, step sequence
    55→├── steps-c/                 # Create-mode steps (sequential execution)
    56→│   ├── step-01-*.md
    57→│   ├── step-02-*.md
    58→│   └── ...
    59→├── data/                    # Reference data — schemas, rules, patterns
    60→│   └── *.md
    61→├── templates/               # Output skeletons (only analyze-source, test-skill)
    62→│   └── *-template.md
    63→├── workflow-plan-*.md       # Design plan (build artifact)
    64→└── validation-report.md     # BMAD validation results (build artifact)
    65→```
    66→
    67→### Step Loading
    68→
    69→Steps execute sequentially via just-in-time loading. Only the current step is in context. Each step explicitly names the next step file. Data and template files are loaded on demand by the steps that need them.
    70→
    71→## Workflow Details
    72→
    73→### setup-forge (SF)
    74→
    75→**4 steps** | **Data:** tier-rules.md
    76→
    77→Detects available tools (ast-grep, gh, QMD), determines the capability tier (Quick/Forge/Deep), writes `forge-tier.yaml` to the sidecar, and optionally indexes the project. Run this first — all other workflows adapt behavior to the detected tier.
    78→
    79→### analyze-source (AN)
    80→
    81→**7 steps** | **Data:** skill-brief-schema.md, unit-detection-heuristics.md | **Templates:** analysis-report-template.md
    82→
    83→Brownfield onboarding entry point. Scans project structure, identifies skillable units using confidence-tiered heuristic signals, maps exports and integration points, presents recommendations for user confirmation, then generates `skill-brief.yaml` files ready for `create-skill --batch`.
    84→
    85→### brief-skill (BS)
    86→
    87→**5 steps** | **Data:** skill-brief-schema.md
    88→
    89→Interactive guided discovery. Gathers user intent (target repo, language, what to skill), analyzes the target to understand boundaries, walks through scope definition with the user, confirms the brief, then writes a validated `skill-brief.yaml`.
    90→
    91→### create-skill (CS)
    92→
    93→**8 steps** | **Data:** extraction-patterns.md, skill-sections.md
    94→
    95→The core compilation engine. Loads a brief, checks ecosystem context, extracts source with AST-backed provenance (T1 confidence when ast-grep available), enriches with usage patterns, compiles into agentskills.io-compliant sections, validates structural integrity, generates the `SKILL.md` artifact, and produces an evidence report. Supports `--batch` for processing multiple briefs.
    96→
    97→### quick-skill (QS)
    98→
    99→**6 steps** | **Data:** registry-resolution.md, skill-template.md
   100→
   101→Fastest path to a skill. Accepts a GitHub URL or package name, resolves to source via registry lookup, performs ecosystem check, extracts public API surface without requiring a brief, compiles best-effort `SKILL.md`, validates, and writes output.
   102→
   103→### create-stack-skill (SS)
   104→
   105→**9 steps** | **Data:** integration-patterns.md, manifest-patterns.md, stack-skill-template.md
   106→
   107→Analyzes dependency manifests (package.json, requirements.txt, Cargo.toml, etc.) to detect libraries, ranks by import frequency, discovers co-import integration patterns between libraries, compiles a consolidated stack skill documenting how libraries connect, validates, and generates output.
   108→
   109→### update-skill (US)
   110→
   111→**7 steps** | **Data:** manual-section-rules.md, merge-conflict-rules.md
   112→
   113→Surgical update engine. Loads the existing skill, detects what changed in source since last compilation, re-extracts only affected exports with fresh provenance, merges new extractions while preserving all `[MANUAL]` developer-authored content, validates the merged result, writes the updated skill, and produces a change report.

   116→
   117→**6 steps** | **Data:** drift-report-template.md, severity-rules.md
   118→
   119→Drift detection engine. Loads the skill under audit, re-indexes current source to build a fresh reference, performs structural diff (signature changes, missing exports), performs semantic diff (behavioral divergence), classifies each finding by severity using defined rules, and produces a graded drift report.
   120→
   121→### test-skill (TS)
   122→
   123→**6 steps** | **Data:** output-section-formats.md, scoring-rules.md | **Templates:** test-report-template.md
   124→
   125→Quality gate before export. Loads the skill, detects test mode (naive for Quick tier, contextual for Forge/Deep), runs coverage checks against source, runs coherence checks for internal consistency, scores using weighted rubric, and produces a completeness report with pass/fail gate decision.
   126→
   127→### export-skill (EX)
   128→
   129→**6 steps** | **Data:** managed-section-format.md, snippet-format.md
   130→
   131→Distribution packaging. Loads the completed skill, packages as agentskills.io-compliant bundle, generates context snippets optimized for token efficiency, updates managed sections in `CLAUDE.md` / `AGENTS.md` with platform-aware injection, produces a token budget report, and summarizes the export.

1→# CLAUDE.md
     2→
     3→This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.
     4→
     5→## Project Overview
     6→
     7→Amytis is a static "digital garden" blog built with Next.js 15+ (App Router), React 19, and Tailwind CSS v4. Content is authored in MDX/Markdown files and statically generated at build time. Features include series support, multi-language (i18n), configurable themes, and comments integration.
     8→
     9→## Commands
    10→
    11→```bash
    12→# Development
    13→bun dev                    # Start dev server at localhost:3000
    14→bun run lint               # Run ESLint
    15→
    16→# Testing
    17→bun test                   # Run all tests
    18→bun run test:unit          # Run unit tests (src/)
    19→bun run test:int           # Run integration tests
    20→bun run test:e2e           # Run end-to-end tests
    21→bun test path/to/file.test.ts  # Run a single test file
    22→
    23→# Build
    24→bun run build              # Full production build (copies assets, builds Next.js, optimizes images)
    25→bun run build:dev          # Development build (no image optimization, faster) — also regenerates Pagefind search index in public/pagefind/
    26→bun run clean              # Remove .next, out, public/posts directories
    27→
    28→# Deploy
    29→bun run deploy             # Deploy out/ to Linux/nginx server via rsync+sshpass (reads .env.local)
    30→
    31→# Content creation
    32→bun run new "Post Title"              # Create new post
    33→bun run new-series "Series Name"      # Create new series
    34→bun run new-from-pdf doc.pdf          # Create post from PDF
    35→bun run new-from-images ./photos      # Create post from image folder
    36→bun run new-flow                      # Create today's flow note
    37→bun run new-flow-from-chat            # Import all new files from imports/chats/
    38→bun run sync-book                     # Sync chapters list for all books from disk
    39→bun run sync-book <slug>              # Sync chapters list for one book
    40→```
    41→
    42→## Architecture
    43→
    44→### Data Flow
    45→
    46→1. **Content source**: MDX/Markdown files in `content/posts/` and `content/series/`
    47→2. **Data layer**: `src/lib/markdown.ts` - reads files with Node `fs`, parses frontmatter with `gray-matter`, validates with Zod
    48→3. **Static generation**: Routes use `generateStaticParams` to pre-render at build time
    49→4. **Rendering**: `react-markdown` with remark/rehype plugins for GFM, math (KaTeX), syntax highlighting, and Mermaid diagrams
    50→
    51→### Key Files
    52→
    53→- `site.config.ts` - Site configuration (nav, social, pagination, themes, i18n, analytics, comments)
    54→- `src/lib/markdown.ts` - Data access layer with all content query functions
    55→- `src/lib/urls.ts` - Central URL helpers (`getPostUrl`, `getPostsBasePath`, `getSeriesCustomPaths`, etc.) — always use these instead of hardcoding `/posts/[slug]`
    56→- `src/lib/search-utils.ts` - Pure search utilities (URL type detection, date extraction, title cleaning, markdown stripping) shared by `Search` and the search index route
    57→- `src/app/globals.css` - Theme CSS variables and color palettes
    58→- `src/components/MarkdownRenderer.tsx` - MDX rendering with all plugins
    59→- `src/i18n/translations.ts` - Language strings for i18n
    60→
    61→### Route Structure
    62→
    63→- `/` - Homepage with hero, featured series, featured posts, latest writing
    64→- `/posts/[slug]` - Individual post pages
    65→- `/posts/page/[page]` - Paginated post listing
    66→- `/series` - All series overview
    67→- `/series/[slug]` - Single series with its posts
    68→- `/series/[slug]/page/[page]` - Series pagination
    69→- `/tags` - Tag cloud with post counts
    70→- `/tags/[tag]` - Posts filtered by tag
    71→- `/authors/[author]` - Posts filtered by author
    72→- `/archive` - Chronological listing grouped by year/month
    73→- `/books` - All books overview
    74→- `/books/[slug]` - Single book with chapter listing
    75→- `/books/[slug]/[chapter]` - Individual chapter page
    76→- `/flows` - Flow notes listing (paginated)
    77→- `/flows/page/[page]` - Paginated flow listing
    78→- `/flows/[year]` - Flows filtered by year
    79→- `/flows/[year]/[month]` - Flows filtered by month
    80→- `/flows/[year]/[month]/[day]` - Single flow detail page
    81→- `/[slug]` - Static pages (about, subscribe, etc.) and custom posts/series listing pages
    82→- `/[prefix]/[slug]` - Posts at custom URL prefixes (e.g. `/articles/my-post`, `/weeklies/my-post`)
    83→- `/[prefix]/page/[page]` - Paginated listing at custom URL prefixes
    84→
    85→### Content Structure
    86→
    87→**Posts** support two formats:
    88→- **Flat file**: `content/posts/my-post.mdx`
    89→- **Nested folder**: `content/posts/my-post/index.mdx` (allows co-located images in `./images/`)
    90→
    91→**Series** live in `content/series/[slug]/index.mdx` with optional `images/` folder for cover images.
    92→
    93→**Books** live in `content/books/[slug]/` with `index.mdx` for metadata and separate `.mdx` files per chapter. The `index.mdx` frontmatter defines chapter ordering with an optional parts structure.
    94→
    95→**Flows** (daily notes) live in `content/flows/YYYY/MM/DD.md` (or `.mdx`). Each flow has a date, title, excerpt, tags, and markdown content.
    96→
    97→Date-prefixed filenames (`2026-01-01-my-post.mdx`) extract dates automatically.
    98→
    99→## Configuration (`site.config.ts`)
   100→
   101→Key configuration options:
   102→- `nav` - Navigation links with weights
   103→- `social` - GitHub, Twitter, email links for footer
   104→- `series.navbar` - Series slugs to show in navbar dropdown
   105→- `series.customPaths` - Per-series custom URL prefix e.g. `{ 'weeklies': 'weeklies' }` → posts at `/weeklies/[slug]`
   106→- `pagination.posts`, `pagination.series` - Items per page
   107→- `themeColor` - 'default' | 'blue' | 'rose' | 'amber'
   108→- `hero` - Homepage hero title and subtitle
   109→- `i18n` - Default locale and supported locales
   110→- `featured.series` - Scrollable series: `scrollThreshold` (default: 2), `maxItems` (default: 6)
   111→- `featured.stories` - Scrollable stories: `scrollThreshold` (default: 1), `maxItems` (default: 5)
   112→- `analytics.provider` - 'umami' | 'plausible' | 'google' | null
   113→- `comments.provider` - 'giscus' | 'disqus' | null
   114→- `posts.basePath` - Custom URL prefix for all posts (default: `'posts'`); e.g. `'articles'` → posts at `/articles/[slug]`
   115→- `posts.authors.default` - Fallback authors when a post has none set in frontmatter
   116→- `posts.authors.showInHeader` - Show author byline below post title (default: true)
   117→- `posts.authors.showAuthorCard` - Show author card at end of post (default: true)
   118→- `posts.excludeFromListing` - Series slugs whose posts are hidden from `/posts` listing pages
   119→- `authors` - Per-author profiles: `bio`, `avatar` (image path), `social` (array of `{ image, description }`)
   120→
   121→## Content Frontmatter
   122→
   123→### Posts
   124→
   125→```yaml
   126→---
   127→title: "Post Title"
   128→date: "2026-01-01"
   129→excerpt: "Optional summary (auto-generated if omitted)"
   130→category: "Category Name"
   131→tags: ["tag1", "tag2"]
   132→authors: ["Author Name"]
   133→series: "series-slug"      # Link to a series
   134→draft: true                # Hidden in production
   135→featured: true             # Show in featured section
   136→pinned: true               # Always shown in featured section; never shuffled away (hero = most recent pinned)
   137→coverImage: "./images/cover.jpg"  # Local or external URL
   138→latex: true                # Enable KaTeX math
   139→toc: false                 # Hide table of contents
   140→layout: "simple"           # Use simple layout (default: "post")
   141→externalLinks:             # Links to external discussions
   142→  - name: "Hacker News"
   143→    url: "https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=12345"
   144→  - name: "V2EX"
   145→    url: "https://v2ex.com/t/123456"
   146→---
   147→```
   148→
   149→### Series (`content/series/[slug]/index.mdx`)
   150→
   151→```yaml
   152→---
   153→title: "Series Title"
   154→excerpt: "Series description"
   155→date: "2026-01-01"
   156→coverImage: "./images/cover.jpg"
   157→featured: true             # Show in featured series
   158→draft: true                # Hidden in production (default: false)
   159→sort: "date-asc"           # 'date-asc' | 'date-desc' | 'manual'
   160→posts: ["post-1", "post-2"] # Manual post ordering (optional)
   161→---
   162→```
   163→
   164→### Books (`content/books/[slug]/index.mdx`)
   165→
   166→```yaml
   167→---
   168→title: "Book Title"
   169→excerpt: "Book description"
   170→date: "2026-01-01"
   171→coverImage: "text:DG"           # Cover image or text placeholder
   172→featured: true                  # Show in featured books
   173→draft: false
   174→authors: ["Author Name"]
   175→chapters:
   176→  - part: "Part I: Getting Started"    # Optional part grouping
   177→    chapters:
   178→      - title: "Chapter Title"
   179→        id: "chapter-file"             # Maps to chapter-file.mdx or chapter-file/index.mdx
   180→  - part: "Part II: Advanced"
   181→    chapters:
   182→      - title: "Another Chapter"
   183→        id: "another-chapter"
   184→---
   185→```
   186→
   187→## Key Components
   188→
   189→- `PostLayout` / `SimpleLayout` - Post page layouts with TOC, series sidebar, external links, comments
   190→- `Hero` - Configurable homepage hero section with collapsible intro
   191→- `HorizontalScroll` - Scrollable container with navigation arrows for featured content
   192→- `PostList` - Card-based post listing with thumbnails, metadata, excerpts, and tags
   193→- `SeriesCatalog` - Timeline-style series post listing with numbered entries and progress indicator
   194→- `SeriesSidebar` - Series navigation sidebar with progress bar and color-coded states
   195→- `SeriesList` - Mobile-optimized series navigation matching sidebar design
   196→- `Search` - Full-text search (Cmd/Ctrl+K) powered by Pagefind (build-time index); features type filter tabs (All/Post/Flow/Book), recent searches, keyboard navigation (arrows + number keys), debounced input, body scroll lock, focus trap, ARIA accessibility, and search syntax tips (`"phrase"`, `-exclude`)
   197→- `TableOfContents` - Sticky TOC with scroll tracking, reading progress, and back-to-top
   198→- `MarkdownRenderer` - MDX rendering with GFM, math, syntax highlighting, diagrams
   199→- `CoverImage` - Optimized image component with WebP support
   200→- `Comments` - Giscus or Disqus integration (theme-aware)
   201→- `Analytics` - Umami, Plausible, or Google Analytics integration
   202→- `FlowContent` - Client wrapper for flow pages with tag filtering state management
   203→- `FlowCalendarSidebar` - Calendar sidebar with date navigation, browse panel, and clickable tag filters
   204→- `FlowTimelineEntry` - Individual flow entry in timeline list
   205→- `LanguageSwitch` - i18n language selector
   206→- `ThemeToggle` - Light/dark mode toggle
